metadata.title: EAU Guidelines on Non-Neurogenic Male Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms (LUTS)
metadata.summary: This guideline addresses the assessment, treatment and follow-up of adult men seeking care for non-neurogenic, non-malignant lower urinary tract symptoms. It covers symptoms associated with prostatic obstruction, bladder dysfunction, nocturia and urinary incontinence, including conservative, pharmacological and procedural approaches. Treatment selection is considered alongside symptom burden, clinical findings and patient preferences.

conditions_covered: Non-Neurogenic Male Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms (LUTS)
target_population: Adult men seeking professional help for non-neurogenic, non-malignant LUTS
therapeutic_areas: Bladder wall injection of botulinum Toxin-A

prevention: Inform older patients receiving non-selective α1-blockers about orthostatic hypotension.
Consider susceptibility to vasodilatation in patients with cardiovascular co-morbidity or vaso-active co-medication.

toxicities.incidence: In a retrospective cohort of men aged > 66 years receiving α1-blockers, the odds ratios were 1.14 for falls and 1.16 for fractures.
A population-based study reported HR: 1.22 with long-term α-blocker use; risk was higher with nonselective α-blockers.

prevention: Avoid initiating α1-blockers before scheduled cataract surgery.
Inform the ophthalmologist about α1-blocker exposure; the reported risk was particularly high with tamsulosin.

toxicities.incidence: A review reported abnormal ejaculation with α1-blockers at OR: 7.53. A meta-analysis reported EjD versus placebo at OR: 5.88; the corresponding OR values were 8.57 for tamsulosin, 32.5 for silodosin, 0.80 for doxazosin and 1.78 for terazosin.
recognition: Reduced or absent seminal fluid during ejaculation
prevention: Discuss EjD risk with sexually active patients receiving selective α1-blockers.

toxicities.incidence: Gynaecomastia develops in 1-2% of patients receiving 5-ARIs.
recognition: Retrograde ejaculation, ejaculation failure or reduced semen volume
Breast enlargement or breast or nipple tenderness
prevention: Discuss treatment-related adverse events when selecting pharmacological therapy.

toxicities.incidence: A Swedish cohort study reported HR 1.61 for finasteride and HR 1.68 for dutasteride.
A British-Taiwanese cohort found higher risk with 5-ARIs than with tamsulosin, without a difference between dutasteride and finasteride.
Two studies suggested a higher incidence of high-grade cancers during 5-ARI treatment, but a causal relationship has not been established.
prevention: Account for the effect of 5-ARIs on PSA when assessing for PCa; evaluate any confirmed PSA increase during treatment.

toxicities.incidence: Trials reported dry mouth in up to 16%, constipation in up to 4%, micturition difficulties in up to 2%, nasopharyngitis in up to 3% and dizziness in up to 5%; approximately 3-10% withdrew, a proportion similar to placebo.
prevention: Reassess symptom scores and PVR regularly.
toxicities.dose_modifications: Advise men to stop treatment if voiding LUTS or urinary stream worsen after initiation.

toxicities.event: Increased PVR and urinary retention during antimuscarinic treatment
toxicities.incidence: In men without BOO, PVR changes were +20.2 mL with fesoterodine 8 mg, +9.6 mL with fesoterodine 4 mg and -0.6 mL with placebo. Urinary retention with tolterodine was 0-1.3% versus 0-1.4% with placebo. Retention symptoms occurred in 5.3% with fesoterodine 8 mg versus 0.8% with fesoterodine 4 mg and 0.8% with placebo. In a twelve week study of men with mild-to-moderate BOO, PVR was 49 mL with tolterodine versus 16 mL with placebo, while AUR occurred in 3% in both arms.
recognition: Worsening voiding symptoms or urinary stream
Retention symptoms with fesoterodine 8 mg arose during the first two weeks, mainly in men aged 66 years or older.
prevention: Do not use antimuscarinic OAB medication when baseline PVR is > 150 mL.
Monitor PVR and symptoms during treatment.
toxicities.dose_modifications: Advise discontinuation if voiding LUTS or urinary stream deteriorate.

toxicities.event: Adverse effects of combined α1-blocker and antimuscarinic treatment
toxicities.incidence: AUR risk was described as low during treatment for up to one year in men with baseline PVR < 150 mL.
prevention: Measure PVR during combination treatment.
Do not prescribe this combination when PVR is > 150 mL.

toxicities.event: Hypertension and other adverse effects during mirabegron treatment
prevention: Measure blood pressure before treatment and monitor it regularly.
Do not use mirabegron in severe uncontrolled hypertension, defined as systolic blood pressure ≥ 180 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure ≥ 110 mmHg, or both.

toxicities.event: Adverse events and retention during combined mirabegron and solifenacin treatment
toxicities.incidence: In an eighteenweek study, adverse events occurred in 40% with solifenacin 5 mg plus mirabegron 25 mg versus 32% with mirabegron 25 mg alone. Events recorded as urinary retention were < 1% and slightly more frequent with combination treatment than with monotherapy or placebo.
recognition: Slight increase in PVR relative to the comparison groups

toxicities.event: Urinary retention during combined α1-blocker and mirabegron treatment
toxicities.incidence: The PLUS trial recorded six retention episodes (1.7%).

toxicities.event: Adverse effects and contraindications of tadalafil and PDE5Is
prevention: Do not use tadalafil with nitrates or guanylate cyclase stimulators such as riociguat, or in men whose cardiac disease makes sexual activity inadvisable.

Tadalafil is also contraindicated after myocardial infarction within the last 90 days; with unstable angina or angina during intercourse; with New York Heart Association Class 2 or greater heart failure in the last six months; with uncontrolled arrhythmias, hypotension (< 90/50 mm Hg) or uncontrolled hypertension; after stroke within the last six months; or with known anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy with sudden visual loss, including after previous PDE5Is use.

toxicities.event: Adverse events during combined α1-blocker and 5-ARI treatment
toxicities.incidence: A meta-analysis reported a three-fold higher EjD risk with α1-blocker and 5-ARI combination treatment than with either monotherapy.
recognition: Adverse effects characteristic of both drug classes
prevention: Inform patients about pharmacological treatment-related adverse events when choosing therapy.

toxicities.incidence: Systematic reviews reported mean incidence 3.8%.

In three titrated-dose studies including men, seventeen of 530 patients (3.2%) developed hyponatraemia. With desmopressin ODT 50 mcg, clinically significant hyponatraemia occurred in 11% of men aged ≥ 65 years versus 0% of men aged < 65 years. Severe hyponatraemia, defined as serum sodium ≤ 125 mmol/L, affected 22 of 1,431 (2%) patients overall in an analysis of ODT trials. In a case series of men aged more than 60 receiving 50 mcg ODT, 12/80 had non-severe hyponatraemia after one week; it persisted in 4/12 after reduction to 25 mcg. With desmopressin acetate nasal spray, reported risks were 1.2% at 1.5 mcg and 0.9% at 0.75 mcg.
recognition: Potentially life-threatening consequences, particularly in older patients
prevention: Check serum sodium at baseline, day three, day seven, one month after starting treatment and periodically thereafter; check more frequently in patients > 65 years or at increased risk.
Restart the monitoring sequence after dose escalation.
For men ≥ 65 years, do not use low-dose desmopressin if serum sodium is below normal.
Advise patients to avoid fluids for at least one hour before and eight hours after the dose.
Assess potentially non-urological causes before prescribing desmopressin and use caution in patients > 75 years, who were under-represented in trials.

toxicities.event: Other adverse effects of antidiuretic treatment
toxicities.incidence: Three titrated-dose studies including men reported seven serious adverse events among 530 patients (1.3%), including one death; hypertension occurred in seven (1.3%), headache in 53 (10%) and nausea in fifteen (2.8%).
prevention: Discuss the potential benefit and risks of desmopressin with patients, particularly men > 65 years.

toxicities.incidence: For M-TURP, TUR-syndrome risk was < 1.1%; bleeding requiring transfusion occurred in 2.9% of 10,654 procedures. An analysis of RCT comparator arms reported transfusion for 2% (0-9%) and TUR-syndrome for 0.8% (0-5%). A meta-analysis estimated twenty fewer TUR-syndrome events and 28 fewer transfusions per 1,000 participants with B-TURP than with M-TURP.
prevention: B-TURP uses saline irrigation and local bipolar circuitry, eliminating TUR-syndrome.
The panel suggests an 80 mL upper limit for M-TURP and notes that the procedure is safest when completed in under 90 minutes.

toxicities.incidence: An RCT comparator analysis reported AUR in 4.5% (0-13.3%), clot retention in 4.9% (0-39%) and UTI in 4.1% (0-22%).

Estimated transfusion rate was about 7-14%; transient UI occurred in up to 10%, and BNC and urethral stricture in about 6%. A study of 1,286 men reported mortality of 0.2% at 30 days and 0.4% at 90 days.
A study reported adverse events in 31% of cases, including 6.6% with complications greater than Clavien grade 2.

toxicities.event: Bleeding and sexual adverse effects after Aquablation
toxicities.incidence: In WATER, one patient required transfusion after Aquablation versus none after TURP; persistent adverse events of Clavien-Dindo grade 1 or 2 or higher occurred in 26% versus 42% at three months. Anejaculation among sexually active men occurred in 10% after Aquablation versus 36% after TURP. In WATER II, bleeding-related events affected fourteen patients (13.9%): eight (7.9%) before discharge and six (5.9%) within one month after discharge. Eight required transfusion, three returned for fulguration, and two required both. WATER II reported 2% de novo incontinence at twelve months.

management.actions: The WATER II study reported transfusion, return to theatre for fulguration, or both.

prevention: Inform patients about bleeding risk and the lack of long-term follow-up data.

toxicities.event: Adverse events after prostatic artery embolisation
toxicities.incidence: One review reported adverse events in 41.6% after PAE versus 30.4% after TURP/OP, and post-procedural AUR in 9.4% versus 2.0%; other reviews reported conflicting comparative findings. A review of radiation exposure estimated a median cancer-related death risk of 0.117% for a 66-year-old patient, equivalent to 5.4 days of reduced life expectancy.
prevention: Include radiation exposure in counselling before PAE.
Perform PAE in units where urologists collaborate with interventional radiologists who have specific mentored training and expertise.

toxicities.event: Post-operative symptoms and retreatment after prostatic urethral lift
toxicities.incidence: Reported post-operative ranges were haematuria 16-63%, dysuria 25-58%, pelvic pain 5-17.9%, urgency 7.1-10%, transient incontinence 3.6-16% and UTI 2.9-11%. A review estimated surgical re-intervention at 6% per year (95% CI: 3.0-8.9); a multicentre study reported retreatment in 13.6% over five years.
prevention: Discuss uncertainty about long-term effects, including retreatment.

toxicities.incidence: A narrative review reported post-procedural retention in 3-17% and UTI in 6-7%.

toxicities.event: Complications and failure of male slings
toxicities.incidence: With non-adjustable slings, chronic pain was reported in 1.3%, transient voiding dysfunction in 4.3-10.3%, and erosion and chronic pain were uncommon at 0-0.4% in reported series. With adjustable slings, chronic pain was reported in 1.5%, re-adjustment in 8-38.6%, explantation in 10-15.8% and erosion around 10%; reported reasons for explantation included infection (4.1-8%), erosion (4-12%) and urethral perforation (2.7-16%).
prevention: Inform candidates for non-adjustable slings that severe incontinence, previous pelvic radiotherapy or transurethral surgery may worsen outcomes.

toxicities.incidence: Reported AUS complications included infection/erosion in 8.5%, mechanical failure in 6.2% and urethral atrophy in 7.9%; revision for any reason at three years was 10-29.1%. For ZSI 375, urethral erosion risk was 8.2-13.3% and mechanical failure risk 2.2-2.5%. In a retrospective study of 168 AMS 800 recipients, 63 (37.5%) required explantation or revision for failure at a median follow-up of 2.7 year.
recognition: Difficulty operating the pump if cognition or manual dexterity declines
prevention: Offer implantation in expert centres.
Warn patients about complications, mechanical failure and possible explantation.
Before implantation, establish that the patient can operate the pump; previous pelvic radiotherapy may adversely affect outcomes.

toxicities.incidence: A meta-analysis estimated bladder or urethral perforation at 5.3% and overall revision at 22.2%, including erosion at 3.8%, device leaking at 4.1% and migration at 6.5%. Prospective series reported explantation in 11-58%.
prevention: Offer implantation only in expert centres and warn about complications, mechanical failure and explantation.
Do not offer ProACT© to men with prior pelvic radiotherapy.

toxicities.event: Adverse effects of bladder wall onabotulinumtoxinA injections
toxicities.incidence: A retrospective cohort reported CISC after treatment in 28.6% of men without prior prostate surgery, 7.5% after TURP and 4.2% after radical prostatectomy.

management.actions: Clean intermittent self-catheterisation may be needed for a prolonged period.

prevention: Before injection, warn patients about UTI, the limited duration of response and possible prolonged CISC; ensure that they are willing and able to perform it.

toxicities.incidence: Reported rates were implant-site pain 13-42%, lead migration 4.0-21%, leg or back pain 3.0-18%, wound infection 5.7-6.7% and surgical revision 29-33%.

management.actions: Surgical revision may be required for malfunction, battery or device replacement, or lead migration.

toxicities.event: Complications of augmentation cystoplasty and urinary diversion
recognition: Early infection, bowel obstruction, bleeding or cardiorespiratory complications
Later metabolic disturbance, altered bowel habits, excess mucus, stones, bladder perforation or, rarely, bladder cancer
Hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis if ileum is used

management.actions: Most patients require self-catheterisation for bladder emptying after augmentation cystoplasty or diversion; patients with a urinary conduit require lifelong urine bags.

prevention: Before augmentation cystoplasty, explain the substantial complication risk, possible need for CISC and lifelong surveillance.
Counsel patients before urinary diversion about the stoma and long-term requirements.

toxicities.event: Adverse effects leading to duloxetine discontinuation
toxicities.incidence: A review reported discontinuation in 38% of cases; fatigue, somnolence and nausea were reported in 18% of patients.
prevention: Inform patients about potential adverse events and the off-label status of duloxetine for this indication in Europe.

recognition: Mild pain or discomfort at the puncture site
prevention: Avoid PTNS in patients with a cardiac pacemaker or skin disease at the stimulation site.

toxicities.event: Complications of long-term indwelling urinary catheters
prevention: Avoid long-term indwelling catheterisation unless other drainage options are unsuitable or have failed.
If an indwelling catheter is needed, prefer a suprapubic rather than urethral route because of traumatic hypospadias risk.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Measure serum sodium before desmopressin, on day three and day seven, one month after initiation and periodically thereafter. Increase testing frequency in patients > 65 years or at higher risk, and restart the sequence after a dose increase.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients receiving desmopressin, especially older or higher-risk patients

prophylaxis.recommendation: Avoid drinking fluids around the time desmopressin is taken.
prophylaxis.duration: At least one hour before and eight hours after each dose

prophylaxis.recommendation: Do not initiate α1-blockers before scheduled cataract surgery, and make the ophthalmologist aware of α1-blocker use.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients scheduled for cataract surgery who use or may start α1-blockers

prophylaxis.recommendation: Reassess symptoms and PVR regularly during antimuscarinic therapy; measure PVR during treatment combining an α1-blocker with an antimuscarinic.
prophylaxis.target_population: Men receiving antimuscarinic treatment, alone or with an α1-blocker

prophylaxis.recommendation: Measure blood pressure before mirabegron and monitor it regularly thereafter.
Establish a new PSA baseline at six months, use serial PSA testing when PCa diagnosis could alter management, and evaluate confirmed PSA rises during 5-ARI treatment.
prophylaxis.target_population: Men receiving 5-ARIs whose life expectancy is greater than ten years and for whom a PCa diagnosis could change management

prophylaxis.recommendation: Initiate clean intermittent self-catheterisation when upper-tract injury is a risk or PVR is > 300mL; prefer it to an indwelling catheter for persistent incomplete emptying.
prophylaxis.target_population: Men with UAB and risk of upper-tract damage or PVR > 300mL

infection_management.prevention: In men with UAB and persistently elevated PVR, clean intermittent self-catheterisation is preferred to indwelling catheterisation because it may reduce complications including UTI. Incomplete emptying with PVR above 300mls is associated with increased UTI risk.
infection_management.management: Urinalysis may identify UTI during assessment of LUTS or UI; abnormal findings warrant further evaluation according to the applicable EAU Guidelines. Recurrent UTIs are listed among the usual absolute indications for surgery in LUTS/BPO.

conditions.name: Non-Neurogenic Male Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms (LUTS)
conditions.description: A multifactorial group of urinary symptoms in men that may arise from prostatic obstruction, bladder dysfunction, nocturnal urine production or other conditions. Symptoms alone do not establish their underlying cause.
conditions.epidemiology: LUTS are common in adult men, become more prevalent with ageing, impair quality of life and create a substantial economic burden. Most elderly men have at least one symptom, although symptoms are often mild or minimally bothersome. Symptoms may persist, worsen or remit. Moderate-to-severe LUTS may be associated with increased risk of major adverse cardiac events.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Symptoms are categorised as storage, voiding or post-micturition symptoms. More than one contributing factor commonly occurs in the same man.

subtypes.name: storage symptoms
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May include frequency, urgency and nocturia.

subtypes.name: voiding symptoms
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May reflect obstruction or impaired detrusor function; symptoms do not reliably distinguish these mechanisms.

subtypes.name: post-micturition symptoms
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Includes post-micturition dribble.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify possible causes, co-morbidities, medications, lifestyle factors and psychological or emotional factors.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Consider neurological disease and prior lower urinary tract disease or surgery when deciding whether broader assessment is needed.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Quantify symptoms, bother and quality of life and monitor change.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial assessment and reassessment during or after treatment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Questionnaires identify predominant symptoms but do not independently diagnose their cause.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess urinary symptoms and quality of life.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Its categories are ‘asymptomatic’ (0 points), ‘mildly symptomatic’ (1-7 points), ‘moderately symptomatic’ (8-19 points) and ‘severely symptomatic’ (20-35 points). It does not assess incontinence, post-micturition symptoms or bother from each individual symptom.

diagnostic_workup.test: The International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire for Male LUTS (ICIQ-MLUTS)
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess male LUTS, including incontinence and bother associated with individual symptoms.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Includes subscales for nocturia and OAB.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess LUTS, incontinence and bother associated with individual symptoms.

diagnostic_workup.test: The Symptoms of Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction Research Network (LURN-SI-10)
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify symptoms including incontinence and bladder pain.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Correlates strongly with IPSS while identifying additional symptoms.

diagnostic_workup.test: Frequency volume charts and/or bladder diaries
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Document voiding times and volumes; a diary can additionally record intake, pad use, activities and symptom characteristics.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Particularly useful with storage symptoms or nocturia; a bladder diary should cover at least three days.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Can establish daytime and night-time frequency, total and individual voided volumes, and the nocturnal polyuria index.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify associated sexual symptoms.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Clinical assessment, preferably using a validated questionnaire such as the International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF).

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Examine the suprapubic region, external genitalia, perineum and lower limbs, and assess prostate size and texture.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Exclude urethral discharge, meatal stenosis, phimosis and penile cancer. Digital-rectal estimation of prostate volume correlates poorly with actual volume.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify findings suggesting infection, haematuria, proteinuria or glycosuria.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Primary assessment; abnormal findings warrant assessment under relevant guidance.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Inform management when a prostate cancer diagnosis would alter care or when PSA assists treatment selection.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After discussion of the implications of testing and an elevated result.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: PSA also predicts prostate volume, prostate growth and some BPO-related outcomes.

diagnostic_workup.test: Serum creatinine or estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess renal function.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suspected renal impairment, hydronephrosis or consideration of surgery.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess bladder emptying.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An elevated value may reflect obstruction, impaired detrusor function or both; no PVR threshold for treatment decisions has been established.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure Qmax, voided volume and flow pattern and provide an objective measure for monitoring.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial assessment and before medical or invasive treatment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Preferably assess a voided volume > 150 mL. Repeat testing is useful when volume is < 150 mL or Qmax or flow pattern is abnormal. A low Qmax cannot distinguish BOO from DU or an under-filled bladder.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate the upper tract and potentially assess bladder, PVR and prostate.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be used in men with LUTS, particularly with large PVR, haematuria or previous urolithiasis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess size and shape to inform treatment choice.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When considering surgery, or medical treatment if imaging would help select a drug.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Transrectal ultrasound (TRUS) measures prostate volume more accurately than digital-rectal examination or transabdominal ultrasound; a middle lobe may affect eligibility for some minimally invasive procedures.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess urethral or bladder pathology and anatomy relevant to an intervention.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: History of microscopic or gross haematuria, urethral stricture or bladder cancer; before minimally invasive or surgical treatment if findings could change its selection.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Cystoscopic appearances do not reliably establish urodynamic obstruction.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Clarify functional mechanisms and support decisions about invasive treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected patients with specific indications rather than routine use, including unsuccessful prior invasive treatment, inability to void > 150 mL, bothersome predominantly voiding symptoms with Qmax > 10 mL/s or PVR > 300 mL, and selected men aged > 80 years or < 50 years considering invasive treatment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Pressure-flow studies distinguish obstruction from impaired detrusor contraction.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate suspected vesico-ureteral reflux, bladder diverticula or urethral disease.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Can be combined with urodynamics as video-urodynamics.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide a visual symptom assessment option.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be useful in men with limited literacy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Has shown a positive correlation with IPSS.

follow_up.schedule: For watchful waiting, review at six months and then annually if symptoms do not deteriorate and no absolute surgical indication develops. For most specified drug regimens, assess response four to six weeks after initiation, then at six months and annually under the same conditions. After prostate surgery, review four to six weeks after catheter removal; further assessment is unnecessary if symptoms improve without adverse events.
recommended_tests: During watchful waiting: history, bladder diary, IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry and PVR.
During medical treatment: history, IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry and PVR; use a frequency volume chart or bladder diary for predominant storage symptoms or nocturnal polyuria.
After prostate surgery: IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry, erectile and ejaculatory function assessment, and PVR.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Follow-up schedules are based on empirical or theoretical considerations rather than evidence-based follow-up studies.

conditions.name: Benign prostatic obstruction
conditions.description: A form of bladder outlet obstruction in which benign prostatic enlargement is known to cause the outflow obstruction. It is distinct from BPH, which denotes a histological pattern.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Can contribute to male LUTS and may occur alongside bladder dysfunction. Signs or symptoms of BPO are associated with more frequent hydronephrosis, renal insufficiency or urinary retention, although the mechanism linking BPO to these complications is not conclusively established.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish whether outflow obstruction is present and distinguish it from DU.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected patients when clarification of the underlying mechanism is needed.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Obstruction features increased detrusor pressure with reduced urinary flow during voiding.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help estimate prostate volume and risk of progression when relevant to management.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When its result assists treatment decisions or a prostate cancer diagnosis would alter management.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: In a community-based study, 1.5 ng/mL best predicted prostate volume > 30 mL, with PPV 78%. Baseline PSA predicted AUR and BPO-related surgery in cited studies; the reported PPV for detecting BPO was 68%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure volume and assess a middle lobe before selecting an intervention.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When considering surgery, and when size would affect medical treatment selection.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: TRUS is more accurate for volume assessment than transabdominal ultrasound.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate emptying and monitor change.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: PVR alone does not establish BPO. At a threshold of 50 mL, its PPV for BOO was 63% and NPV was 52%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate urinary flow and monitor treatment response.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Reduced Qmax does not by itself distinguish obstruction from DU.

diagnostic_workup.test: Ultrasound measurement of intravesical prostatic protrusion (IPP)
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess a possible non-invasive indicator of obstruction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Its role as an alternative to pressure-flow studies remains under evaluation.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: With bladder volume 150-250 mL, grade I is 0-4.9 mm, grade II is 5-10 mm and grade III is > 10 mm. A cited review reported sensitivity 0.71 and specificity 0.77 for urodynamic BOO at cut-off > 10mm.

follow_up.schedule: Follow the schedule appropriate to watchful waiting, the selected medication or prostate surgery.

conditions.name: Bladder outlet obstruction
conditions.description: Obstruction during voiding, characterised by higher detrusor pressure and lower urinary flow. BPO is one possible form.
conditions.clinical_presentation: May cause LUTS, but symptoms and reduced flow alone cannot reliably distinguish it from DU.

subtypes.name: Benign prostatic obstruction
subtypes.distinguishing_features: BOO attributable to benign prostatic enlargement.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Diagnose and grade obstruction and differentiate it from DU.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected patients when invasive investigation is justified.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The stated obstruction calculation is pdetQmax - 2Qmax: BOO > 40 = obstructed; BOO 20-40 = equivocal; BOO < 20 = unobstructed.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide a non-invasive assessment of flow.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial assessment and before medical or invasive treatment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: At Qmax 10 mL/s, reported specificity was 70%, PPV 70% and sensitivity 47% for BOO; at Qmax 15 mL/s, specificity was 38%, PPV 67% and sensitivity 82%. Qmax > 15 mL/s does not exclude BOO.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess incomplete emptying.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An elevated PVR may result from BOO, DU or both and cannot establish obstruction by itself.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate potential indicators of obstruction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Not as substitutes for urodynamics/pressure-flow studies when diagnosing obstruction.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The reported accuracy of IPP, bladder or detrusor wall thickness, ultrasound-estimated bladder weight, penile cuff testing and other non-invasive methods varies substantially across studies.

definitions.description: Obstruction is present according to pdetQmax - 2Qmax.
The obstruction result is equivocal according to pdetQmax - 2Qmax.
The result is unobstructed according to pdetQmax - 2Qmax.

conditions.name: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
conditions.description: The term is reserved for the characteristic histological disease pattern; it does not itself establish that a man's LUTS are caused by prostatic obstruction.

genetic_molecular.clinical_significance: The guideline describes potential use as a biomarker and novel target for early BPH diagnosis and therapy; this is not presented as an established diagnostic test.

conditions.name: Benign prostatic enlargement
conditions.description: Prostatic enlargement that may cause BPO when it produces bladder outlet obstruction.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure prostate volume to inform treatment selection.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When considering surgical treatment or treatment for which prostate size matters.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: More accurate for prostate volume than digital-rectal examination or transabdominal ultrasound.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess prostate size and shape.
Estimate prostate size and assess texture.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Tends to underestimate volume, particularly when TRUS volume is > 30 mL.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help predict prostate volume and growth.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A pooled analysis reported AUC 0.76-0.78 across prostate-volume thresholds of 30 mL, 40 mL and 50 mL. For glands exceeding 40 mL, approximate criteria were PSA > 1.6 ng/mL, > 2.0 ng/mL and > 2.3 ng/mL in men with BPH in their 50s, 60s and 70s, respectively, at specificity 70% and sensitivity 65-70%.

conditions.name: Acute retention of urine
conditions.description: An inability to pass any urine accompanied by a painful bladder that can be palpated or detected by percussion.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Painful urinary retention with a palpable or percussible bladder.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify inability to void and assess for a painful, palpable or percussible bladder.

conditions.name: Chronic retention of urine
conditions.description: Persistent, painless bladder distension that remains palpable or percussible after voiding.
conditions.clinical_presentation: A palpable or percussible bladder after passing urine; incontinence can also occur.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify persistent, painless bladder distension after voiding.
Quantify urine remaining after voiding.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Elevated PVR alone does not distinguish obstruction from impaired detrusor function.

conditions.name: Detrusor overactivity
conditions.description: An urodynamic finding of involuntary detrusor contractions during bladder filling, arising spontaneously or after provocation.
conditions.epidemiology: In a cited study of men whose LUTS were attributed to BPO, DO occurred in 61% and was independently associated with obstruction grade and ageing.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Commonly accompanies OAB symptoms, but its identification requires urodynamic assessment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify involuntary detrusor contractions during filling.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Observed contractions may be spontaneous or provoked.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate accompanying BOO or impaired detrusor function.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When the underlying mechanisms of LUTS require clarification.

conditions.name: Overactive bladder
conditions.description: A syndrome centred on urinary urgency, with or without urgency urinary incontinence, usually accompanied by increased daytime frequency and nocturia when no proven infection or other evident pathology explains the symptoms.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Urgency, potentially with urgency urinary incontinence, increased daytime frequency and nocturia.

diagnostic_workup.test: Medical history and symptom score questionnaire
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterise urgency, storage symptoms, bother and treatment response.
Record storage symptoms, voiding frequency and nocturia.
Identify findings suggesting infection or other conditions requiring assessment.
Assess emptying when considering or monitoring storage-symptom medication.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Baseline assessment and reassessment with muscarinic receptor antagonists.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline advises against antimuscarinic OAB medication when PVR is > 150 mL.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Clarify DO and coexisting voiding abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected patients when the underlying mechanism needs clarification or invasive treatment is considered.

follow_up.schedule: For applicable drug treatment, assess response four to six weeks after initiation, then at six months and annually if symptoms remain stable and no absolute surgical indication develops.
recommended_tests: Bladder diary for predominant storage symptoms

conditions.name: Detrusor underactivity
conditions.description: A urodynamic condition in which reduced strength and/or duration of contraction causes prolonged emptying and/or failure to empty the bladder completely within a normal period. It differs from the symptom-based term UAB.
conditions.epidemiology: Its prevalence in the general population is unknown. Clinical studies in men with non-neurogenic LUTS referred for video-urodynamics reported 10%, rising up to 48% among elderly men aged ≥ 70 years. Its untreated course was described as relatively stable in available observations.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Can occur without symptoms or present with non-specific voiding symptoms resembling those of BPO; incomplete emptying and storage symptoms may coexist.

subtypes.name: Neurogenic
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May follow peripheral or central nervous system disease; addressed in separate neuro-urological guidance.

subtypes.name: Myogenic
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May involve detrusor muscle or extracellular-matrix changes; BOO and diabetic cystopathy are discussed as possible causes.

subtypes.name: Iatrogenic
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May occur following pelvic surgery, radiation therapy or medication affecting detrusor contractility.

subtypes.name: Idiopathic
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Ageing has been proposed as a contributor, but the cited evidence does not strongly establish declining detrusor contractility with usual ageing.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess symptoms, co-morbidities, medications and possible causes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Assessment of suspected DU or UAB.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: No single symptom identifies UAB or reliably separates DU from BOO.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess flow and voiding pattern.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Proposed models for distinguishing UAB from BOO lack established diagnostic accuracy and external validation.

diagnostic_workup.test: Ultrasound scan and post-void residual measurement
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess bladder characteristics and incomplete emptying.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A study of 143 adult males associated detrusor wall thickness ≤ 1.23 mm and bladder capacity > 445 mL with urodynamically proven DU; sensitivity was 42% and specificity 100%. No agreed PVR cut-off diagnoses DU.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish DU and investigate accompanying obstruction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When a urodynamic diagnosis is needed.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: It is the only widely accepted diagnostic method for DU, although no consensus urodynamic definition or optimal quantification method has been established.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Quantify detrusor contractility from pressure-flow measurements.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: BCI=pdetQmax + 5Qmax; BCI>150 denotes strong, 100-150 normal and <100 weak contractility. The proposed diagnostic models are not validated for DU.

prognostic_tools.name: Bladder contractility index (BCI)
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Calculated as BCI=pdetQmax + 5Qmax; it is widely used, but the guideline states that proposed DU diagnostic models lack validation.

prognostic_tools.name: Griffiths’ Watt factor
components: Bladder volume at each point of micturition
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Expresses detrusor power as W/m2. The appropriate calculation and threshold remain disputed; expert opinion has suggested Wmax 7.0 W/m2.

prognostic_tools.name: Schafer’s detrusor-adjusted mean PURR factor (DAMPF)

risk_groups.criteria: Classification according to the length of linPURR on the Schafer nomogram.
Classification according to the length of linPURR on the Schafer nomogram.
Classification according to the length of linPURR on the Schafer nomogram.
Classification according to the length of linPURR on the Schafer nomogram.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: Proposed to quantify detrusor strength; it has not been validated as a DU diagnostic model.

follow_up.schedule: The interval between visits depends on patient characteristics, treatment and frequency of urinary complications; a fixed long-term schedule is not specified.
long_term_effects: Available retrospective observations suggest detrusor contractility may remain impaired without necessarily worsening over time; TURP has not been shown to restore contractility.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: The long-term natural history of men with UAB is insufficiently documented.

conditions.name: underactive bladder
conditions.description: A clinical symptom complex suggestive of DU, generally involving prolonged urination, with or without a sensation of incomplete emptying.
conditions.clinical_presentation: May range from no symptoms to symptomatic chronic retention. Hesitancy, reduced filling sensation and slow or interrupted stream may occur; voiding symptoms predominate, although storage symptoms can coexist.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify symptoms, medications, co-morbidities and potential causes.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: No pivotal symptom or validated clinical model reliably separates UAB from BOO.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Describe symptom burden.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: There is no UAB-specific validated questionnaire, and benefit for monitoring UAB treatment is uncertain.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess Qmax and flow pattern.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Its proposed diagnostic models require external validation.

diagnostic_workup.test: Ultrasound scan and post-void residual measurement
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess bladder characteristics and emptying.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Elevated PVR may accompany DU, but no diagnostic PVR cut-off has been agreed.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine whether DU is present and distinguish it from obstruction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When confirmation of the underlying urodynamic mechanism is required.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: UAB remains a clinical diagnosis; DU denotes the urodynamic finding.

follow_up.schedule: Individualise visit intervals according to patient characteristics, treatment and urinary complications.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Long-term clinical evolution is not well documented.

conditions.name: Nocturia
conditions.description: Waking during the main sleep period to pass urine. Potential causes include urinary tract dysfunction, excessive urine production, behavioural factors, systemic disease and sleep disturbance, often in combination.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Night-time waking to void, which may or may not be bothersome. It should be regarded as LUTS only when lower urinary tract dysfunction contributes.

subtypes.name: 24-hour polyuria
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Urine output > 40 mL/kg over a 24-hour period.

subtypes.name: nocturnal polyuria
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Excess urine production during the main sleep period; the stated thresholds are nocturnal output exceeding 20% of 24-hour urine output in the young or 33% in people > 65.

subtypes.name: sleep disorders
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Sleep disturbance may lead to awareness of bladder filling rather than waking primarily because of lower urinary tract dysfunction.

subtypes.name: mixed aetiology
subtypes.distinguishing_features: More than one nocturia mechanism is present.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess urinary, behavioural, systemic and sleep-related causes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: All presentations, including non-bothersome nocturia when history or examination suggests underlying disease.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Consider renal failure, diabetes mellitus, cardiac failure, obstructive sleep apnoea and relevant medication.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify severity and bother of individual LUTS.

diagnostic_workup.test: Validated bladder diary or frequency volume chart
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterise night-time voids, urine production and possible mechanisms.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: A validated bladder diary is mandatory in the described diagnostic assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Helps distinguish polyuria, nocturnal polyuria and other contributing mechanisms.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess potential urinary or systemic contributors.
Identify incomplete emptying as a possible contributor.
Inform management if prostate cancer diagnosis would alter care.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After discussion with the patient when indicated.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate associated LUTS or suspected prostatic contribution.

diagnostic_workup.test: Renal function assessment and kidney ultrasound
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate possible renal or upper-tract abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: According to clinical findings, including significant PVR.

follow_up.schedule: For men receiving desmopressin, measure serum sodium at day three and seven, one month after starting treatment and periodically thereafter. If values remain normal, subsequent screening can occur every three months. Restart this sequence after dose escalation; monitor more frequently in patients ≥ 65 years of age or at increased risk of hyponatremia.
recommended_tests: Serum sodium concentration during desmopressin treatment
long_term_effects: Hyponatraemia is a particularly important risk of antidiuretic therapy, especially in older patients.

conditions.name: nocturnal polyuria
conditions.description: Excessive urine production during an individual's main sleep period.
conditions.clinical_presentation: May contribute to nocturia, including in patients with additional urinary, systemic or sleep-related causes.

diagnostic_workup.test: Validated bladder diary or frequency volume chart
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Compare urine output during sleep with total 24-hour output and identify coexisting causes of nocturia.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Defined by nocturnal output exceeding 20% of 24-hour urine output in the young or 33% of urine output in people > 65.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate potential systemic disease, sleep disorders, fluid habits and medication effects.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before attributing nocturia to lower urinary tract dysfunction or considering antidiuretic therapy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess and monitor hyponatraemia risk with desmopressin.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At baseline, after starting treatment or changing dose, and during treatment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Low-dose desmopressin should not be used in men ≥ 65 years if serum sodium is below normal.

follow_up.schedule: During desmopressin therapy, check sodium at day three and day seven, at one month and periodically afterward; screening can subsequently occur every three months if sodium remains normal. Resume the initial monitoring sequence after a dose increase.
long_term_effects: Monitor for hyponatraemia, particularly in patients ≥ 65 years of age and those at increased risk.

conditions.name: male urinary incontinence
conditions.description: Unintentional urine loss in men. The guideline addresses stress, urgency and mixed urinary incontinence; other specified forms fall outside its current management scope.
conditions.epidemiology: Reported prevalence ranges from 11% in men aged 60 to 64 years old to 31% in men ≥ 85 years; it affects up to 32% of men with LUTS.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The timing and circumstances of leakage help distinguish stress-related, urgency-related and mixed symptoms.

subtypes.name: Stress UI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Leakage during effort, movement or increased abdominal pressure.

subtypes.name: Urgency UI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Leakage occurring with or immediately after urgency.

subtypes.name: Mixed UI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Stress-related and urgency-related leakage occur together.

subtypes.name: Overflow UI
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Identified as a separate form outside the current management scope.

subtypes.name: post-micturition dribble
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Identified as a separate form outside the current management scope.

subtypes.name: nocturnal enuresis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Identified as a separate form outside the current management scope.

subtypes.name: total incontinence
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Identified as a separate form outside the current management scope.

diagnostic_workup.test: Medical history and focused physical examination
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Categorise UI, assess co-morbidities and medications, and identify patients needing specialist referral.
Quantify incontinence severity.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Assessment of UI; ICIQ-UI-SF is given as an example.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Document leakage episodes, voiding frequency and urine volumes.
Quantify leakage severity and monitor response.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Its usefulness for distinguishing UI types or predicting treatment outcomes is uncertain.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess emptying and help distinguish overflow incontinence from other UI types.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The broader clinical significance of PVR in non-neurogenic male UI is uncertain.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Objectively characterise UI and detect additional storage or voiding dysfunction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider in selected patients, particularly before invasive treatment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Evidence that it changes management or predicts outcomes in uncomplicated male UI remains limited.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess selected patients for urethral or bladder-neck strictures and bladder pathology.
Investigate anatomical or functional abnormalities relevant to UI.
Identify findings suggesting infection, proteinuria, haematuria or glycosuria.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Abnormal results may require further investigation.

recommended_tests: Pad test when quantifying response is useful

conditions.name: stress urinary incontinence
conditions.description: Urine loss associated with movement, physical effort or increased abdominal pressure; the overview attributes it to sphincter deficiency.
conditions.epidemiology: The guideline's male UI overview reports prevalence < 10%. It lists surgery for BPO, pelvic or urethral surgery, radical prostatectomy and neurogenic conditions among associated factors.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Leakage during activity, exercise, coughing or sneezing, usually without leakage during sleep or nocturnal enuresis.

subtypes.name: post-prostatectomy incontinence
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Incontinence following prostatectomy; sphincter deficiency is frequently implicated, although accompanying detrusor dysfunction may occur.

diagnostic_workup.test: Medical history and focused physical examination
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish the circumstances of leakage and relevant surgical or radiotherapy history.
Observe whether leakage coincides with coughing.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Leakage may be seen during coughing.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Document activity-related leakage and quantify severity.
Characterise sphincter and coexisting bladder dysfunction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider particularly when invasive treatment is planned.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Following radical prostatectomy or BPO surgery, sphincter weakness is common but need not be the only finding.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess emptying and help distinguish other types of UI.

recommended_tests: Pad test when quantifying treatment response is useful
long_term_effects: Prior pelvic radiotherapy and severe baseline incontinence may adversely affect outcomes with non-adjustable male slings.
Artificial urinary sphincter devices may require later revision or replacement.

conditions.name: urgency urinary incontinence
conditions.description: Urine loss occurring at the same time as, or immediately after, an episode of urgency.
conditions.epidemiology: The guideline's overview reports prevalence 40-80% among male UI types.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Leakage with urgency, commonly accompanied by increased frequency and nocturia. The overview lists DO, urothelial stimulation and increased afferent signalling among possible mechanisms.

diagnostic_workup.test: Medical history and validated symptom score questionnaire
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterise urgency-related leakage and its severity.
Document urgency, frequency, nocturia and incontinence episodes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Assessment of storage symptoms and UI.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Quantify leakage and monitor response.
Identify findings suggesting infection or another condition requiring assessment.
Assess emptying and inform treatment selection.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: UI evaluation and when relevant to medication or invasive treatment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify DO and additional storage or voiding abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected patients, particularly when invasive treatment is considered.

long_term_effects: After bladder-wall onabotulinumtoxinA injection, monitor for urinary tract infection and retention that may require clean intermittent self-catheterisation.

conditions.name: mixed urinary incontinence
conditions.description: Urinary incontinence combining stress-related and urgency-related leakage.
conditions.epidemiology: The guideline's overview reports prevalence 10-30% among male UI types.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Leakage occurs both with effort and in association with urgency; a cough stress test may show leakage.

diagnostic_workup.test: Medical history and focused physical examination
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify both stress and urgency components.
Assess symptom severity.
Document patterns and quantify leakage.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Diary findings can vary.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess effort-related leakage.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Leakage may accompany coughing.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess bladder emptying.
Clarify the mechanisms and any additional dysfunction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected patients, especially when invasive treatment is considered.

conditions.name: post-prostatectomy incontinence
conditions.description: Urinary incontinence following prostatectomy; the guideline discusses both conservative care and procedures for persistent post-prostatectomy leakage.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Post-surgical leakage may involve sphincter weakness, sometimes alongside DO or reduced bladder compliance.

diagnostic_workup.test: Medical history and focused physical examination
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterise leakage, prior surgery and associated symptoms.

diagnostic_workup.test: Validated symptom score questionnaire and bladder diary
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Quantify symptoms and document leakage patterns.
Quantify leakage and monitor continence recovery.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Early postoperative pad testing may predict later continence after radical prostatectomy, although the broader predictive value of pad tests remains uncertain.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess emptying and other possible mechanisms of leakage.
Assess sphincter deficiency and possible accompanying detrusor abnormalities.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected patients, particularly before invasive treatment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A cited review found intrinsic urethral sphincter deficiency as the sole cause following radical prostatectomy in 8-71% of cases, with variable associations with detrusor dysfunction.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate suspected urethral or bladder-neck stricture or other bladder pathology.

recommended_tests: Pad test when measuring continence recovery or treatment response

therapies_index.name: Watchful waiting
approved_indications: Mild-to-moderate uncomplicated LUTS that cause little bother
therapies_index.administration: Use with periodic assessment; education and lifestyle advice may be included.
monitoring: Review at six months and then annually if symptoms do not deteriorate and no absolute indication for surgery develops.
Assess history, bladder diary, IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry and PVR volume.

therapies_index.name: Behavioural and dietary modifications
approved_indications: Self-care for men with LUTS
therapies_index.administration: May include adjusting fluid intake at inconvenient times, moderating caffeine or alcohol, relaxed or double voiding, urethral milking, distraction and bladder retraining, medication review, assistance with functional limitations, and treatment of constipation.

therapies_index.name: alfuzosin
therapies_index.mechanism: As an α1-blocker, reduces the effect of noradrenaline on prostatic smooth muscle and thereby aims to lower prostatic tone and BOO; other mechanisms may contribute.
approved_indications: Moderate-to-severe male LUTS
key_toxicities: Asthenia, dizziness and orthostatic hypotension are reported for α1-blockers.
Vascular adverse events and IFIS have been associated with alfuzosin.
Abnormal ejaculation is a class-associated adverse effect.
monitoring: Assess response and adverse events four to six weeks after starting treatment.
Inform the ophthalmologist of α1-blocker use before cataract surgery.

therapies_index.name: doxazosin
therapies_index.mechanism: As an α1-blocker, aims to reduce noradrenaline-mediated prostatic smooth-muscle tone and BOO; other mechanisms may contribute.
approved_indications: Moderate-to-severe male LUTS
key_toxicities: Asthenia, dizziness and orthostatic hypotension; vasodilating effects are particularly pronounced.
Vascular adverse events and IFIS have been associated with doxazosin.
monitoring: Assess response and adverse events four to six weeks after starting treatment.
Discuss orthostatic hypotension with older patients receiving non-selective α1-blockers.
Inform the ophthalmologist of α1-blocker use before cataract surgery.

therapies_index.name: silodosin
therapies_index.mechanism: As an α1-blocker, aims to inhibit noradrenaline-mediated prostatic smooth-muscle tone; the guide also describes its α1A selectivity.
approved_indications: Moderate-to-severe male LUTS
therapies_index.administration: A pooled analysis evaluated silodosin 8 mg.
key_toxicities: Ejaculatory dysfunction, particularly with selective α1-blockers.
Asthenia and dizziness are reported for the α1-blocker class; hypotension frequency with silodosin was comparable to placebo.
monitoring: Assess response and adverse events four to six weeks after starting treatment.
Counsel sexually active patients about ejaculatory dysfunction.
Inform the ophthalmologist of α1-blocker use before cataract surgery.

therapies_index.name: tamsulosin
therapies_index.mechanism: As an α1-blocker, aims to reduce noradrenaline-mediated prostatic smooth-muscle tone and BOO; other mechanisms may contribute.
approved_indications: Moderate-to-severe male LUTS
key_toxicities: Ejaculatory dysfunction and IFIS; the reported IFIS association was particularly marked for tamsulosin.
Asthenia, dizziness and orthostatic hypotension are α1-blocker adverse effects.
monitoring: Assess response and adverse events four to six weeks after starting treatment.
Discuss ejaculatory dysfunction with sexually active patients.
Inform the ophthalmologist of α1-blocker use before cataract surgery.

therapies_index.name: terazosin
therapies_index.mechanism: As an α1-blocker, aims to reduce noradrenaline-mediated prostatic smooth-muscle tone and BOO; other mechanisms may contribute.
approved_indications: Moderate-to-severe male LUTS
key_toxicities: Asthenia, dizziness and orthostatic hypotension; vasodilating effects are particularly pronounced.
Vascular adverse events and IFIS have been associated with terazosin.
monitoring: Assess response and adverse events four to six weeks after starting treatment.
Discuss orthostatic hypotension with older patients receiving non-selective α1-blockers.
Inform the ophthalmologist of α1-blocker use before cataract surgery.

therapies_index.name: naftopidil
therapies_index.mechanism: As an α1-blocker, aims to reduce noradrenaline-mediated prostatic smooth-muscle tone and BOO; other mechanisms may contribute.
approved_indications: Moderate-to-severe male LUTS
key_toxicities: Asthenia, dizziness and orthostatic hypotension are reported for α1-blockers.
Abnormal ejaculation is a class-associated adverse effect.
monitoring: Assess response and adverse events four to six weeks after starting treatment.

therapies_index.name: finasteride
therapies_index.mechanism: Inhibits 5α-reductase type 2, reducing conversion of testosterone to DHT and promoting apoptosis of prostatic epithelial cells.
approved_indications: Moderate-to-severe LUTS with increased risk of progression, such as prostate volume > 40 mL
therapies_index.administration: Long-term treatment is needed because clinical effects develop slowly.
key_toxicities: Reduced libido, ED and less frequent ejaculation disorders.
Gynaecomastia and breast or nipple tenderness.
A Swedish cohort reported an association with depression (HR 1.61); a causal relationship with high-grade cancer has not been established.
monitoring: Review after twelve weeks and six months, including symptoms, adverse events, uroflowmetry and PVR.

If life expectancy exceeds ten years and a PCa diagnosis could change management, perform serial PSA testing; establish a new PSA baseline at six months and evaluate any confirmed rise during treatment.

therapies_index.name: dutasteride
therapies_index.mechanism: Inhibits both 5α-reductase types, reducing DHT and promoting apoptosis of prostatic epithelial cells.
approved_indications: Moderate-to-severe LUTS with increased risk of progression, such as prostate volume > 40 mL
therapies_index.administration: Long-term treatment is needed because clinical effects develop slowly.
key_toxicities: Reduced libido, ED and less frequent ejaculation disorders.
Gynaecomastia and breast or nipple tenderness.
A Swedish cohort reported an association with depression (HR 1.68); a causal relationship with high-grade cancer has not been established.
monitoring: Review after twelve weeks and six months, including symptoms, adverse events, uroflowmetry and PVR.

If life expectancy exceeds ten years and a PCa diagnosis could change management, perform serial PSA testing; establish a new PSA baseline at six months and evaluate any confirmed rise during treatment.

therapies_index.name: darifenacin
therapies_index.mechanism: Antagonises muscarinic receptors involved in detrusor contractions; effects through other tissues may also contribute.
approved_indications: OAB/storage symptoms
key_toxicities: Antimuscarinic class effects include dry mouth, constipation, difficulty voiding, nasopharyngitis and dizziness.
PVR may increase; urinary retention is possible.
monitoring: Regularly reassess symptom scores and PVR.
Advise discontinuation if voiding symptoms or urinary stream worsen.

therapies_index.name: fesoterodine
therapies_index.mechanism: Antagonises muscarinic receptors involved in detrusor contractions.
approved_indications: OAB/storage symptoms
therapies_index.administration: The guide reports studies of fesoterodine 4 mg and fesoterodine 8 mg.
key_toxicities: Dry mouth, constipation, difficulty voiding, nasopharyngitis and dizziness are antimuscarinic class effects.
Fesoterodine 8 mg produced higher PVR than placebo or fesoterodine 4 mg; symptoms of urinary retention were also more frequent with fesoterodine 8 mg.
monitoring: Regularly reassess symptom scores and PVR.
Advise discontinuation if voiding symptoms or urinary stream worsen.

therapies_index.name: mirabegron
therapies_index.mechanism: Beta-3 adrenoceptor stimulation is thought to relax the detrusor, although its mode of action is not fully established.
approved_indications: OAB in adults
Moderate-to-severe male LUTS predominantly involving bladder storage
UUI after conservative treatment has failed
therapies_index.administration: Mirabegron 50 mg is described as clinically available; studies also evaluated 25 mg daily.
key_toxicities: Hypertension, UTI, headache and nasopharyngitis.
monitoring: Measure blood pressure before treatment and regularly during treatment.
Assess response and adverse events four to six weeks after treatment starts.

therapies_index.name: vibegron
therapies_index.mechanism: Beta-3 adrenoceptor stimulation is thought to relax the detrusor; the precise mode of action of beta-3 agonists is not fully established.
therapies_index.administration: The EMPOWUR trial studied 75 mg once daily.

therapies_index.name: tadalafil
therapies_index.mechanism: Inhibits phosphodiesterase 5, increasing intracellular cyclic guanosine monophosphate and reducing smooth-muscle tone in the detrusor, prostate and urethra; its precise action on LUTS remains uncertain.
approved_indications: Male LUTS with or without ED
therapies_index.administration: 5 mg once daily is the licensed regimen for male LUTS.
key_toxicities: PDE5I trial reports include flushing, gastroesophageal reflux, headache, dyspepsia, back pain and nasal congestion.

therapies_index.name: sildenafil
therapies_index.mechanism: As a PDE5I, increases intracellular cyclic guanosine monophosphate and reduces lower urinary tract smooth-muscle tone; the precise mechanism for LUTS is unclear.
therapies_index.administration: Combination trials included sildenafil 25 mg.
key_toxicities: PDE5I trial reports include flushing, gastroesophageal reflux, headache, dyspepsia, back pain and nasal congestion.

therapies_index.name: vardenafil
therapies_index.mechanism: As a PDE5I, increases intracellular cyclic guanosine monophosphate and reduces lower urinary tract smooth-muscle tone; the precise mechanism for LUTS is unclear.
therapies_index.administration: A combination trial included vardenafil 20 mg.
key_toxicities: PDE5I trial reports include flushing, gastroesophageal reflux, headache, dyspepsia, back pain and nasal congestion.

therapies_index.name: hexane extracted Serenoa repens
therapies_index.mechanism: The precise mechanism of plant extracts remains unclear.
approved_indications: Men with LUTS who wish to avoid potential adverse effects, particularly sexual adverse effects
Well-established use for symptomatic treatment of BPH under the cited HMPC monograph
therapies_index.administration: Extracted with hexane; the guide does not provide a dose.
key_toxicities: Gastrointestinal disorders were the most frequent adverse effects in the cited reviews.

therapies_index.name: Serenoa repens
therapies_index.mechanism: The precise mechanism of plant extracts remains unclear.
approved_indications: The cited HMPC monograph lists traditional use of the ethanol extract for LUTS related to BPH after serious conditions have been excluded.
therapies_index.administration: The document distinguishes ethanol-extracted preparations from hexane-extracted preparations.

therapies_index.name: Cucurbita pepo L, semen
therapies_index.mechanism: The precise mechanism of plant extracts remains unclear.
approved_indications: The cited HMPC monograph lists traditional use for LUTS related to BPH or an OAB after serious conditions have been excluded.

therapies_index.name: Prunus africana (Hook f.) Kalkm., cortex
therapies_index.mechanism: The precise mechanism of plant extracts remains unclear.
approved_indications: The cited HMPC monograph lists traditional use for LUTS related to BPH after serious conditions have been excluded.

therapies_index.name: Urtica dioica L., Urtica urens L., their hybrids or their mixtures, radix
therapies_index.mechanism: The precise mechanism of plant extracts remains unclear.
approved_indications: The cited HMPC monograph lists traditional use for LUTS related to BPH after serious conditions have been excluded.

therapies_index.name: Epilobium angustifolium L. and/or Epilobium parviflorum Schreb., herba
therapies_index.mechanism: The precise mechanism of plant extracts remains unclear.
approved_indications: The cited HMPC monograph lists traditional use for LUTS related to BPH after serious conditions have been excluded.

therapies_index.name: α1-blockers + 5α-reductase inhibitors
therapies_index.mechanism: Combines the comparatively rapid effect of an α1-blocker on prostatic tone with the slower prostate-reducing effect of a 5-ARI.
approved_indications: Moderate-to-severe LUTS with increased risk of progression, such as prostate volume > 40 mL
therapies_index.administration: Intended for long-term treatment of more than twelve months; stopping the α1-blocker after six months may be considered in men with moderate LUTS.
key_toxicities: Adverse effects of both component classes occur more frequently with combination treatment.
Ejaculatory dysfunction risk was higher than with either monotherapy in a cited meta-analysis.
monitoring: Review four to six weeks after treatment initiation and subsequently at six months and annually if stable.
For the 5-ARI component, assess treatment response and adverse events after twelve weeks and six months, with PSA follow-up when indicated.

therapies_index.name: dutasteride and tamsulosin
therapies_index.mechanism: Combines an α1-blocker with a 5-ARI.
approved_indications: Moderate-to-severe LUTS with increased risk of progression
therapies_index.administration: The guide describes a fixed-dose combination; component doses are not specified.
key_toxicities: Adverse effects associated with both α1-blockers and 5-ARIs.
monitoring: Assess response and adverse events after starting treatment.
Apply the guide's follow-up and PSA precautions for 5-ARI treatment.

therapies_index.name: doxazosin and finasteride
therapies_index.mechanism: Combines an α1-blocker with a 5-ARI.
approved_indications: Moderate-to-severe LUTS with increased risk of progression
key_toxicities: The MTOPS study reported more treatment-related adverse events during the first year of this combination.
monitoring: Assess response and adverse events after starting treatment.
Apply the guide's follow-up and PSA precautions for 5-ARI treatment.

therapies_index.name: α1-blockers + muscarinic receptor antagonists
therapies_index.mechanism: Targets α1-adrenoceptors and muscarinic receptors together.
approved_indications: Moderate-to-severe LUTS with inadequate relief of storage symptoms from either monotherapy
key_toxicities: Adverse effects of both classes, especially dry mouth; ejaculation failure may occur.
PVR may rise, although the guide describes a low AUR risk in studied men with baseline PVR < 150 mL.
monitoring: Measure PVR during combination treatment.
Assess response and adverse effects four to six weeks after starting treatment.

therapies_index.name: α1-blockers + Beta-3 agonist
therapies_index.mechanism: Adds a beta-3 agonist to α1-blocker therapy for persisting OAB symptoms.
approved_indications: Persistent storage LUTS after α1-blocker monotherapy
therapies_index.administration: Add-on treatment; the guide describes short-term studies rather than a general dosing regimen.
key_toxicities: Adverse effects of both component classes.
monitoring: Assess response and adverse events after starting treatment.

therapies_index.name: tamsulosin plus mirabegron
therapies_index.mechanism: Combines α1-blockade with beta-3 adrenoceptor stimulation.
approved_indications: Persistent OAB or storage symptoms during tamsulosin treatment
therapies_index.administration: Studies used mirabegron 50 mg with tamsulosin 0.2 mg; another used tamsulosin 0.4 mg with mirabegron 25 mg increased to 50 mg after one month.
key_toxicities: Hypertension, headache and nasopharyngitis were commonly reported in the PLUS trial; retention episodes were also recorded.
monitoring: Measure blood pressure before and during mirabegron treatment.
Assess response and adverse events.

therapies_index.name: α1-blockers + Phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors
therapies_index.mechanism: Combines α1-blockade and phosphodiesterase 5 inhibition to improve LUTS.
approved_indications: Bothersome LUTS, particularly when improvement in erectile function is also desired
key_toxicities: In the cited RCT comparison, adding PDE5Is did not increase adverse-event incidence over α-blocker monotherapy.

therapies_index.name: finasteride and tadalafil
therapies_index.mechanism: Combines 5α-reductase inhibition with phosphodiesterase 5 inhibition.
therapies_index.administration: A cited trial evaluated finasteride with tadalafil 5 mg.

therapies_index.name: HESr with silodosin
therapies_index.mechanism: Combines a plant extract whose precise mechanism is unclear with an α1-blocker.
therapies_index.administration: A cited study assessed patients treated for at least twelve months.

therapies_index.name: mirabegron and solifenacin
therapies_index.mechanism: Combines beta-3 adrenoceptor stimulation with muscarinic receptor antagonism.
therapies_index.administration: Studies evaluated mirabegron 25/50 mg with solifenacin 5/10 mg, and solifenacin 5 mg with mirabegron 25 mg or 50 mg.
key_toxicities: In a cited study, adverse events were more frequent with solifenacin 5 mg plus mirabegron 25 mg than with mirabegron 25 mg alone; retention was uncommon but somewhat more frequent with combination treatment, and PVR increased slightly.

therapies_index.name: Mirabegron + Doxazosin
therapies_index.mechanism: Combines beta-3 adrenoceptor stimulation with α1-blockade.

therapies_index.name: solifenacin, tadalafil, and dutasteride
therapies_index.mechanism: Combines muscarinic receptor antagonism, phosphodiesterase 5 inhibition and 5α-reductase inhibition.
therapies_index.administration: A cited study examined simultaneous administration in patients with OAB and LUT obstruction unresponsive to prior treatment.

therapies_index.name: desmopressin
therapies_index.mechanism: A synthetic AVP analogue with high V2 receptor affinity that promotes renal water reabsorption and reduces urine production.
approved_indications: Nocturia due to nocturnal polyuria in men < 65 years of age
Low-dose treatment for men > 65 years of age with nocturia at least twice nightly due to nocturnal polyuria
therapies_index.administration: For men < 65 years, start at 0.1 mg/day and, if needed, increase weekly up to 0.4 mg/day; take once daily before sleep. Avoid fluids for at least one hour before and eight hours after dosing. Low-dose ODT 50 mcg for men is described for nocturia with ≥ 2 episodes.
key_toxicities: Hyponatraemia, potentially life-threatening, particularly in older patients.
Headache, insomnia, dry mouth, hypertension, abdominal pain, peripheral edema and nausea.
monitoring: Measure serum sodium at baseline, day three, day seven and one month after treatment begins, and periodically thereafter.
Increase sodium-monitoring frequency for patients > 65 years and those at increased risk of hyponatraemia.
Restart the monitoring sequence after dose escalation.
Use FVC at follow-up.

therapies_index.name: desmopressin acetate nasal spray
therapies_index.mechanism: As a desmopressin formulation, acts at renal V2 receptors to reduce urine production.
approved_indications: The guide reports FDA approval for nocturia due to nocturnal polyuria; this formulation is not available in Europe.
therapies_index.administration: Cited trials evaluated 1.5 mcg and 0.75 mcg doses.
key_toxicities: Hyponatraemia.
monitoring: The guide requires sodium assessment at baseline and during desmopressin treatment.

therapies_index.name: diuretics
approved_indications: Timed diuretic therapy may be offered for nocturia due to nocturnal polyuria.
therapies_index.administration: The guide describes timed treatment but does not specify a drug or dose.
monitoring: Screen for hyponatraemia at baseline and during treatment.

therapies_index.name: duloxetine
approved_indications: Male stress urinary incontinence; use for this indication is off label in Europe.
key_toxicities: Fatigue, somnolence and nausea; treatment discontinuation was frequent in the cited review.
monitoring: Inform patients of potential adverse events and off-label use.

therapies_index.name: Botulinum toxin-A
therapies_index.mechanism: Inhibits neurotransmitter release from cholinergic neurons.
therapies_index.administration: Intraprostatic injection was studied for LUTS, but the guideline recommends against offering it for male LUTS.

therapies_index.name: fexapotide triflutate (NX-1207)
therapies_index.mechanism: The mechanism is not fully understood; experimental findings suggest apoptosis-mediated prostatic atrophy.
therapies_index.administration: Evaluated as a transrectal intraprostatic injection.

therapies_index.name: PRX302
therapies_index.mechanism: The mechanism is not fully understood; experimental findings suggest apoptosis-mediated prostatic atrophy.
therapies_index.administration: Evaluated as an intraprostatic injection.

therapies_index.name: onabotulinumtoxinA
therapies_index.mechanism: Inhibits neurotransmitter release from cholinergic neurons.
approved_indications: OAB with persistent or refractory non-neurogenic UUI in adults
therapies_index.administration: 100 U injected into the bladder wall.
key_toxicities: Urinary retention and UTI; haematuria, dysuria and post-treatment pain are also reported.
Response has limited duration and repeat injections may be needed.
monitoring: Before treatment, discuss UTI risk and the possible prolonged need for clean intermittent self-catheterisation; establish whether the patient is willing and able to perform it.

therapies_index.name: parasympathomimetics
therapies_index.administration: The guide advises against routine use for men with UAB.
key_toxicities: Potential serious adverse effects are noted without specification.

therapies_index.name: bethanechol chloride
therapies_index.administration: A cited trial combined it with intravesical PGE2.

therapies_index.name: PGE2
therapies_index.mechanism: Prostaglandins E2 and F2a are described as predominant prostaglandin subtypes stimulating detrusor contractions.
therapies_index.administration: Studied by intravesical instillation; clinical utility for UAB remains uncertain.

therapies_index.name: PGF2a
therapies_index.mechanism: Prostaglandins E2 and F2a are described as predominant prostaglandin subtypes stimulating detrusor contractions.
therapies_index.administration: Studied by intravesical instillation; clinical utility for UAB remains uncertain.

therapies_index.name: Monopolar-TURP
therapies_index.mechanism: Resects prostatic transition-zone tissue to relieve obstruction.
approved_indications: Surgical treatment of moderate-to-severe LUTS with prostate size 30-80 mL
therapies_index.administration: The guide suggests an upper prostate-volume limit of 80 mL and notes that the procedure is safest when completed in under 90 minutes.
key_toxicities: Bleeding, transfusion, TUR-syndrome, clot retention, AUR and UTI.
Later complications include UI, urinary retention, BNC, urethral stricture, retrograde ejaculation and ED.
monitoring: Review four to six weeks after catheter removal, assessing IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry, erectile and ejaculatory function, and PVR.

therapies_index.name: B-TURP
therapies_index.mechanism: Resects prostatic transition-zone tissue using a locally completed bipolar electrical circuit and saline irrigation.
approved_indications: Surgical treatment of moderate-to-severe LUTS with prostate size 30-80 mL
