key_toxicities: Bleeding, urinary retention, UI, urethral stricture and BNC can occur; the guide describes a more favourable peri-operative safety profile than M-TURP.
monitoring: Review four to six weeks after catheter removal, assessing IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry, erectile and ejaculatory function, and PVR.

therapies_index.name: HoLRP
therapies_index.mechanism: Holmium-laser resection of prostatic tissue.
therapies_index.administration: The guide states that HoLRP no longer has a role in contemporary treatment algorithms.

therapies_index.name: ThuVARP
therapies_index.mechanism: Uses a continuous-wave Tm:YAG laser for prostatic vaporesection.
approved_indications: Alternative to TURP for surgical treatment of LUTS
key_toxicities: The guide reports blood loss and potential late urethral stricture or BNC, while noting limited longer-term comparative evidence.
monitoring: Review four to six weeks after catheter removal, assessing symptoms, uroflowmetry, sexual function and PVR.

therapies_index.name: TUIP
therapies_index.mechanism: Incises the bladder outlet without substantial tissue removal.
approved_indications: Surgical treatment of moderate-to-severe LUTS with prostate size < 30 mL and no middle lobe
therapies_index.administration: Conventionally performed using a Collins knife and electrocautery; holmium laser has also been studied.
key_toxicities: Re-operation is more frequent than after M-TURP; retrograde ejaculation can occur but was less frequent than after M-TURP.
monitoring: Review four to six weeks after catheter removal, assessing symptoms, uroflowmetry, sexual function and PVR.

therapies_index.name: OP
therapies_index.mechanism: Enucleates obstructing prostatic adenoma through a transvesical or anterior-capsule approach.
approved_indications: Moderate-to-severe LUTS with prostate size > 80 mL when anatomical endoscopic enucleation is unavailable
therapies_index.administration: Open surgery through the bladder (Freyer procedure) or anterior prostatic capsule (Millin procedure).
key_toxicities: Blood transfusion, transient UI, BNC and urethral stricture; the guide identifies it as the most invasive surgical method.
monitoring: Review four to six weeks after catheter removal, assessing symptoms, uroflowmetry, erectile and ejaculatory function, and PVR.

therapies_index.name: B-TUEP
therapies_index.mechanism: Endoscopically enucleates obstructing adenoma using bipolar energy, followed by morcellation or resection.
approved_indications: Alternative to TURP for men with moderate-to-severe LUTS
key_toxicities: Urinary retention, bleeding, transfusion, urethral stricture and BNC are assessed in comparative studies; the guide describes a favourable peri-operative safety profile.
monitoring: Review four to six weeks after catheter removal.

therapies_index.name: PKEP
therapies_index.mechanism: Plasmakinetic bipolar transurethral enucleation of obstructing prostatic adenoma.
approved_indications: Alternative to TURP for men with moderate-to-severe LUTS
key_toxicities: Comparative studies report bleeding, transfusion, urinary retention, BNC and retrograde ejaculation.
monitoring: Review four to six weeks after catheter removal.

therapies_index.name: BPEP
therapies_index.mechanism: Bipolar plasma enucleation of obstructing prostatic adenoma.
key_toxicities: Comparative studies assess blood transfusion, urethral stricture and UI.
monitoring: Review four to six weeks after catheter removal.

therapies_index.name: HoLEP
therapies_index.mechanism: Uses pulsed Ho:YAG laser energy absorbed by water-containing tissue to enucleate the prostate while providing limited-depth coagulation.
approved_indications: Alternative to TURP or OP for moderate-to-severe LUTS
key_toxicities: Urinary stricture, UI, UTI and retrograde ejaculation are reported; bleeding and transfusion were less frequent than with M-TURP in cited comparisons.
monitoring: Review four to six weeks after catheter removal, assessing symptoms, uroflowmetry, erectile and ejaculatory function, and PVR.

therapies_index.name: ThuLEP
therapies_index.mechanism: Blunt prostatic enucleation using thulium laser energy absorbed by water-containing tissue.
approved_indications: Alternative to TURP, HoLEP or bipolar transurethral enucleation for moderate-to-severe LUTS
Tm:YAG laser enucleation is offered to patients receiving anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy.
key_toxicities: Bleeding, clot retention and urethral or bladder-neck stricture were assessed in comparative studies.
monitoring: Review four to six weeks after catheter removal.

therapies_index.name: ThuVEP
therapies_index.mechanism: Thulium-laser vapoenucleation of prostatic tissue.
approved_indications: Alternative to TURP, HoLEP or bipolar transurethral enucleation for moderate-to-severe LUTS
key_toxicities: Post-operative adverse events were reported in a cited study; the guide notes limited trial evidence.
monitoring: Review four to six weeks after catheter removal.

therapies_index.name: DiLEP
therapies_index.mechanism: Diode-laser enucleation of prostatic tissue.
approved_indications: Alternative to bipolar transurethral enucleation or B-TURP for moderate-to-severe LUTS
therapies_index.administration: The recommendation specifies 120-W 980 nm, 1,318 nm or 1,470 nm diode laser enucleation.
key_toxicities: Bleeding and peri-operative complications were assessed in trials; the guide notes uncertain retreatment findings.
monitoring: Review four to six weeks after catheter removal.

therapies_index.name: MISP
therapies_index.mechanism: Performs simple prostatectomy through a laparoscopic or robot-assisted transcapsular or transvesical approach.
therapies_index.administration: Includes LSP and RASP; described as feasible for prostate sizes > 80 mL, but further RCTs are needed.
key_toxicities: Blood loss, transfusion and peri-operative complications are reported in comparisons.
monitoring: Review after prostate surgery as described in the guide.

therapies_index.name: LSP
therapies_index.mechanism: Laparoscopic simple prostatectomy through a transcapsular or transvesical approach.
key_toxicities: Catheterisation and hospitalisation requirements were reported in comparative studies.
monitoring: Review after prostate surgery as described in the guide.

therapies_index.name: RASP
therapies_index.mechanism: Robot-assisted simple prostatectomy through a transcapsular or transvesical approach.
key_toxicities: Blood loss and peri-operative complications were reported in comparative studies.
monitoring: Review after prostate surgery as described in the guide.

therapies_index.name: GreenLEP
therapies_index.mechanism: Anatomically enucleates adenoma by blunt dissection with the sheath and laser-assisted incision.
therapies_index.administration: Described as under investigation; the guide reports a lack of adequate high-quality RCTs.

therapies_index.name: B-TUVP
therapies_index.mechanism: A bipolar electrode and high-frequency generator form a plasma field that vaporises prostatic tissue.
approved_indications: Alternative to TURP for moderate-to-severe LUTS with prostate volume 30-80 mL
key_toxicities: Reported outcomes include clot retention, transfusion, urethral stricture, UI and other peri-operative complications.
monitoring: Review four to six weeks after catheter removal.

therapies_index.name: PVP
therapies_index.mechanism: Photoselective laser vaporisation removes obstructing prostatic tissue.
approved_indications: An alternative to TURP for moderate-to-severe LUTS with prostate volume 30-80 mL when using the recommended 80-W KTP, 120-W LBO or 180-W LBO laser options
therapies_index.administration: The guide separately recommends 80-W 532-nm KTP, 120-W 532-nm LBO and 180-W 532-nm LBO approaches.
key_toxicities: Re-operation, urinary retention, UTI, urethral stricture, BNC and haematuria are reported; bleeding outcomes vary across comparisons.
monitoring: Review four to six weeks after catheter removal.

therapies_index.name: Diode laser vaporisation of the prostate
therapies_index.mechanism: Vaporises prostatic tissue with diode laser energy.
therapies_index.administration: The guide discusses 120-W 980 nm treatment as a technique under investigation.
key_toxicities: Post-operative dysuria, persistent SUI and re-operation were reported; retreatment results remain uncertain.

therapies_index.name: Aquablation
therapies_index.mechanism: A targeted, high-velocity saline stream ablates prostatic tissue under real-time transrectal ultrasound guidance without generating thermal energy.
approved_indications: Alternative to TURP for moderate-to-severe LUTS with prostate volume 30-80 mL; the guide states that it remains under investigation.
therapies_index.administration: Haemostasis may use a Foley balloon under light traction, diathermy or a low-powered laser.
key_toxicities: Bleeding and possible transfusion; the guide specifically requires counselling about bleeding risk and limited long-term follow-up.
monitoring: Review after prostate surgery as described in the guide.

therapies_index.name: PAE
therapies_index.mechanism: Selectively embolises arteries supplying the prostate to produce stasis in treated vessels.
approved_indications: Moderate-to-severe LUTS in men considering minimally invasive treatment who accept less favourable outcomes than TURP; the guide states that PAE remains under investigation.
therapies_index.administration: May be performed as a day procedure under local anaesthesia through femoral or radial arterial access; requires appropriately trained interventional radiologists working with urologists.
key_toxicities: AUR, possible non-target embolisation and radiation exposure; comparative adverse-event findings conflict.
monitoring: Urologists working with trained interventional radiologists should conduct patient selection, work-up and follow-up.
Discuss radiation exposure during patient counselling.

therapies_index.name: The Rezum system
therapies_index.mechanism: Radiofrequency-generated water vapour transfers heat into prostatic tissue, producing cellular necrosis.
therapies_index.administration: Can be performed in an office setting; typically one to three injections per lateral lobe and, when indicated, one to two into the median lobe. The guide classifies it as under investigation.
key_toxicities: Reported adverse events were generally mild-to-moderate and resolved rapidly.

therapies_index.name: Prostatic urethral lift (Urolift®)
therapies_index.mechanism: Permanent suture-based implants compress the lateral prostatic lobes and open an anterior urethral channel.
approved_indications: LUTS in men seeking preservation of ejaculatory function, with prostate size < 70 mL and no middle lobe
therapies_index.administration: Implants are placed under cystoscopic guidance with local or general anaesthesia.
key_toxicities: Haematuria, dysuria, pelvic pain, urgency, transient incontinence and UTI.
Retreatment may be required.
monitoring: Review after prostate surgery as described in the guide.

therapies_index.name: iTIND
therapies_index.mechanism: An expanded nitinol device compresses obstructing prostatic tissue, producing radial pressure and ischaemic necrosis.
therapies_index.administration: Placed under direct vision, left for five days and removed by outpatient urethroscopy; the guide lists it as under investigation.
key_toxicities: Transient urinary retention, device displacement with transient incontinence, infection and other usually mild transient adverse events.

therapies_index.name: Prompted voiding
therapies_index.mechanism: A carer prompts toileting rather than leaving initiation to the patient.
approved_indications: Urinary incontinence when appropriate

therapies_index.name: Bladder training
therapies_index.mechanism: Retrains voiding habits to improve urgency control, extend intervals between voids and increase functional bladder capacity.
approved_indications: Complementary treatment for UI

therapies_index.name: PFMT
therapies_index.mechanism: Trains pelvic floor muscles to assist recovery of continence.
approved_indications: Alone or with biofeedback and/or electrostimulation to hasten UI recovery in men undergoing radical prostatectomy
therapies_index.administration: The guide describes starting between seven and ten days after urethral catheter withdrawal.

therapies_index.name: Electrical stimulation
approved_indications: Studied as an adjunct to PFMT for male UI
therapies_index.administration: Studies included surface and intra-anal electrostimulation.
key_toxicities: Pain and discomfort occurred more often than with sham stimulation in a cited review.

therapies_index.name: PTNS
therapies_index.mechanism: Stimulates the posterior tibial nerve to deliver signals through the S2-S4 sacral plexus to the sacral micturition centre.
approved_indications: The guide says it may be offered to male patients as an alternative before more invasive OAB treatments, while noting insufficient male-specific evidence for a formal recommendation.
therapies_index.administration: Percutaneous treatment typically comprises twelve weekly sessions of 30 minutes; transcutaneous treatment typically comprises self-administered daily sessions of twenty minutes after instruction.
key_toxicities: Puncture-site pain or discomfort; small haematomas, swelling, leg tingling and vasovagal reactions are also reported.

therapies_index.name: pads
therapies_index.mechanism: Absorb urine as a containment measure.
approved_indications: Palliative containment of UI

therapies_index.name: penile sheaths
therapies_index.mechanism: Provide external urine collection.
approved_indications: Palliative containment of UI

therapies_index.name: penile clamps
therapies_index.mechanism: Externally compress the penis to contain urinary leakage.
approved_indications: Containment for selected activities in men with UI
key_toxicities: Discomfort or pain was commonly reported by men using a hinge-type clamp in a cited trial.

therapies_index.name: bulking agents
therapies_index.mechanism: Adds material around a damaged sphincter region to improve urethral coaptation.
approved_indications: The guide notes a possible option for men unfit for more invasive treatment, but recommends against offering bulking agents for post-prostatectomy incontinence.
therapies_index.administration: Urethral injection.
key_toxicities: Transient dysuria and haematuria, urinary retention, UTI, possible allergic reactions and material migration.

therapies_index.name: Macroplastique
therapies_index.mechanism: Injected urethral bulking material improves coaptation of a damaged sphincter zone.
therapies_index.administration: Evaluated by urethral injection.
key_toxicities: Bulking-agent-associated dysuria, haematuria, urinary retention, UTI, allergic reactions and potential migration are described at class level.

therapies_index.name: Opsys
therapies_index.mechanism: As a bulking agent, adds urethral bulk to improve sphincter-zone coaptation.
therapies_index.administration: Evaluated as an injectable bulking agent.
key_toxicities: The guide describes possible bulking-agent-associated dysuria, haematuria, retention, UTI, allergic reactions and migration at class level.

therapies_index.name: Durasphere
therapies_index.mechanism: As a bulking agent, adds urethral bulk to improve sphincter-zone coaptation.
therapies_index.administration: Evaluated as an injectable bulking agent.
key_toxicities: The guide describes possible bulking-agent-associated dysuria, haematuria, retention, UTI, allergic reactions and migration at class level.

therapies_index.name: Urolastic
therapies_index.mechanism: As a bulking agent, adds urethral bulk to improve sphincter-zone coaptation.
therapies_index.administration: Evaluated as an injectable bulking agent.
key_toxicities: The guide describes possible bulking-agent-associated dysuria, haematuria, retention, UTI, allergic reactions and migration at class level.

therapies_index.name: non-adjustable transobturator slings
therapies_index.mechanism: A fixed suburethral sling restores continence by urethral compression and/or repositioning of the urethral bulb.
approved_indications: Mild-to-moderate post-prostatectomy incontinence; the guide notes that these severity categories remain undefined
therapies_index.administration: Positioned under the urethra; tension is set during surgery and cannot subsequently be adjusted.
key_toxicities: Pain, superficial wound infection, temporary voiding dysfunction, de novo urgency or urinary retention; chronic pain and erosion are uncommon.
monitoring: Counsel that severe incontinence, previous pelvic radiotherapy or transurethral surgery may worsen outcomes.

therapies_index.name: AdVanceXP
therapies_index.mechanism: Repositioning sling placed under the urethra to improve continence.
key_toxicities: The guide reports male-sling-associated pain, infection and transient voiding dysfunction; outcomes may be worse after radiotherapy.

therapies_index.name: I-Stop TOMS
therapies_index.mechanism: A transobturator compressive male sling provides urethral support.

therapies_index.name: Remeex®
therapies_index.mechanism: A male sling whose tension can be adjusted after implantation.
therapies_index.administration: Post-operative readjustment is possible.
key_toxicities: Mechanical failure was reported in one cited study; adjustable-sling complications also include pain, erosion and infection.

therapies_index.name: Argus®
therapies_index.mechanism: A male sling whose tension can be adjusted after implantation.
therapies_index.administration: Post-operative readjustment is possible.
key_toxicities: Pain, erosion and infection are reported for adjustable male slings; a cited comparison reported more inguinal pain and explantation with Argus T.

therapies_index.name: ATOMS®
therapies_index.mechanism: An adjustable male sling whose tension can be changed after implantation.
therapies_index.administration: Post-operative adjustment is possible.
key_toxicities: Complications and device expulsion were reported in cited reviews.

therapies_index.name: autologous vas deferens sling
therapies_index.mechanism: An autologous sling is positioned beneath the vesico-urethral anastomosis with the aim of improving early continence recovery.
therapies_index.administration: Studied during RARP; the guide reports no established improvement in continence at six months.

therapies_index.name: AUS
therapies_index.mechanism: An implanted inflatable cuff and patient-operated control system compress the urethra to restore continence.
approved_indications: Moderate-to-severe male SUI
therapies_index.administration: Implantation should be offered in expert centres; the patient must be able to operate the pump.
key_toxicities: Infection, erosion, mechanical failure and urethral atrophy; revision or explantation may be needed.
monitoring: Assess the patient's ability to operate the pump and explain the likelihood of long-term maintenance operations.
Counsel regarding complications, mechanical failure and possible explantation.

therapies_index.name: AMS 800
therapies_index.mechanism: A three-component AUS uses an inflatable cuff, control pump and pressure-regulating balloon.
approved_indications: Moderate-to-severe male SUI as an AUS device
therapies_index.administration: Implantation should be performed in an experienced centre.
key_toxicities: Device malfunction, urethral atrophy, erosion and infection were recorded among AUS failures.
monitoring: Counsel about pump operation and possible revision or explantation.

therapies_index.name: ZSI 375
therapies_index.mechanism: A two-component AUS comprises an inflatable cuff and control pump.
therapies_index.administration: Implanted artificial urinary sphincter.
key_toxicities: Urethral erosion and mechanical failure were reported.
monitoring: Counsel about pump operation and possible revision or explantation.

therapies_index.name: ProACT®
therapies_index.mechanism: Adjustable balloons positioned beside the bladder neck compress the urethral outlet.
approved_indications: The guide discusses its use for male UI but advises against offering it after pelvic radiotherapy.
therapies_index.administration: Two devices are inserted through perineal incisions under fluoroscopy; balloon volume may be adjusted through scrotal ports. Implantation should only be offered in expert centres.
key_toxicities: Bladder or urethral perforation, erosion, device leakage and migration; revision and explantation may be needed.
monitoring: Counsel about complications, mechanical failure and possible explantation.

therapies_index.name: Bladder wall injections of onabotulinumtoxinA
therapies_index.mechanism: Injected onabotulinumtoxinA inhibits cholinergic neurotransmitter release.
approved_indications: OAB/UUI refractory to medical therapy
therapies_index.administration: Inject 100 U into the bladder wall.
key_toxicities: Urinary retention, UTI, haematuria, dysuria and post-treatment pain; repeated treatment may be needed.
monitoring: Counsel about limited response duration and possible prolonged clean intermittent self-catheterisation.

therapies_index.name: SNM
therapies_index.mechanism: An implanted electrode delivers low-amplitude impulses to sacral nerve roots, modulating neural activity through a mechanism that remains uncertain.
approved_indications: UUI refractory to medical therapy in patients willing to undergo surgery
Test phase for men with DU without BPO
therapies_index.administration: Initial percutaneous test near S3, or S4 if needed, precedes full implantation when symptoms decrease by more than 50%.
key_toxicities: Implant-site pain, lead migration, leg or back pain and wound infection; device revision may be required.
monitoring: Assess response during the test phase before proceeding to full implantation.

therapies_index.name: augmentation cystoplasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Places a detubularised bowel segment into the opened bladder wall to increase capacity and reduce OAB symptoms.
approved_indications: OAB/UUI after all other treatment options have failed, in patients able and willing to self-catheterise
therapies_index.administration: Major reconstructive surgery.
key_toxicities: Early infection, bowel obstruction, bleeding and cardiorespiratory complications.
Long-term metabolic disturbance, altered bowel habits, mucus production, stones, bladder perforation and rare bladder cancer; self-catheterisation is commonly required.
monitoring: Counsel about complications, potential clean intermittent self-catheterisation and lifelong surveillance.

therapies_index.name: urinary diversion
therapies_index.mechanism: Diverts urine as a reconstructive option for intractable UUI.
approved_indications: OAB/UUI after less invasive treatments have failed, in patients who will accept a stoma
therapies_index.administration: Major surgery; patients with a urinary conduit rely on lifelong urine bags.
key_toxicities: Early infection, bowel obstruction, bleeding and cardiorespiratory complications.
Long-term metabolic and bowel effects, mucus production, stones and other major complications.
monitoring: Provide thorough pre-operative counselling, including access to stoma or continence nursing expertise.

therapies_index.name: CIC
therapies_index.mechanism: Intermittently empties the bladder to provide timely drainage.
approved_indications: UAB when upper-tract damage is a risk or PVR is > 300mL
therapies_index.administration: May be performed by the patient or another person; self-administration requires adequate dexterity and cognition.
monitoring: Assess PVR and urinary complications.

therapies_index.name: suprapubic cystostomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Provides continuous bladder drainage through a suprapubic catheter.
approved_indications: Urinary drainage when other modalities have failed or are unsuitable
therapies_index.administration: If long-term indwelling drainage is necessary, the guide favours the suprapubic route over urethral catheterisation.
key_toxicities: Indwelling catheters are associated with complications and increased UTI risk.

therapies_index.name: indwelling transurethral catheterisation
therapies_index.mechanism: Provides continuous bladder drainage through a urethral catheter.
approved_indications: Urinary drainage only when other modalities have failed or are unsuitable
therapies_index.administration: Long-term use should be avoided where possible.
key_toxicities: UTI and other catheter complications, including risk of traumatic hypospadias.

therapies_index.name: IVES
therapies_index.mechanism: Stimulates A-delta mechanoreceptor afferents to reinforce bladder contractions.
therapies_index.administration: Daily stimulation; ten to fifteen sessions are described as a trial period.
monitoring: Assess voiding response during the trial period.

therapies_index.name: ESWT
therapies_index.mechanism: Promotes neovascularisation and tissue regeneration and could theoretically improve detrusor contractility.

therapies_index.name: Pelvic floor muscle relaxation training with biofeedback
therapies_index.mechanism: Aims to facilitate relaxation of the pelvic floor and urinary sphincter during voiding.
therapies_index.administration: Described as usual first-line physiotherapy for voiding dysfunction; no adult male RCT establishes its effect on UAB.

therapies_index.name: timed or scheduled voiding
therapies_index.mechanism: Uses planned toileting intervals to support bladder emptying.
approved_indications: May be recommended for UAB with sensory impairment
therapies_index.administration: Voiding is scheduled at predetermined intervals.

therapies_index.name: double or triple voiding
therapies_index.mechanism: Repeated attempts to void may reduce PVR.
approved_indications: May be tried for bothersome frequency in UAB; the guide states that clinical-trial evidence of benefit or harm in non-neurogenic men is unavailable.

therapies_index.name: Valsalva or the Credé maneuver
therapies_index.mechanism: Raises abdominal pressure to assist bladder emptying.
approved_indications: May be tried for bothersome frequency in UAB, except in patients with poorly compliant bladders
key_toxicities: The guide cautions against increasing intra-abdominal pressure with these manoeuvres in poorly compliant bladders.

recommendations.statement: Obtain a comprehensive medical history from men with LUTS.
At the initial assessment of male LUTS, and when reassessing during or after treatment, use a validated symptom questionnaire that covers bother and quality of life.
Use a bladder diary when assessing male LUTS with a storage component, particularly nocturia.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.3 Frequency volume charts and/or bladder diaries

recommendations.statement: Ask the patient to record a bladder diary for at least three days.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.3 Frequency volume charts and/or bladder diaries

recommendations.statement: Include a physical examination and digital-rectal examination when assessing male LUTS.
Assess male LUTS with urinalysis performed by dipstick or microscopy.
Measure PSA when a diagnosis of prostate cancer would alter management.
Measure PSA when the result would help guide treatment or other clinical decisions.
Explain PSA testing and the implications of an elevated result to patients.
Assess renal function when history and examination suggest renal impairment, hydronephrosis is present, or surgery for male LUTS is being considered.
Measure post-void residual when assessing male LUTS.
Include uroflowmetry in the initial evaluation of male LUTS.
Perform uroflowmetry before starting medical or invasive treatment.
Perform upper urinary tract ultrasound in men with LUTS.
When considering medical treatment for male LUTS, image the prostate if the findings would help select the appropriate drug.
Image the prostate when surgical treatment is under consideration.
Before minimally invasive or surgical treatment for male LUTS, perform urethrocystoscopy if its findings could alter the treatment selected.
Reserve UDS for individual patients with specific indications before invasive treatment, or when further investigation of the pathophysiology of LUTS is warranted.
Perform UDS before further invasive treatment in men whose previous invasive treatment for LUTS was unsuccessful.
Perform UDS in men considering invasive treatment who cannot void > 150 mL.
When considering surgery for men with bothersome, predominantly voiding LUTS and Qmax > 10 mL/s, perform UDS.
Perform UDS before considering invasive therapy for men with bothersome, predominantly voiding LUTS and post-void residual > 300 mL.
Perform UDS when considering invasive treatment for men aged > 80 years who have bothersome, predominantly voiding LUTS.
Perform UDS when considering invasive treatment for men aged < 50 years who have bothersome, predominantly voiding LUTS.
Do not substitute non-invasive tests for urodynamics/pressure-flow studies when diagnosing bladder outflow obstruction in men.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.13 Non-invasive tests in diagnosing bladder outlet obstruction in men with LUTS

recommendations.statement: Offer watchful waiting to men whose mild/moderate symptoms cause minimal bother.
Provide men with LUTS with lifestyle guidance and self-care information before treatment or alongside it.
Offer α1-blockers to men with moderate-to-severe LUTS.
Use 5α-reductase inhibitors (5-ARIs) for men with moderate-to-severe LUTS who have increased risk of progression, such as prostate volume > 40 mL.
Explain to patients that 5-ARIs take time to act.
Use muscarinic receptor antagonists for men with moderate-to-severe LUTS when bladder storage symptoms predominate.
Do not use antimuscarinic overactive bladder medications in men whose post-void residual volume is > 150 mL.
Use beta-3 agonists for men with moderate-to-severe LUTS whose symptoms are predominantly related to bladder storage.
Use phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors for men with moderate-to-severe LUTS, whether or not erectile dysfunction is present.
Offer hexane extracted Serenoa repens to men with LUTS who want to avoid potential adverse effects, particularly those affecting sexual function.
Tell patients that the treatment effect of hexane extracted Serenoa repens may be modest.
Offer an α1-blocker together with a 5α-reductase inhibitor to men with moderate-to-severe LUTS and increased progression risk, such as prostate volume > 40 mL.
Use an α1-blocker with a muscarinic receptor antagonist for moderate-to-severe LUTS when either drug alone has provided insufficient relief of storage symptoms.
Do not prescribe an α1-blocker plus a muscarinic receptor antagonist to men with post-void residual volume > 150 mL.
Use an α1-blocker together with mirabegron when storage LUTS persist despite α1-blocker monotherapy.
Use α1-blockers + Phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors for bothersome LUTS, particularly when patients also want improved erectile function.
Explain to patients that the benefit of α1-blockers + Phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors is modest in magnitude.
Offer bipolar or monopolar transurethral resection of the prostate as surgery for moderate-to-severe LUTS in men with prostate size 30-80 mL.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.3.1.1 Monopolar and bipolar transurethral resection of the prostate

recommendations.statement: Offer Tm:YAG laser prostate resection (ThuVARP) as an alternative to TURP.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.3.1.3 Thulium:yttrium-aluminium-garnet laser vaporesection of the prostate

recommendations.statement: Offer transurethral incision of the prostate for surgical treatment of moderate-to-severe LUTS when prostate size is < 30 mL and there is no middle lobe.
If anatomical endoscopic enucleation of the prostate is unavailable, offer open prostatectomy for moderate-to-severe LUTS in men with prostate size > 80 mL.
Offer bipolar transurethral (plasmakinetic) enucleation of the prostate as an alternative to transurethral resection for men with moderate-to-severe LUTS.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.3.2.2 Bipolar transurethral enucleation of the prostate

recommendations.statement: Offer Ho:YAG laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) to men with moderate-to-severe LUTS as an alternative to transurethral resection or open prostatectomy.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.3.2.3 Holmium laser enucleation of the prostate

recommendations.statement: Offer Tm:YAG laser enucleation of the prostate (ThuLEP, ThuVEP) to men with moderate-to-severe LUTS as an alternative to transurethral resection, holmium laser enucleation or bipolar transurethral (plasmakinetic) enucleation.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.3.2.4 Thulium:yttrium-aluminium-garnet laser enucleation of the prostate

recommendations.statement: Offer Tm:YAG laser enucleation of the prostate to patients receiving anticoagulant or antiplatelet treatment.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.3.2.4 Thulium:yttrium-aluminium-garnet laser enucleation of the prostate

recommendations.statement: Offer 120-W 980 nm, 1,318 nm or 1,470 nm diode laser prostate enucleation to men with moderate-to-severe LUTS as a comparable alternative to bipolar transurethral (plasmakinetic) enucleation or bipolar transurethral resection.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.3.2.5 Diode laser enucleation of the prostate

recommendations.statement: Offer bipolar transurethral vaporisation of the prostate as an alternative to transurethral resection for surgical treatment of moderate-to-severe LUTS when prostate volume is 30-80 mL.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.3.3.1 Bipolar transurethral vaporisation of the prostate

recommendations.statement: Offer 80-W 532-nm Potassium-Titanyl-Phosphate (KTP) laser prostate vaporisation as an alternative to TURP for men with moderate-to-severe LUTS and prostate volume 30-80 mL.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.3.3.2 532 nm (‘Greenlight’) laser vaporisation of the prostate

recommendations.statement: Offer 120-W 532-nm Lithium Borat (LBO) laser prostate vaporisation as an alternative to TURP for men with moderate-to-severe LUTS and prostate volume 30-80 mL.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.3.3.2 532 nm (‘Greenlight’) laser vaporisation of the prostate

recommendations.statement: Offer 180-W 532-nm LBO laser prostate vaporisation as an alternative to TURP for men with moderate-to-severe LUTS and prostate volume 30-80 mL.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.3.3.2 532 nm (‘Greenlight’) laser vaporisation of the prostate

recommendations.statement: Offer prostate vaporisation using 80-W KTP, 120- or 180-W LBO lasers to patients on antiplatelet or anticoagulant treatment whose prostate volume is < 80 mL.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.3.3.2 532 nm (‘Greenlight’) laser vaporisation of the prostate

recommendations.statement: Offer Aquablation as an alternative to transurethral resection for patients with moderate-to-severe LUTS and prostate volume 30-80 mL.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.3.4.1 Aquablation – image guided robotic waterjet ablation: AquaBeam

recommendations.statement: Inform patients considering Aquablation about bleeding risk and the absence of long-term follow-up data.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.3.4.1 Aquablation – image guided robotic waterjet ablation: AquaBeam

recommendations.statement: Offer PAE to men with moderate-to-severe LUTS who want to consider a minimally invasive procedure and accept outcomes less favourable than those of transurethral resection.
Perform PAE only in centres where urologists carry out assessment and follow-up in collaboration with interventional radiologists trained to identify suitable PAE candidates.
Offer Prostatic urethral lift (Urolift®) to men with LUTS who wish to preserve ejaculatory function, have prostates < 70 mL and have no middle lobe.
Do not offer intraprostatic Botulinum toxin-A injections to patients with male LUTS.
recommendations.rationale: Clinical trials showed no clinical benefit over placebo for LUTS due to BPO.

recommendations.statement: Treat contributory causes of nocturia, whether behavioural, systemic, sleep-related, related to lower urinary tract dysfunction, or combined.
Discuss behavioural measures with patients to reduce night-time urine production and nocturia episodes and to improve sleep quality.
Offer desmopressin to men aged < 65 years to reduce nocturia caused by nocturnal polyuria.
Offer low dose desmopressin to men aged > 65 years who have nocturia at least twice nightly because of nocturnal polyuria.

Screen for hyponatraemia before treatment, on day three and day seven, at one month after treatment begins, and periodically thereafter; check serum sodium more often in patients aged > 65 years and those at increased risk of hyponatraemia.
Discuss the potential benefits and associated risks of desmopressin with patients, particularly men aged > 65 years.
Offer α1-adrenergic antagonists for nocturia associated with LUTS in men.
Offer antimuscarinic drugs for nocturia associated with overactive bladder in men.
Offer 5α-reductase inhibitors for nocturia in men with associated LUTS and prostate enlargement > 40 mL.
Do not offer phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors to treat nocturia.
For men with UI, obtain a comprehensive history covering symptoms, co-morbidities and medications, and perform a focused physical examination.
Assess UI with a validated symptom questionnaire, bladder diary and pad-test.
Measure post-void residual when assessing UI.
Perform urodynamics for UI if invasive treatment is being considered.
Offer patients lifestyle guidance that may improve UI, while explaining that evidence supporting these measures is lacking.
Review medications that may have contributed to the onset or worsening of UI.
Use pads and/or penile sheaths as palliative management for UI.
Use prompted voiding for patients with UI when appropriate.
Offer bladder training as an adjunctive treatment for UI.
Offer men undergoing radical prostatectomy pelvic floor muscle training, alone or with biofeedback and/or electrostimulation, to accelerate recovery from UI.
Offer antimuscarinic drugs or mirabegron to adults with urgency urinary incontinence when conservative treatment has failed.
Offer duloxetine to men with stress urinary incontinence.
Explain duloxetine’s potential adverse effects and its off-label status for this indication in Europe.
Do not offer bulking agents to men with post-prostatectomy incontinence.
Offer non-adjustable transobturator slings to men with mild-to-moderate postprostatectomy incontinence.
recommendations.context: The guideline does not define mild or moderate PPI.

recommendations.statement: Inform men that severe incontinence, previous pelvic radiotherapy or transurethral surgery may adversely affect outcomes after non-adjustable male sling surgery.
Offer an artificial urinary sphincter (AUS) to men with moderate-to-severe stress urinary incontinence.
Offer AUS or ProACT© implantation for men only at expert centres.
Warn men receiving AUS or ProACT© that cure is possible but complications, mechanical failure and explantation carry a high risk.
Do not offer the non-circumferential compression device ProACT© to men previously treated with pelvic radiotherapy.
Offer onabotulinumtoxinA (100 U) bladder wall injections when overactive bladder/urgency urinary incontinence has not responded to medical treatment.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.6.6.1 Bladder wall injection of botulinum Toxin-A

recommendations.statement: Warn patients receiving onabotulinumtoxinA about the limited duration of benefit, UTI risk and potentially prolonged need for clean intermittent self-catheterisation; confirm that they are willing and able to perform it.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.6.6.1 Bladder wall injection of botulinum Toxin-A

recommendations.statement: Offer sacral neuromodulation to patients with urgency urinary incontinence refractory to medical treatment who are willing to have surgery.
Offer augmentation cystoplasty to patients with OAB/UUI only after all other treatment options have failed and if they are able and willing to self-catheterise.
Before augmentation cystoplasty, inform patients about the high complication risk, possible need for clean intermittent self-catheterisation and requirement for lifelong surveillance.
Offer urinary diversion for OAB/UUI only to patients who have failed less invasive treatments and accept a stoma.
Start clean intermittent self-catheterisation if upper urinary tract damage is a risk or PVR exceeds > 300mL.
Offer an indwelling transurethral catheter or suprapubic cystostomy only if other approaches to urinary drainage have failed or are unsuitable.
Do not recommend parasympathomimetics routinely for men with underactive bladder.
Offer alpha-adrenergic blockers before using more invasive approaches.
Counsel patients with DU or an acontractile detrusor plus benign prostatic enlargement about the possible subjective and objective benefits of benign prostatic surgery.
Offer a test phase of sacral neuromodulation to men with DU but without benign prostatic obstruction.
Provide follow-up to every patient managed conservatively, medically or surgically.
Set the examinations and intervals for follow-up according to the treatment received.

special_populations.considerations: The visual prostate symptom score (VPSS) may provide an alternative way to assess symptoms.

special_populations.population: Men with neurological disease or previous radical pelvic surgery
special_populations.considerations: These circumstances may require a broader evaluation than the one addressed by this guideline. The document directs assessment of neurological disease to the EAU Guidelines on Neuro-Urology.

special_populations.population: Men aged < 50 years or > 80 years considering invasive treatment
special_populations.considerations: For bothersome, predominantly voiding LUTS, the guideline recommends UDS before invasive treatment with a Weak strength rating. It notes that evidence for these age-specific indications is limited.

special_populations.population: Men aged > 65 years with nocturia due to nocturnal polyuria
special_populations.considerations: Hyponatraemia is an important risk of desmopressin, particularly with increasing age. The guideline recommends more frequent serum sodium monitoring in men aged > 65 years and cautions that patients aged > 75 years were under-represented in trials.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For men aged > 65 years who void at least twice nightly, low-dose desmopressin may be offered. In men aged ≥ 65 years, it should not be used when serum sodium is below normal. Check sodium at baseline, day three, day seven, one month after starting treatment and periodically thereafter; repeat the monitoring sequence after dose escalation.

special_populations.population: Men aged < 65 years with nocturia due to nocturnal polyuria
special_populations.considerations: Potential non-urological causes, including sleep apnoea, should be assessed before prescribing desmopressin.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Desmopressin may be started at 0.1 mg/day and increased every week, if needed, to a maximum of 0.4 mg/day. It is taken before sleep; fluids should be avoided for at least one hour beforehand and eight hours afterward.

special_populations.population: Men with severe uncontrolled hypertension or specified cardiac and vascular conditions
special_populations.considerations: Mirabegron is contraindicated with severe uncontrolled hypertension, defined as systolic blood pressure ≥ 180 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure ≥ 110 mmHg, or both. Tadalafil has additional cardiovascular contraindications, including cardiac disease for which sexual activity is inadvisable, myocardial infarction within the last 90 days, and stroke within the last six months.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Measure blood pressure before and regularly during mirabegron treatment. Do not use tadalafil in patients taking nitrates or guanylate cyclase stimulators, such as riociguat, or in those meeting its stated cardiovascular contraindications.

special_populations.considerations: Exposure to α1-blockers is associated with intra-operative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS), with a particularly high reported risk for tamsulosin.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: The guideline considers it prudent not to start α1-blockers before scheduled cataract surgery and advises informing the ophthalmologist about their use.

special_populations.population: Men receiving anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy
special_populations.considerations: The document discusses bleeding and peri-operative outcomes separately for several prostate procedures. Evidence for some approaches, particularly in anticoagulated patients, is limited.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Tm:YAG laser enucleation may be offered to patients receiving anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy. Laser vaporisation using 80-W KTP, 120- or 180-W LBO lasers may be offered when prostate volume is < 80 mL.

special_populations.population: Men with prior pelvic radiotherapy and stress urinary incontinence
special_populations.considerations: Previous pelvic radiotherapy may reduce the benefit of non-adjustable male slings and adversely affect outcomes after artificial urinary sphincter implantation. ProACT® has poorer reported outcomes and more urethral erosion after radiotherapy.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Inform men that prior radiotherapy may worsen sling outcomes. Do not offer ProACT© to men who have undergone pelvic radiotherapy.

special_populations.population: Men with impaired manual dexterity or cognition
special_populations.considerations: Operating an artificial urinary sphincter pump may become difficult if dexterity or cognition declines. Clean intermittent self-catheterisation requires sufficient dexterity and cognition when performed independently, although a caregiver may perform it.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Assess the ability to operate an artificial urinary sphincter pump before implantation. For underactive bladder requiring drainage, an indwelling catheter is reserved for circumstances in which other drainage methods fail or are unsuitable.

special_populations.population: Men with detrusor underactivity or acontractile detrusor and concomitant benign prostatic obstruction
special_populations.considerations: De-obstructive surgery may improve symptoms and voiding measures, but outcomes vary. Older age, weaker contractility and lack of obstruction are associated with poorer outcomes; available long-term data suggest that benefits may not be durable.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Counsel patients with DU or acontractile detrusor and concomitant benign prostatic enlargement about the potential subjective and objective benefits of benign prostatic surgery. In severe DU with 20 ≤ BOOI < 40, TURP should be considered carefully and only after adequate counselling.

special_populations.population: Men with detrusor underactivity without benign prostatic obstruction
special_populations.considerations: Evidence for sacral neuromodulation in men with DU is scarce and comes from retrospective studies.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Offer a test phase of sacral neuromodulation to men with DU and no benign prostatic obstruction.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with uncomplicated mild-to-moderate symptoms that cause little bother.
decision_rules: Assess symptom severity and distinguish uncomplicated from complicated LUTS before selecting treatment.
Choose watchful waiting when symptoms cause little bother; reconsider treatment if bother, PVR, complications, or an indication for surgery develops.

recommended_regimens.name: Watchful waiting
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer observation with periodic review to men minimally troubled by mild-to-moderate LUTS.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Approximately 85% of men with mild LUTS remained stable at one year in one study. A separate comparison reported that 36% of the WW group proceeded to surgery within five years, while 64% continued to do well with WW.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Review at six months and annually thereafter if symptoms do not worsen and no absolute surgical indication arises.

recommended_regimens.name: Lifestyle advice and self-care
recommended_regimens.summary: Provide education and self-management information before treatment or alongside it.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In one study, three self-management sessions added to standard care improved symptoms and QoL for up to a year compared with standard care alone.

response_assessment.timepoint: six months and annually thereafter
response_assessment.method: History, bladder diary, IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry and PVR volume.
response_assessment.interpretation: Reassess the approach if symptoms deteriorate or an absolute indication for surgery develops.

supportive_care: Discuss timing of fluid intake, caffeine and alcohol moderation, relaxed or double voiding, urethral milking, urgency-control techniques, bladder retraining, medication review, assistance with functional limitations and constipation management as appropriate.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The individual components of lifestyle advice have not been studied separately.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with moderate-to-severe LUTS, particularly when a rapid pharmacological effect is desired.
decision_rules: Offer an α1-blocker for moderate-to-severe LUTS; prostate size does not determine short-term eligibility.
Explain that α1-blockers do not prevent long-term urinary retention or the need for surgery.

recommended_regimens.name: α1-blockers
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer an α1-blocker for symptom relief. Available agents named in the guideline are alfuzosin hydrochloride (alfuzosin), doxazosin mesylate (doxazosin), silodosin, tamsulosin hydrochloride (tamsulosin), terazosin hydrochloride (terazosin) and naftopidil.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Controlled studies typically reported an approximately 30-40% IPSS reduction and an approximately 20-25% Qmax increase with α1-blockers; substantial improvement also occurred with placebo.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Effects develop fully over a few weeks; reported improvements appear maintained for at least four years.

response_assessment.timepoint: four to six weeks after initiation; subsequently at six months and annually
response_assessment.method: Assess symptoms, adverse events, IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry and PVR volume.
response_assessment.interpretation: Continue treatment if symptom relief occurs without troublesome adverse events.

supportive_care: Discuss treatment-related adverse events, particularly orthostatic hypotension in older men receiving non-selective α1-blockers and EjD in sexually active men receiving selective α1-blockers.
Inform the ophthalmologist of α1-blocker use before cataract surgery.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline advises against starting an α1-blocker before scheduled cataract surgery.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with moderate-to-severe LUTS and increased risk of progression, such as prostate volume > 40 mL; elevated PSA concentration > 1.4-1.6 ng/mL is also discussed.
decision_rules: Use a 5-ARI when reducing the longer-term risk of AUR or surgery is an objective.
Account for the delayed symptom response and the effect of treatment on PSA.

recommended_regimens.name: 5α-reductase inhibitors (5-ARIs)
recommended_regimens.summary: Use dutasteride or finasteride for men with moderate-to-severe LUTS at increased risk of progression, and explain the slow onset.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: After two to four years, studies reported approximately 15-30% improvement in IPSS, 18-28% reduction in prostate volume and a 1.5-2.0 mL/s increase in Qmax among patients with LUTS due to prostate enlargement.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Clinical effects relative to placebo require at least six months; treatment is intended for years rather than short-term use.

response_assessment.timepoint: twelve weeks and six months
response_assessment.method: History, adverse events, IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry and PVR volume.
response_assessment.interpretation: Determine symptomatic response and tolerability.

response_assessment.timepoint: six months and during subsequent regular follow-up
response_assessment.method: Establish a new baseline PSA at six months; use serial PSA tests when life expectancy exceeds ten years and a PCa diagnosis could alter management.
response_assessment.interpretation: Evaluate any confirmed PSA increase during 5-ARI treatment.

supportive_care: Counsel about delayed benefit and possible sexual and breast-related adverse effects.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Finasteride may not outperform placebo for prostates < 40 mL; the guideline describes possible benefit from dutasteride at volumes between 30 and 40 mL.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with moderate-to-severe LUTS in whom bladder storage symptoms predominate.
decision_rules: Offer a muscarinic receptor antagonist for predominantly storage LUTS.
Do not use antimuscarinic overactive bladder medication when PVR is > 150 mL.

recommended_regimens.name: Muscarinic receptor antagonists
recommended_regimens.summary: Use an antagonist for predominantly storage symptoms. Licensed agents named in the guideline are darifenacin hydrobromide (darifenacin), fesoterodine fumarate (fesoterodine), oxybutynin hydrochloride (oxybutynin), propiverine hydrochloride (propiverine), solifenacin succinate (solifenacin), tolterodine tartrate (tolterodine) and trospium chloride.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Monotherapy can significantly improve urgency, UUI and increased daytime frequency.

not_recommended.name: antimuscarinic overactive bladder medications
not_recommended.reason: The guideline advises against their use when post-void residual volume is > 150 mL.

response_assessment.timepoint: four to six weeks after initiation; subsequently at six months and annually
response_assessment.method: Assess symptoms and adverse events, IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry and PVR; use a bladder diary or FVC for predominant storage symptoms.
response_assessment.interpretation: Reassess regularly and stop medication if voiding symptoms or urinary stream worsen after treatment begins.

supportive_care: Discuss possible adverse events and monitor PVR.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence in men was generally short-term, and studies enrolled patients with low baseline PVR.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with moderate-to-severe LUTS in whom bladder storage symptoms predominate.
decision_rules: A beta-3 agonist is an option for predominantly storage LUTS.

recommended_regimens.name: beta-3 agonists
recommended_regimens.summary: Use a beta-3 agonist for predominantly storage symptoms; the guideline discusses mirabegron.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Mirabegron improved frequency, urgency and UUI in the evidence reviewed.

response_assessment.timepoint: four to six weeks after initiation; subsequently at six months and annually
response_assessment.method: Assess symptoms, adverse events, IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry and PVR; use a diary or FVC to assess storage symptoms.
response_assessment.interpretation: Continue if relief is achieved without troublesome adverse events.

supportive_care: Measure blood pressure before starting mirabegron and monitor it regularly during treatment.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Mirabegron is contraindicated with severe uncontrolled hypertension, defined as systolic blood pressure ≥ 180 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure ≥ 110 mmHg, or both. Vibegron was not licensed in Europe at the time described.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with moderate-to-severe LUTS, with or without erectile dysfunction.
decision_rules: Offer a phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor regardless of whether erectile dysfunction is present.

recommended_regimens.name: phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors
recommended_regimens.summary: Use this drug class for moderate-to-severe LUTS; tadalafil 5 mg once daily is the agent licensed for this indication in the guideline.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The cited updated meta-analysis reported an IPSS mean difference of 1.89 lower than placebo (95% CI: 2.27 lower to 1.50 lower; n = 4,293). The evidence summary reports improvement in IPSS and IIEF score, but not Qmax.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: tadalafil 5 mg once daily; evidence was predominantly for treatment up to twelve weeks, with one trial followed for one year.

response_assessment.timepoint: four to six weeks after initiation; subsequently at six months and annually
response_assessment.method: Assess symptoms, adverse events, IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry and PVR volume.
response_assessment.interpretation: Continue when symptom relief is achieved without troublesome adverse events.

supportive_care: Discuss treatment-related adverse events and contraindications before prescribing.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Tadalafil is contraindicated with nitrates or guanylate cyclase stimulators such as riociguat, and in the specified cardiac, vascular and visual conditions described in the guideline. Data on disease progression are unavailable.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with LUTS who particularly wish to avoid potential adverse effects on sexual function.
decision_rules: If phytotherapy is selected on this basis, use the specifically identified hexane extract rather than assuming that findings apply to every Serenoa repens preparation.
Explain that the size of the benefit may be modest.

recommended_regimens.name: hexane extracted Serenoa repens
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer the hexane-extracted preparation to men prioritising avoidance of potential adverse events, particularly sexual adverse events.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The cited updated review reported 0.64 (95% CI: 0.98 - 0.31) fewer voids/night and an additional mean Qmax increase of 2.75 mL/s (95% CI: 0.57 - 4.93) versus placebo.

supportive_care: Tell the patient that efficacy may be modest.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Findings for hexane extracted Serenoa repens cannot automatically be transferred to extracts made by other methods or brands.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with moderate-to-severe LUTS and increased risk of progression, for example prostate volume > 40 mL, when prolonged treatment is planned.
decision_rules: Offer an α1-blocker with a 5-ARI when both symptom relief and prevention of progression are treatment goals.
Reserve the combination primarily for patients at increased progression risk, and explain its higher adverse-event rate.
Discontinuation of the α1-blocker after six months may be considered in men with moderate LUTS; severe baseline symptoms may warrant longer combination therapy.

recommended_regimens.name: α1-blockers + 5α-reductase inhibitors
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer combination treatment for moderate-to-severe symptoms with increased progression risk. Combinations discussed include dutasteride with tamsulosin and finasteride with an α1-blocker.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In CombAT, combination treatment reduced relative risks of AUR by 68%, BPO-related surgery by 71% and symptom deterioration by 41% versus tamsulosin after four years. In MTOPS, combined therapy reduced long-term clinical progression by 66% versus placebo.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Use when treatment for more than twelve months is intended.

response_assessment.timepoint: four to six weeks after initiation; subsequently at six months and annually
response_assessment.method: Assess symptoms, adverse events, IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry and PVR volume.
response_assessment.interpretation: Continue if relief is obtained without troublesome adverse events; reassess the need for the α1-blocker during prolonged treatment.

supportive_care: Counsel about adverse events associated with both drug classes and the intended long-term treatment.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Combination treatment has greater efficacy against progression than α1-blocker monotherapy but a higher frequency of adverse events.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with moderate-to-severe LUTS whose storage symptoms have not been adequately relieved by monotherapy with either drug class.
decision_rules: Add a muscarinic receptor antagonist to an α1-blocker when storage symptom relief from monotherapy is insufficient.
Do not prescribe the combination if PVR is > 150 mL.

recommended_regimens.name: α1-blockers + muscarinic receptor antagonists
recommended_regimens.summary: Use the combination after inadequate storage-symptom control with either constituent class alone.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A cited review reported a small reduction in daily micturitions after adding an antimuscarinic to an α-blocker (standard mean difference - 0.19), without a significant effect on urgency episodes.

not_recommended.name: α1-blockers + muscarinic receptor antagonists
not_recommended.reason: Do not prescribe the combination to men whose post-void residual volume is > 150 mL.

response_assessment.timepoint: during combination treatment
response_assessment.method: Measure PVR and assess storage symptoms and adverse events.
response_assessment.interpretation: Monitor for deterioration in bladder emptying.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Trials predominantly included men with low baseline PVR and were generally short.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with persistent storage LUTS despite α1-blocker monotherapy.
decision_rules: Consider adding mirabegron when storage symptoms persist, while recognising that the observed benefit in voiding frequency is small and short-term benefit remains uncertain.

recommended_regimens.name: α1-blockers + mirabegron
recommended_regimens.summary: Use mirabegron as add-on treatment for persistent storage LUTS during α1-blocker therapy.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: MATCH reported 0.52 fewer voids per day in favour of mirabegron added to tamsulosin; the between-group improvement in total IPSS was not significant. PLUS reported a mean adjusted difference of 0.39 voids per day.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Evidence cited for add-on use comes from short-term trials.

response_assessment.timepoint: four to six weeks after initiation
response_assessment.method: Assess storage symptoms, adverse events, IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS and PVR volume.
response_assessment.interpretation: Weigh the degree of symptom improvement against tolerability.

supportive_care: Check blood pressure before mirabegron and monitor it regularly.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline calls for longer follow-up to clarify the value of add-on treatment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with bothersome LUTS, particularly those wishing to improve erectile function.
decision_rules: Combination of an α1-blocker with a phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitor is an option when erectile-function improvement is also desired.
Explain that the additional clinical effect is modest.

recommended_regimens.name: α1-blockers + Phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors
recommended_regimens.summary: Use the combination for bothersome LUTS, especially when improvement of erectile function is a patient priority.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A cited meta-analysis of five RCTs reported differences versus α-blockers alone of -1.8 in IPSS, +3.6 in IIEF and +1.5 mL/s in Qmax.

supportive_care: Inform patients that the magnitude of the effect is modest and discuss treatment-related adverse events.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline states that larger studies with longer follow-up are needed.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with recurrent or refractory urinary retention, overflow incontinence, recurrent UTIs, bladder stones or diverticula, treatment-resistant macroscopic haematuria due to BPH/BPE, or upper-tract dilatation due to BPO with or without renal insufficiency; also men without adequate LUTS or PVR relief from conservative or medical treatment.
decision_rules: The listed complications are absolute indications for surgery; inadequate relief with non-surgical treatment is a relative indication.
Select the procedure according to prostate size, co-morbidities, anaesthetic suitability, patient preferences, adverse-effect priorities, available equipment and surgeon experience.

response_assessment.timepoint: four to six weeks after catheter removal
response_assessment.method: Assess IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry, erectile and ejaculatory function, PVR, treatment response and adverse events.
response_assessment.interpretation: Further reassessment is unnecessary if symptoms have improved and there are no adverse events.

supportive_care: Discuss procedure-specific adverse effects and the limited long-term trial evidence for some operations.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Individual procedures and their eligibility criteria are specified in the following pathways.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men requiring surgery for moderate-to-severe LUTS with prostate size 30-80 mL.
decision_rules: Offer bipolar or monopolar transurethral resection; the choice can reflect equipment, surgeon experience and patient preference.

recommended_regimens.name: bipolar- or monopolar-transurethral resection of the prostate
recommended_regimens.summary: Use B-TURP or M-TURP as standard surgical treatment in this prostate-size range.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A meta-analysis of twenty RCTs reported mean changes after M-TURP of +162% in Qmax, -70% in IPSS, -69% in QoL score and -77% in PVR. The evidence reviewed found comparable efficacy for B-TURP and M-TURP, with a more favourable peri-operative safety profile for B-TURP.

response_assessment.timepoint: four to six weeks after catheter removal
response_assessment.method: IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry, erectile and ejaculatory function and PVR volume.
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess symptom benefit and adverse events.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The suggested upper limit of 80 mL for M-TURP reflects Panel consensus; complication rates rise with prostate size.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men requiring surgery for moderate-to-severe LUTS with prostate size < 30 mL and no middle lobe.
decision_rules: Offer transurethral incision for an appropriately sized prostate without a middle lobe.

recommended_regimens.name: transurethral incision of the prostate
recommended_regimens.summary: Use TUIP for surgical relief of symptoms in men meeting the size and anatomical criteria.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A cited meta-analysis of six trials reported re-operation in 18.4% after TUIP versus 7.2% after M-TURP.

response_assessment.timepoint: four to six weeks after catheter removal
response_assessment.method: IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry, sexual function and PVR volume.
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess response and complications.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Compared with M-TURP, the evidence summary reports less retrograde ejaculation but more re-operation after TUIP.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with moderate-to-severe LUTS and prostate size > 80 mL who require surgery when anatomical endoscopic enucleation is unavailable.
decision_rules: Offer open prostatectomy in the absence of anatomical endoscopic enucleation.
Consider its greater invasiveness and peri-operative risk in the treatment discussion.

recommended_regimens.name: open prostatectomy
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer OP for a large prostate when anatomical endoscopic enucleation is not available.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Studies cited by the guideline reported LUTS reduction of 63-86% (12.5-23.3 IPSS points), QoL score improvement of 60-87%, mean Qmax increase of 375% (+16.5-20.2 mL/s) and PVR reduction of 86-98%.

response_assessment.timepoint: four to six weeks after catheter removal
response_assessment.method: IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry, erectile and ejaculatory function and PVR volume.
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess relief and adverse events.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: OP is described as the most invasive surgical option; its peri-operative safety is less favourable than B-TUEP or HoLEP.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with moderate-to-severe LUTS being considered for transurethral resection.
decision_rules: Tm:YAG laser vaporesection may be offered as an alternative to TURP, while recognising limited comparative mid- to long-term evidence.

alternative_regimens.name: Tm:YAG laser (ThuVARP)
alternative_regimens.summary: Offer laser vaporesection as an alternative to TURP; comparative evidence found similar IPSS but favoured TURP for Qmax at twelve months.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: When this surgical alternative is selected after discussing the limits of longer-term comparative evidence.

response_assessment.timepoint: four to six weeks after catheter removal
response_assessment.method: IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry, sexual function and PVR.
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess treatment effect and adverse events.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline states that further investigation of ThuVARP is needed.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with moderate-to-severe LUTS for whom transurethral resection is being considered.
decision_rules: Bipolar transurethral plasmakinetic enucleation is an alternative to TURP.

alternative_regimens.name: bipolar transurethral (plasmakinetic) enucleation of the prostate
alternative_regimens.summary: Offer PKEP as an alternative endoscopic operation; the guideline reports favourable mid- to long-term efficacy and peri-operative safety compared with TURP.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: When an enucleation alternative to TURP is appropriate and available.

response_assessment.timepoint: four to six weeks after catheter removal
response_assessment.method: IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry, sexual function and PVR.
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess response and adverse events.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with moderate-to-severe LUTS being considered for transurethral resection or open prostatectomy.
decision_rules: Offer HoLEP as an alternative to either operation.

recommended_regimens.name: Ho:YAG laser (HoLEP)
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer laser enucleation as an alternative to TURP or open prostatectomy.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The evidence summary reports comparable mid- to long-term efficacy to TURP, with a more favourable peri-operative profile despite longer operation times in the comparisons described.

response_assessment.timepoint: four to six weeks after catheter removal
response_assessment.method: IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry, erectile and ejaculatory function and PVR.
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess response and adverse events.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Surgeon experience strongly affects complication occurrence; mentorship programmes are advised.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with moderate-to-severe LUTS considering resection or another enucleation procedure.
decision_rules: Tm:YAG laser enucleation may be offered as an alternative to TURP, HoLEP or bipolar transurethral plasmakinetic enucleation.

alternative_regimens.name: Tm:YAG laser (ThuLEP, ThuVEP)
alternative_regimens.summary: Offer Tm:YAG laser enucleation as a surgical alternative while acknowledging the limited number of comparative RCTs.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: When an available enucleation approach is selected instead of TURP, HoLEP or bipolar transurethral plasmakinetic enucleation.

response_assessment.timepoint: four to six weeks after catheter removal
response_assessment.method: IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry, sexual function and PVR.
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess response and adverse events.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: ThuVEP lacks RCT support; the guideline calls for continued investigation of these approaches.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients receiving anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy who require prostate enucleation.
decision_rules: Tm:YAG laser enucleation may be offered in this medication-exposure setting.

alternative_regimens.name: Tm:YAG laser enucleation of the prostate
alternative_regimens.summary: Offer Tm:YAG enucleation to patients receiving anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy; the safety evidence for ThuVEP in this setting is described as suggestive.

response_assessment.timepoint: four to six weeks after catheter removal
response_assessment.method: IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry, sexual function, PVR and adverse-event review.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The recommendation is graded Weak.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with moderate-to-severe LUTS for whom bipolar transurethral plasmakinetic enucleation or B-TURP is an option.
decision_rules: Diode laser enucleation may be offered as a comparable alternative, while recognising the need for better-quality evidence.

alternative_regimens.name: 120-W 980 nm, 1,318 nm or 1,470 nm diode laser enucleation of the prostate
alternative_regimens.summary: Offer one of the specified diode-laser approaches as an alternative to bipolar plasmakinetic enucleation or B-TURP.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: When the relevant laser technique and surgical expertise are available.

response_assessment.timepoint: four to six weeks after catheter removal
response_assessment.method: IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry, sexual function and PVR.
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess response and adverse events.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline notes limited, predominantly low-quality RCT evidence and uncertainty about retreatment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men requiring surgery for moderate-to-severe LUTS with prostate volume 30-80 mL.
decision_rules: Bipolar transurethral vaporisation may be offered instead of TURP.

alternative_regimens.name: bipolar transurethral vaporisation of the prostate
alternative_regimens.summary: Offer B-TUVP as an alternative to TURP in the specified prostate-volume range; short-term efficacy is similar in the evidence reviewed.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Prostate volume 30-80 mL and selection of vaporisation rather than resection.

response_assessment.timepoint: four to six weeks after catheter removal
response_assessment.method: IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry, sexual function and PVR.
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess benefit and complications.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline states that trial heterogeneity and methodological limitations prevent firm conclusions about longer-term outcomes.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with moderate-to-severe LUTS and prostate volume 30-80 mL.
decision_rules: Offer one of the specified 532-nm laser vaporisation approaches as an alternative to TURP.

recommended_regimens.name: 80-W 532-nm Potassium-Titanyl-Phosphate (KTP) laser vaporisation of the prostate
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer vaporisation as an alternative to TURP within the specified prostate-volume range.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The guideline reports comparable short-term outcomes to TURP for the 80-W KTP laser.

recommended_regimens.name: 120-W 532-nm Lithium Borat (LBO) laser vaporisation of the prostate
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer vaporisation as an alternative to TURP within the specified prostate-volume range.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The guideline reports comparable mid-term outcomes to TURP for the 120-W LBO laser.

recommended_regimens.name: 180-W 532-nm LBO laser vaporisation of the prostate
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer vaporisation as an alternative to TURP within the specified prostate-volume range.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The guideline reports short- to mid-term outcomes comparable to TURP.

response_assessment.timepoint: four to six weeks after catheter removal
response_assessment.method: IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry, sexual function and PVR.
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess response and adverse events.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The 180-W XPS is described as the current standard PVP generator, but supporting evidence is limited, especially for large glands and long-term outcomes.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients receiving antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy who require surgery and have prostate volume < 80 mL.
decision_rules: Laser vaporisation using one of the named KTP or LBO systems may be offered in this setting.

alternative_regimens.name: 80-W KTP, 120- or 180-W LBO lasers
alternative_regimens.summary: Offer laser prostate vaporisation to eligible patients receiving antiplatelet or anticoagulant treatment.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Prostate volume < 80 mL and antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy; evidence for 180-W LBO in this population is graded 3.

response_assessment.timepoint: four to six weeks after catheter removal
response_assessment.method: IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry, sexual function, PVR and adverse-event assessment.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The recommendation is Weak, and the guideline describes low-level evidence for 180-W LBO safety in patients receiving these medications.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with moderate-to-severe LUTS and prostate volume 30-80 mL.
decision_rules: Aquablation may be offered instead of TURP, with counselling about bleeding and the limits of long-term evidence.

alternative_regimens.name: Aquablation
alternative_regimens.summary: Offer waterjet ablation as an alternative to TURP; the guideline continues to classify it as under investigation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Prostate volume 30-80 mL and acceptance of the stated uncertainties and bleeding risk.

response_assessment.timepoint: four to six weeks after catheter removal
response_assessment.method: IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry, sexual function, PVR and adverse events.
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess clinical response and bleeding-related complications.

supportive_care: Inform patients about bleeding risk and the lack of long-term follow-up data.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: In the cited WATER trial, five-year surgical retreatment was 5.1% after Aquablation and 1.5% after TURP.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with moderate-to-severe LUTS who prefer a minimally invasive option and accept outcomes less favourable than TURP.
decision_rules: PAE may be offered after discussing its comparative outcomes.
Perform selection, work-up and follow-up through collaborating urologists and appropriately trained interventional radiologists.

alternative_regimens.name: prostatic artery embolisation (PAE)
alternative_regimens.summary: Offer embolisation to men accepting less optimal outcomes than TURP; it remains under investigation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Preference for a minimally invasive option and access to the specified collaborative service.

response_assessment.timepoint: during follow-up
response_assessment.method: Urological assessment of symptoms, flow, PVR, retreatment needs and adverse events.
response_assessment.interpretation: Evaluate the response in light of PAE's less favourable symptom and functional outcomes compared with TURP in the evidence summary.
