supportive_care: Include radiation exposure in counselling for PAE.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline requires collaborative care with trained interventional radiologists and describes conflicting comparative adverse-event findings.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with LUTS who prioritise preservation of ejaculatory function, have prostate size < 70 mL and have no middle lobe.
decision_rules: Offer PUL when the specified anatomical criteria and ejaculatory-function preference apply.

recommended_regimens.name: Prostatic urethral lift (Urolift®)
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer a prostatic urethral lift to eligible men seeking to preserve ejaculation.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The guideline reports improvement in IPSS, Qmax and QoL that is inferior to TURP at 24 months; a cited multicentre study reported retreatment of 13.6% over five years.

response_assessment.timepoint: four to six weeks after catheter removal
response_assessment.method: IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry, erectile and ejaculatory function and PVR.
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess improvement and procedure-related adverse events.

supportive_care: Discuss the possibility of retreatment.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Effectiveness in large glands has not been established, and evidence for an obstructing or protruding middle lobe is limited.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men being considered for intraprostatic injection to manage LUTS.
decision_rules: Do not offer intraprostatic Botulinum toxin-A injection.

not_recommended.name: intraprostatic Botulinum toxin-A injection
not_recommended.reason: Clinical trials showed no clinical benefit over placebo for LUTS due to BPO.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline reports clinical benefits for NX-1207 versus placebo in cited trials but does not recommend it as a treatment pathway.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with nocturia, including those in whom behavioural, systemic, sleep-related or LUTD causes may coexist.
decision_rules: Identify contributing causes with symptom assessment, a validated bladder diary, medication review and evaluation for relevant medical or sleep conditions.
Treat the underlying cause or combination of causes; pursue a LUTD pathway only when LUTD is justifiably suspected to contribute.

recommended_regimens.name: behavioural changes
recommended_regimens.summary: Discuss changes intended to reduce night-time urine production and nocturia episodes and improve sleep.

response_assessment.timepoint: during diagnostic assessment and follow-up
response_assessment.method: Validated bladder diary or FVC, symptom score, directed history and assessment of relevant systemic and sleep factors.
response_assessment.interpretation: Determine whether polyuria, LUTD, a sleep disorder or a mixture contributes to nocturia.

supportive_care: Involve relevant medical specialties when systemic disease or sleep disturbance may be important.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Nocturia without substantial bother may still merit evaluation if history or examination raises concern for an underlying medical condition.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men < 65 years of age with nocturia attributable to nocturnal polyuria.
decision_rules: Consider non-urological causes before prescribing desmopressin.
Offer desmopressin to reduce nocturia and discuss its potential benefit against its risks.

recommended_regimens.name: desmopressin
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer antidiuretic treatment for nocturia caused by nocturnal polyuria.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A cited review reported -0.46 nocturnal voids versus placebo during follow-up up to three months and a change of -0.85 during follow-up from three to twelve months.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: For men < 65 years, initiate at 0.1 mg/day before sleep and, if needed, increase gradually up to 0.4 mg/day every week until maximum efficacy.

response_assessment.timepoint: baseline, day three, day seven, one month and periodically thereafter; restart this sequence after dose escalation
response_assessment.method: Serum sodium and FVC.
response_assessment.interpretation: Screen for hyponatraemia; if sodium remains normal, subsequent screening can occur every three months.

supportive_care: Avoid fluids at least one hour before and for eight hours after dosing.
Discuss the risk of hyponatraemia.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline states that desmopressin is not recommended in high-risk groups.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men > 65 years of age with nocturia at least twice per night due to nocturnal polyuria.
decision_rules: Offer low-dose desmopressin after considering non-urological causes and discussing benefit relative to risk.
Do not use low-dose desmopressin in men ≥ 65 years if serum sodium is below normal; monitor sodium more frequently in older patients and those at increased hyponatraemia risk.

recommended_regimens.name: low dose desmopressin
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer low-dose treatment for eligible older men with nocturnal polyuria.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Across cited placebo-controlled desmopressin ODT trials, clinically significant hyponatraemia occurred in 11% of men aged ≥ 65 years versus 0% of men aged < 65 years receiving 50 mcg.

not_recommended.name: low dose desmopressin
not_recommended.reason: Do not use in men ≥ 65 years when serum sodium is below normal.

response_assessment.timepoint: baseline, day three, day seven, one month and periodically during treatment; repeat the sequence after dose escalation
response_assessment.method: Serum sodium and FVC, with more frequent sodium measurement for older or higher-risk patients.
response_assessment.interpretation: Detect hyponatraemia and assess nocturia response.

supportive_care: Discuss the potentially serious risk of hyponatraemia.
Avoid fluids at least one hour before and for eight hours after dosing.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline advises particular caution for trial-under-represented patients > 75 years.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men whose nocturia is associated with LUTS, overactive bladder or an enlarged prostate, according to the treatment selected.
decision_rules: Consider medication directed at LUTD only if LUTD contributes to nocturia.
Match the medication to associated LUTS, overactive bladder or prostate enlargement.
Do not offer phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors specifically to treat nocturia.

recommended_regimens.name: α1-adrenergic antagonists
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer for nocturia associated with LUTS.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The evidence summary describes improvements in nocturnal voiding frequency and uninterrupted sleep duration as generally having only marginal clinical significance.

recommended_regimens.name: antimuscarinic drugs
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer when nocturia is associated with overactive bladder.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The evidence summary reports reduced severity of night-time urgency, while changes in overall nocturia frequency are small or non-significant.

recommended_regimens.name: 5α-reductase inhibitors
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer when nocturia accompanies LUTS and prostate enlargement > 40 mL.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The evidence summary reports reduced nocturia severity among men with at least two baseline voids per night.

not_recommended.name: phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors
not_recommended.reason: The guideline advises against offering this drug class for treatment of nocturia.

response_assessment.timepoint: during treatment follow-up
response_assessment.method: FVC or bladder diary to assess predominant storage symptoms or nocturnal polyuria.
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess whether night-time symptoms improve.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: For nocturia specifically, the effect of LUTD medications is generally small or not significantly different from placebo.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with UI; prompted voiding is appropriate particularly when a caregiver can initiate toileting.
decision_rules: Classify UI and offer conservative measures appropriate to the individual.
Review medication potentially contributing to UI and explain the limited evidence supporting lifestyle changes.

recommended_regimens.name: prompted voiding
recommended_regimens.summary: Implement caregiver-initiated toileting where appropriate.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The evidence summary reports better continence among elderly, care-dependent people.

alternative_regimens.name: bladder training
alternative_regimens.summary: Offer as an adjunctive treatment for UI.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: When a complementary behavioural approach is suitable; the recommendation is Weak.

response_assessment.timepoint: during treatment
response_assessment.method: Validated symptom questionnaire, bladder diary and pad test.
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess UI severity and change with treatment.

supportive_care: Offer lifestyle advice that may help UI while explaining the limited evidence; review drugs associated with onset or worsening of UI.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline does not establish which lifestyle measures are most effective for each UI type.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men needing symptom containment for UI.
decision_rules: Use containment when palliation is appropriate to the patient's activities and preferences.

recommended_regimens.name: pads and/or penile sheaths
recommended_regimens.summary: Use absorbent products or penile sheaths as palliative UI management.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: A cited comparison found differing practical advantages and disadvantages among containment devices, and many men preferred a combination.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men undergoing radical prostatectomy for whom faster recovery from UI is sought.
decision_rules: Offer pelvic floor muscle training alone or with biofeedback and/or electrostimulation.

recommended_regimens.name: pelvic floor muscle training
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer PFMT, with optional biofeedback and/or electrostimulation, to accelerate recovery from UI.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The cited evidence on PFMT is conflicting; subsequent reviews reported shorter time to continence recovery, while a 2015 Cochrane review found no overall benefit at twelve months after surgery.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: The guideline advises initiation as soon as possible after surgery, between seven and ten days after removal of the urethral catheter.

response_assessment.timepoint: during recovery
response_assessment.method: Assess continence and pad use.
response_assessment.interpretation: Determine the pace of continence recovery.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The evidence summary states that adding bladder training, electrostimulation or biofeedback to PFMT has conflicting evidence.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with UUI whose conservative treatment has failed.
decision_rules: Offer an antimuscarinic drug or mirabegron after inadequate response to conservative care.

recommended_regimens.name: antimuscarinic drugs
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer pharmacological treatment for UUI after conservative-treatment failure.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The evidence summary reports significant improvement in urgency, UUI and increased daytime frequency with antimuscarinic monotherapy.

recommended_regimens.name: mirabegron
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer as another pharmacological option after conservative-treatment failure.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The evidence summary describes mirabegron as superior to placebo and similarly effective to antimuscarinics for improving UUI.

response_assessment.timepoint: four to six weeks after initiation; subsequently at six months and annually
response_assessment.method: Review symptoms, adverse events, IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry and PVR.
response_assessment.interpretation: Continue treatment if benefit occurs without troublesome adverse events.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The medicine-specific cautions for antimuscarinics and mirabegron also apply.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with SUI.
decision_rules: Duloxetine may be offered, with explicit counselling about adverse events and off-label use in Europe.

alternative_regimens.name: duloxetine
alternative_regimens.summary: Offer to men with SUI; the recommendation is Weak.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: After discussing possible adverse events and the fact that this indication is off label in Europe.

response_assessment.timepoint: during treatment
response_assessment.method: Assess continence, pad use and adverse events.
response_assessment.interpretation: Reassess tolerability, given the substantial discontinuation reported in studies.

supportive_care: Inform patients about adverse events and off-label use in Europe.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: A cited review of post-prostatectomy SUI reported treatment discontinuation in 38% of cases.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men considering urethral bulking after prostatectomy.
decision_rules: Do not offer bulking agents for post-prostatectomy incontinence.

not_recommended.name: bulking agents
not_recommended.reason: The guideline advises against their use for post-prostatectomy incontinence; evidence of effectiveness is very limited and cure rates are low.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline separately discusses bulking as an option for some men unfit for more invasive treatment, but its formal recommendation excludes its use for post-prostatectomy incontinence.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with mild-to-moderate post-prostatectomy incontinence considering surgery.
decision_rules: Offer a non-adjustable transobturator sling.
Explain that severe incontinence, previous pelvic radiotherapy or previous transurethral surgery may worsen the result.

recommended_regimens.name: non-adjustable transobturator slings
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer a fixed transobturator sling for mild-to-moderate incontinence after prostatectomy.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In the cited MASTER Trial, twelve-month continence was 87% with a male sling versus 84.2% with AUS (95% CI: -11.6-4.6, PNI=0.003]), meeting that trial's non-inferiority criterion.

response_assessment.timepoint: after implantation
response_assessment.method: Assess continence, pad use, complications and patient-reported benefit.
response_assessment.interpretation: Evaluate persistent or recurrent incontinence.

supportive_care: Counsel about factors that may reduce the chance of success.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline states that the terms mild and moderate PPI remain undefined.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with moderate-to-severe SUI who can operate an implanted pump.
decision_rules: Offer AUS for moderate-to-severe SUI.
Offer implantation only in an expert centre and discuss device-related complications and possible explantation.

recommended_regimens.name: artificial urinary sphincter (AUS)
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer implantation for moderate-to-severe SUI.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A cited meta-analysis reported an overall cure rate of 56% and a reduction of -3.75 pads used per 24-hours after AUS implantation.

response_assessment.timepoint: after implantation and during device follow-up
response_assessment.method: Assess continence, pump operation, mechanical function, infection, erosion and need for revision.
response_assessment.interpretation: Identify device failure or complications.

supportive_care: Explain the need to operate the pump and the risks of complications, mechanical failure and explantation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Cognitive impairment or reduced manual dexterity may impede pump use. Prior pelvic radiotherapy may worsen outcomes, and long-term maintenance operations are common.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Selected men considering a non-circumferential compression device who have not undergone pelvic radiotherapy.
decision_rules: If ProACT© is considered, offer implantation only in an expert centre.
Do not offer ProACT© after pelvic radiotherapy.

alternative_regimens.name: ProACT©
alternative_regimens.summary: A non-circumferential compression option discussed for selected men, with substantial failure and complication concerns; the expert-centre recommendation is Weak.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Highly selected patients in expert centres without prior pelvic radiotherapy.

not_recommended.name: ProACT©
not_recommended.reason: Do not offer to men who have had pelvic radiotherapy.

response_assessment.timepoint: after implantation
response_assessment.method: Assess continence, device function, complications and need for adjustment, revision or explantation.
response_assessment.interpretation: Identify persistent incontinence or device-related harm.

supportive_care: Warn about complications, mechanical failure and possible explantation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The evidence summary associates ProACT® with high failure and complication rates, especially after pelvic radiotherapy.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with OAB/UUI refractory to medical treatment who are willing and able to perform clean intermittent self-catheterisation if needed.
decision_rules: Offer bladder-wall onabotulinumtoxinA after medical-treatment failure.
Counsel about limited response duration, UTI, urinary retention and possible prolonged catheterisation.

recommended_regimens.name: onabotulinumtoxinA
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer bladder-wall injections of onabotulinumtoxinA (100 U) for refractory OAB/UUI.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a cited RCT, 22.9% of patients receiving onabotA were fully dry versus 6.5% receiving saline.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: 100 U per injection session; response has limited duration and repeat injections may be needed.

response_assessment.timepoint: after injection
response_assessment.method: Assess UUI response, urinary retention, UTI and need for clean intermittent self-catheterisation.
response_assessment.interpretation: Determine benefit and whether treatment-related bladder-emptying problems have developed.

supportive_care: Confirm that the patient is willing and able to perform clean intermittent self-catheterisation if necessary.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Men without prior de-obstructive surgery may be more likely to require catheterisation after treatment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with UUI refractory to medical treatment who accept surgical treatment.
decision_rules: Offer sacral neuromodulation as a surgical option for refractory UUI.
Proceed to full implantation after a successful test phase.

recommended_regimens.name: sacral neuromodulation
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer staged neuromodulation to eligible patients willing to undergo surgery.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A cited meta-analysis found no significant difference from onabotA in successfully treated cases at six months (RR 0.93; 95% CI: 0.63-1.39).
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Initial test phase followed by full implantation if symptoms decrease by more than 50%.

response_assessment.timepoint: test phase
response_assessment.method: Measure change in symptoms.
response_assessment.interpretation: A reduction of more than 50% identifies candidates for full implantation.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Male representation in the cited RCTs was around 10%.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with OAB/UUI who have failed all other treatment options and can and will perform self-catheterisation.
decision_rules: Offer augmentation cystoplasty only after other options fail.
Explain the high complication risk, possible catheterisation requirement and need for lifelong surveillance.

recommended_regimens.name: augmentation cystoplasty
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer bladder augmentation to eligible patients with refractory OAB/UUI.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A cited study reported post-operative continence in 93% of patients with idiopathic detrusor overactivity after three years; evidence specifically relevant to men with idiopathic disease is limited.

response_assessment.timepoint: lifelong
response_assessment.method: Surveillance for complications and assessment of continence and catheterisation needs.
response_assessment.interpretation: Identify short- or long-term harm.

supportive_care: Counsel about complications and the potential need for clean intermittent self-catheterisation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: This is a major operation with substantial long-term risks.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with OAB/UUI who have failed less invasive therapies and will accept a stoma.
decision_rules: Offer urinary diversion only after less invasive therapies fail and the patient accepts a stoma.

alternative_regimens.name: urinary diversion
alternative_regimens.summary: A reconstructive option after less invasive treatment failure; the recommendation is Weak.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Failure of less invasive OAB/UUI therapies and acceptance of a stoma.

response_assessment.timepoint: long-term
response_assessment.method: Assess complications and the practical requirements of urinary diversion.
response_assessment.interpretation: Monitor for treatment-related harm.

supportive_care: Provide thorough pre-operative counselling and access to stoma or continence nursing expertise.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Urinary diversion is major surgery and may require lifelong use of urine bags.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with UAB, including those with sensory impairment or incomplete bladder emptying.
decision_rules: Focus initial management on symptom relief, timely drainage, complication prevention and maintaining QoL.
Consider scheduled voiding for impaired bladder sensation; double or triple voiding may be considered for bothersome frequency.
Avoid Valsalva or Credé manoeuvres in patients with poorly compliant bladders.

alternative_regimens.name: behavioural interventions
alternative_regimens.summary: Individualised scheduled voiding and emptying strategies may be attempted.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: When conservative measures are appropriate; efficacy or harm from the described emptying manoeuvres has not been established in non-neurogenic men.

response_assessment.timepoint: individualised follow-up
response_assessment.method: Assess symptoms, PVR and urinary complications.
response_assessment.interpretation: The visit interval depends on patient characteristics, treatment and complication frequency.

supportive_care: Inform asymptomatic patients at risk of UAB, including those with diabetes mellitus or a history of pelvic surgery or radiotherapy, about this risk.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline reports no high-quality randomised evidence for behavioural interventions in men with UAB.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men at risk of upper-tract damage or with PVR > 300mL.
decision_rules: Initiate clean intermittent self-catheterisation when upper-tract damage is a risk or PVR exceeds the specified threshold.
Prefer intermittent drainage over a long-term indwelling catheter when feasible.

recommended_regimens.name: clean intermittent self-catheterisation
recommended_regimens.summary: Use intermittent catheterisation for complete, timely bladder drainage when the stated risk or PVR criterion applies.

response_assessment.timepoint: individualised follow-up
response_assessment.method: Assess emptying, PVR, UTI and upper-tract concerns.
response_assessment.interpretation: Adjust follow-up to complications and the drainage approach.

supportive_care: Assess the patient's manual dexterity and cognition or identify a caregiver who can perform catheterisation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline notes that UTI risk increases after 300mls, while stating that a universally accepted maximum PVR has not been established.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men needing urinary drainage when other modalities have failed or are unsuitable.
decision_rules: Offer an indwelling transurethral catheter or suprapubic cystostomy only when other drainage methods fail or cannot be used.
If long-term indwelling drainage is necessary, prefer the suprapubic route over the urethral route.

alternative_regimens.name: indwelling transurethral catheterisation or suprapubic cystostomy
alternative_regimens.summary: Use indwelling drainage only when alternatives fail or are unsuitable; the recommendation is Weak.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Other urinary drainage approaches have failed or cannot be used.

response_assessment.timepoint: during ongoing drainage
response_assessment.method: Review UTI and catheter-related complications.
response_assessment.interpretation: Reconsider the drainage approach if complications occur.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The suprapubic route is favoured because of the risk of traumatic hypospadias with urethral catheterisation.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with UAB being considered for pharmacological management before invasive techniques.
decision_rules: Offer alpha-adrenergic blockers before more invasive approaches.
Do not routinely recommend parasympathomimetics.

recommended_regimens.name: alpha-adrenergic blockers
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer a trial aimed at reducing outflow resistance before more invasive management.

not_recommended.name: parasympathomimetics
not_recommended.reason: Do not recommend routinely: evidence of benefit for UAB is insufficient and possible serious adverse effects must be considered.

response_assessment.timepoint: individualised follow-up
response_assessment.method: Assess symptoms, emptying and PVR.
response_assessment.interpretation: Determine whether further treatment is necessary.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline describes limited evidence for alpha-adrenergic blockers and does not establish the efficacy of prostaglandins for UAB.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with DU or acontractile detrusor and concomitant benign prostatic enlargement being considered for benign prostatic surgery.
decision_rules: Counsel patients about possible subjective and objective benefits of surgery.
Weigh expected benefit carefully when obstruction is limited and DU is severe.

alternative_regimens.name: benign prostatic surgery
alternative_regimens.summary: Discuss de-obstructive surgery as an option for concomitant prostatic enlargement; the counselling recommendation is Weak.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Coexisting DU or acontractile detrusor and benign prostatic enlargement after individual assessment and counselling.

response_assessment.timepoint: post-operative follow-up
response_assessment.method: Assess symptoms, QoL, Qmax, PVR and bladder emptying.
response_assessment.interpretation: Determine subjective and objective response; the guideline notes that available long-term data suggest limited durability.

supportive_care: Discuss the possibility of a less favourable outcome with older age, lack of obstruction, concomitant DO or lower bladder contractility.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: For severe DU with 20 ≤ BOOI < 40, the guideline advises particularly careful consideration of TURP after adequate counselling.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with DU and no benign prostatic obstruction.
decision_rules: Offer a test phase of sacral neuromodulation.

recommended_regimens.name: sacral neuromodulation
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer a test phase to men with DU without BPO.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a cited retrospective series including 35 males, 51.4% responded to the first stage and qualified for full implantation; 72% of implanted male patients had favourable responses.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Test phase before any full implantation.

response_assessment.timepoint: test phase
response_assessment.method: Evaluate voiding response before full implantation.
response_assessment.interpretation: Determine candidacy for implantation.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence in men with DU or acontractile detrusor is scarce.

artifacts.title: Medical history: summary of evidence

rows: A medical and surgical history is an integral part of a patient’s medical evaluation.
A medical and surgical history aims to identify the potential causes of LUTS as well as any relevant co-morbidities and to review the patient’s current medication and lifestyle habits.

artifacts.summary: Summarises the evidential basis for taking a medical and surgical history in men with LUTS.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: History helps identify possible causes, co-morbidities and factors relevant to care.

artifacts.title: Medical history: recommendation

rows: Take a complete medical history from men with LUTS.
Strong

artifacts.summary: Specifies the recommended history-taking approach for men with LUTS.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Establishes a component of the initial clinical assessment.

artifacts.title: Symptom score questionnaires: summary of evidence

rows: Symptom questionnaires are sensitive to symptom changes.
Symptom scores can quantify LUTS and identify which types of symptoms are predominant; however, they are not disease-, or age-specific.

artifacts.summary: Describes what symptom questionnaires measure and their limitations.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Supports selection and interpretation of symptom scores.

artifacts.title: Symptom score questionnaires: recommendation

rows: Use a validated symptom score questionnaire including bother and quality of life assessment during the initial assessment of male LUTS and for re-evaluation during and/or after treatment.
Strong

artifacts.summary: Sets out when validated symptom questionnaires should be used.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Enables initial symptom assessment and subsequent evaluation of treatment.

artifacts.title: Frequency volume charts and bladder diaries: summary of evidence
artifacts.source_heading: 4.3 Frequency volume charts and/or bladder diaries

rows: Frequency volume charts (FVC) and/or bladder diaries provide real-time documentation of urinary function and reduce recall bias.
Three day FVCs provide reliable measurement of urinary symptoms in patients with LUTS similar to seven days and without losing the diagnostic accuracy.
2b

artifacts.summary: Summarises evidence on recording urinary function and the duration of FVCs.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Informs the use of diaries to characterise symptoms, particularly nocturia.

artifacts.title: Frequency volume charts and bladder diaries: recommendations
artifacts.source_heading: 4.3 Frequency volume charts and/or bladder diaries

rows: Use a bladder diary to assess male LUTS with a storage component, especially nocturia.
Strong
Tell the patient to complete a bladder diary for at least three days.
Strong

artifacts.summary: Specifies indications and a minimum duration for a bladder diary.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Helps characterise storage symptoms and nocturia before treatment decisions.

artifacts.title: Physical examination: summary of evidence

rows: Physical examination is an integral part of a patient’s medical evaluation.
Digital-rectal examination can be used to assess prostate volume and texture; however, the correlation to actual prostate volume is poor.

artifacts.summary: Summarises the role and limitations of examination and DRE.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Prevents overreliance on DRE when estimating prostate volume.

artifacts.title: Physical examination: recommendation

rows: Perform a physical examination including digital rectal examination in the assessment of male LUTS.
Strong

artifacts.summary: Specifies the examination recommended during LUTS assessment.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Guides the physical component of diagnostic evaluation.

artifacts.title: Urinalysis: summary of evidence

rows: Urinalysis (dipstick or microscopy) may indicate a UTI, proteinuria, haematuria, or glycosuria requiring further assessment.
The benefits of urinalysis outweigh the costs.

artifacts.summary: Identifies findings that urinalysis may reveal.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Abnormal urine findings can prompt assessment for other conditions.

artifacts.title: Urinalysis: recommendation

rows: Use urinalysis (by dipstick or microscopy) in the assessment of male LUTS.
Strong

artifacts.summary: Specifies the recommended use of urinalysis.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Supports detection of conditions requiring separate evaluation.

artifacts.title: Prostate-specific antigen: summary of evidence

rows: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) has a good predictive value for assessing prostate volume and is a strong predictor of prostate growth.
1b
Baseline PSA can predict the risk of AUR and BPO-related surgery.
1b

artifacts.summary: Summarises the prognostic uses of PSA in men with LUTS.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: PSA may inform prostate-related treatment planning and progression risk.

artifacts.title: Prostate-specific antigen: recommendations

rows: Measure prostate-specific antigen (PSA) if a diagnosis of prostate cancer will change management.
Strong
Measure PSA if it assists in the treatment and/or decision-making process.
Strong
Counsel patients about PSA testing and the implications of a raised PSA test.
Strong

artifacts.summary: Sets out circumstances for PSA measurement and patient counselling.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Links testing to decisions that could change management.

artifacts.title: Renal function: summary of evidence

rows: Decreased Qmax and a history of hypertension and/or diabetes are associated with CKD in patients who present with LUTS.
Patients with renal insufficiency are at an increased risk of developing post-operative complications.

artifacts.summary: Summarises associations relevant to renal assessment and operative risk.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Helps identify patients for whom renal function affects evaluation or surgery.

artifacts.title: Renal function: recommendation

rows: Assess renal function if renal impairment is suspected based on history and clinical examination, or in the presence of hydronephrosis, or when considering surgical treatment for male LUTS.
Strong

artifacts.summary: Defines circumstances in which renal function should be assessed.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Informs investigation and operative planning.

artifacts.title: Post-void residual: summary of evidence

rows: The diagnostic accuracy of PVR measurement, using a PVR threshold of 50 mL, has a PPV of 63% and a NPV of 52% for the prediction of BOO.
Monitoring of changes in PVR over time may allow for identification of patients at risk of AUR.

artifacts.summary: Reports the diagnostic limitations and potential monitoring value of PVR.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: A PVR measurement alone has limited ability to establish BOO.

artifacts.title: Post-void residual: recommendation

rows: Measure post-void residual in the assessment of male LUTS.
Strong

artifacts.summary: Specifies PVR measurement during LUTS assessment.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Provides information about bladder emptying.

artifacts.title: Uroflowmetry: summary of evidence

rows: The diagnostic accuracy of uroflowmetry for detecting BOO varies considerably and is substantially influenced by threshold values. Specificity can be improved by repeated flow rate testing.
2b

artifacts.summary: Describes the threshold-dependent accuracy of uroflowmetry.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Informs interpretation of flow measurements when assessing BOO.

artifacts.title: Uroflowmetry: recommendations

rows: Perform uroflowmetry in the initial assessment of male LUTS.
Weak
Perform uroflowmetry prior to medical or invasive treatment.
Strong

artifacts.summary: Distinguishes initial from pretreatment use of uroflowmetry.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Supports objective assessment before choosing treatment.

artifacts.title: Upper urinary tract imaging: summary of evidence

rows: Men with LUTS are not at increased risk for upper tract malignancy or other abnormalities when compared to the overall population.
Ultrasound can be used for the evaluation of men with large PVR, haematuria, or a history of urolithiasis.

artifacts.summary: Summarises upper-tract risk and potential uses of ultrasound.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Provides context for selecting imaging in men with LUTS.

artifacts.title: Upper urinary tract imaging: recommendation

artifacts.title: Figure 2: Assessment algorithm of LUTS in men aged 40 years or older
artifacts.description: Step 1: For male LUTS, assess history and sexual function, symptom score, urinalysis, physical examination and PVR; discuss PSA when a PCa diagnosis would change management. Step 2: Determine whether symptoms are bothersome and whether DRE, PSA or urinalysis is abnormal, neurological disease is suspected, or PVR is significant. Step 3: Evaluate abnormal findings under the relevant guidelines or clinical standard; consider kidney US and renal function assessment for significant PVR. Step 4: For bothersome benign bladder or prostate symptoms, use a bladder diary when storage LUTS or nocturia predominates, assess the prostate by US and perform uroflowmetry. Step 5: Plan treatment under the male LUTS treatment algorithm; consider endoscopy when it would change the surgical modality and pressure-flow studies for the indications described in the guideline.
artifacts.summary: Shows how initial findings direct further evaluation and treatment planning in men aged 40 years or older.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Connects baseline assessment, investigation of concerning findings and selection of treatment.

artifacts.title: Conservative treatment: summary of evidence

rows: Watchful waiting is usually a safe alternative for men who are less bothered by urinary difficulty or who wish to delay treatment. The treatment failure rate over a period of five years was 21%; 79% of patients were clinically stable.
1b
An additional study reported 81% of patients were clinically stable on WW after a mean follow-up of seventeen months.

Men randomised to three self-management sessions in addition to standard care had better symptom improvement and QoL than men treated with standard care alone at up to a year. Self-care management as part of WW reduces both symptoms and progression.
1b

Self-management achieved a clinically meaningful reduction in symptom severity at six months compared to usual care. There was also a small but significant additional benefit of adding selfmanagement to drug therapy.
1b

artifacts.title: α1-blockers: summary of evidence

rows: Alpha 1-blockers are effective in reducing urinary symptoms (IPSS) and increasing the peak urinary flow rate (Qmax) compared with placebo.
1a

1a
Alfuzosin, doxazosin, tamsulosin and terazosin exposure has been associated with an increased risk of IFIS.
1a
Ejaculatory dysfunction is significantly more common with α1-blockers than with placebo, particularly with more selective α1-blockers such as tamsulosin and silodosin.
1a

artifacts.title: 5α-reductase inhibitors: summary of evidence

rows: After two to four years of treatment, 5-ARIs improve IPSS by approximately 15-30%, decrease prostate volume by 18-28%, and increase Qmax by 1.5-2.0 mL/s in patients with LUTS due to prostate enlargement.
1b
5α-reductase inhibitors can prevent disease progression with regard to AUR and the need for surgery. Due to 5-ARIs slow onset of action, they are suitable only for long-term treatment (years).
1a

The most relevant adverse effects of 5-ARIs are related to sexual function, and include reduced libido, ED and less frequently, ejaculation disorders such as retrograde ejaculation, ejaculation failure, or decreased semen volume as well as breast enlargement and breast tenderness.

artifacts.title: α1-blockers plus 5α-reductase inhibitors: summary of evidence

rows: Long-term data (four years) from the MTOPS and CombAT studies showed that combination treatment is superior to monotherapy for symptoms and Qmax, and superior to α1-blocker alone in reducing the risk of AUR or need for surgery.
1b

The MTOPS study found that the risk of long-term clinical progression (primarily due to increasing IPSS) was reduced by 66% with combined therapy vs. placebo and to a greater extent than with either finasteride or doxazosin monotherapy.
1b
The CombAT study found that combination therapy reduced the relative risks of AUR by 68%, BPHrelated surgery by 71%, and symptom deterioration by 41% compared with tamsulosin, after four years.
1b
Adverse events of both drug classes are seen with combined treatment using α1-blockers and 5-ARIs.
1b

Adverse events of both drug classes are seen with combined treatment using α1-blockers and antimuscarinics.

artifacts.source_heading: 5.3.1.3 Thulium:yttrium-aluminium-garnet laser vaporesection of the prostate

rows: Laser vaporesection of the prostate using Tm:YAG laser (ThuVARP) has similar operation, catheterisation and hospitalisation times compared to TURP. ThuVARP and TURP are equivalent in terms of IPSS but not Qmax, with TURP deemed superior at twelve months follow-up. ThuVARP and TURP show similar short-term safety. Mid- to long-term results on efficacy and safety compared to TURP are very limited.

Open prostatectomy has a less favourable peri-operative safety profile compared to B-TUEP and HoLEP.

artifacts.title: Greenlight laser vaporisation: summary of evidence
artifacts.source_heading: 5.3.3.2 532 nm (‘Greenlight’) laser vaporisation of the prostate

rows: Laser vaporisation of the prostate using the 80-W KTP and the 120-W LBO laser (PVP) demonstrated higher intra-operative safety with regard to haemostatic properties when compared to TURP. Perioperative parameters such as catheterisation time and hospital stay are in favour of PVP, whereas operation time and risk of re-operation are in favour of TURP. Short-term results for the 80-W KTP laser and mid-term results for the 120-W LBO laser were comparable to TURP.
1a

Laser vaporisation of the prostate using the 180-W LBO laser (PVP) demonstrated higher intraoperative safety with regard to haemostatic properties when compared to TURP. artifacts.title: Figure 3: Treatment algorithm of male LUTS using medical and/or conservative treatment options
artifacts.description: Step 1: In male LUTS without an indication for surgery, determine whether symptoms are bothersome. If not, use WW with or without education and lifestyle advice. Step 2: If symptoms are bothersome and nocturnal polyuria predominates, provide education and lifestyle advice with or without a vasopressin analogue. Step 3: Otherwise, identify predominant storage symptoms; provide education and lifestyle advice with or without a muscarinic receptor antagonist or beta-3 agonist. Step 4: For the remaining patients, assess whether prostate volume is > 40 mL and whether long-term treatment is intended. Options shown include education and lifestyle advice with or without an α1-blocker/PDE5I, or with or without a 5α-reductase inhibitor ± α1-blocker/PDE5I. Step 5: For residual storage symptoms, consider adding a muscarinic receptor antagonist/beta-3 agonist. Patient preferences may alter these choices.
artifacts.summary: Organises conservative and medical options by bother, predominant symptom and prostate volume.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Helps tailor nonsurgical treatment to the assessed patient profile.

artifacts.title: Figure 4: Treatment algorithm of bothersome LUTS refractory to conservative/medical treatment or in cases of absolute operation indications
artifacts.description: Step 1: Consider active procedural treatment for absolute surgical indications, inadequate response to medication, or a request for active treatment without medication. Step 2: Assess high-risk status, ability to undergo anaesthesia and whether anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy can be stopped. Step 3: Stratify available approaches by prostate volume: < 30 mL, 30 – 80 mL or > 80 mL. The diagram lists TUIP and TURP for < 30 mL; TURP, laser enucleation, bipolar enucleation, laser vaporisation and PU lift for 30 – 80 mL; and open prostatectomy, HoLEP, bipolar enucleation, laser vaporisation, thulium enucleation and TURP for > 80 mL. It also displays laser vaporisation or laser enucleation, and PU lift, in branches concerning procedural risk and suitability. Its marked current standards/first choices are TUIP or TURP, TURP, and open prostatectomy or HoLEP or bipolar enucleation in their respective volume branches; other options are alternatives.

artifacts.description: Step 1: For a man presenting with UI, obtain medical history, focused examination, urinalysis, PVR and uroflowmetry. Step 5: After further failure, the diagram shows a non-adjustable transobturator sling or AUS for stress UI, with qualified roles for ProACT® or bulking agents, and sacral neuromodulation or bladder-wall onabotulinum toxin A for urgency UI. Step 6: After failure of urgency-UI interventions, consider augmentation cystoplasty or urinary diversion.

document_sections.heading: 1.1 Aim and objectives
document_sections.content: LUTS are common in adult men, substantially affect QoL and impose economic costs. These guidelines address assessment and treatment of non-neurogenic, benign male LUTS. Because the LUT functions as a unit and symptoms have multiple causes, the focus is LUTS rather than BPH; BPO is treated when obstruction substantially contributes to symptoms. Recommendations inform, but do not replace, individual clinical judgment or consideration of patient preferences and circumstances.

document_sections.heading: 1.2 Panel composition
document_sections.content: The panel brings together international expertise in urology and clinical epidemiology.

document_sections.heading: 1.4.1 Publication history
document_sections.content: The guideline was first published in 2000. Newly published research is assessed annually to inform updates. The 2025 edition reproduces the 2024 version; the next update is planned for 2026.

document_sections.heading: 1.4.2 Summary of changes
document_sections.content: The 2024 chapters were updated from the 2022 version. Changes include material on LURN-SI-10, bladder voiding efficiency, α1-blockers + Phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors, urodynamics in male urinary incontinence, an incontinence algorithm and management of underactive bladder. A recommendation on open prostatectomy and evidence statements concerning compression devices were also added.

document_sections.heading: 2.1 Introduction
document_sections.content: For the 2024 edition, the panel systematically identified and appraised relevant evidence across the guideline. Searches of Medline, EMBASE and the Cochrane Libraries covered May 1st 2021 to May 1st 2023 and English-language systematic reviews with meta-analysis, randomised controlled trials and prospective non-randomised comparative studies. Screening involved 3,608 unique records. Recommendation strength considers evidence quality, effect magnitude and certainty, benefits against harms, and patient values and preferences. Strong recommendations generally reflect higher-quality evidence and/or a favourable benefit–harm balance and preferences; Weak recommendations may reflect poorer evidence, an uncertain balance or variable preferences.

document_sections.heading: 2.2 Review
document_sections.content: The guideline underwent peer review before its 2016 publication. The newly introduced male underactive bladder section underwent peer review before publication in 2024.

document_sections.heading: 2.3 Patients to whom the guidelines apply
document_sections.content: Recommendations concern men seeking professional assessment for LUTS associated with non-neurogenic, nonmalignant conditions, including BPO, DO/OAB, urinary incontinence and nocturnal polyuria. Concomitant neurological disease, young age, or previous LUT disease or surgery may require a broader assessment outside this guideline's scope.

document_sections.heading: 3. EPIDEMIOLOGY, AETIOLOGY AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
document_sections.content: LUTS comprise storage, voiding and post-micturition symptoms. They are prevalent, troublesome, impair QoL and are strongly associated with ageing; their population burden may consequently grow. Potentially modifiable associations include metabolic syndrome. Men with moderate-to-severe LUTS may have increased major adverse cardiac event risk. Most older men have at least one symptom, often mild or minimally bothersome. Symptoms can persist, worsen or remit. Although BOO can arise as histological BPH progresses through BPE to BPO, LUTS frequently have causes unrelated to the prostate. DO/OAB, DU/UAB, urinary tract abnormalities, prostatic inflammation and non-urological conditions may contribute, often simultaneously. Acute retention denotes inability to pass urine with a painful, palpable or percussible bladder; chronic retention denotes a painless bladder remaining palpable or percussible after voiding, sometimes with incontinence. BOO describes increased detrusor pressure with reduced urinary flow during voiding and is generally diagnosed with invasive urodynamics or pressure-flow studies. BPO denotes BOO attributable to BPE; BPH specifically denotes a histological pattern. DO consists of spontaneous or provoked involuntary filling-phase detrusor contractions and is usually associated with OAB: urgency, with or without UUI, commonly accompanied by daytime frequency and nocturia without established infection or another evident cause. DU involves reduced voiding pressure and flow and can produce UAB symptoms resembling BPO. Figure 1 depicts possible contributors to male LUTS, several of which commonly coexist.

document_sections.heading: 4. DIAGNOSTIC EVALUATION
document_sections.content: Assessment helps establish diagnoses, monitor disease, estimate progression risk, plan treatment and anticipate outcomes. Its principal aims are to identify alternative causes of multifactorial male LUTS and characterise the patient's clinical profile and progression risk.

document_sections.heading: 4.1 Medical history
document_sections.content: History-taking assesses possible causes, medical or neurological co-morbidities, medicines, lifestyle and emotional or psychological factors. Discussions should incorporate the patient's perspective and explain that LUTS have no definite association with PCa. A validated self-completed symptom questionnaire helps quantify LUTS; bladder diaries or FVC are particularly useful. Sexual function should also be assessed, preferably with a validated measure such as IIEF. Evidence summaries assign LE 4 to the importance and aims of medical and surgical history. Obtain a complete history in men with LUTS (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 4.2 Symptom score questionnaires
document_sections.content: Validated scores quantify symptom burden, identify predominant symptom types and track changes during treatment, but are not specific to disease, gender or age. A systematic review comparing symptoms and questionnaires with urodynamics found no significant association between individual symptoms and questionnaire findings for diagnosing BOO. Evidence summaries grade sensitivity to change and symptom characterisation LE 3. Use a validated questionnaire covering bother and QoL at initial evaluation and during and/or after treatment (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 4.2.1 The International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS)
document_sections.content: IPSS contains eight items: seven concerning symptoms and one concerning QoL. Its categories are asymptomatic (0 points), mildly symptomatic (1-7 points), moderately symptomatic (8-19 points) and severely symptomatic (20-35 points). It does not assess incontinence, post-micturition symptoms or bother attributable to each symptom.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.2 The International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire for Male LUTS (ICIQ-MLUTS)
document_sections.content: ICIQ-MLUTS is a validated patient-completed questionnaire derived from the ICS Male questionnaire. Its thirteen items include incontinence and symptom-specific bother; it has nocturia and OAB subscales, examines male LUTS subtypes in greater detail and is available in 24 languages.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.3 Danish Prostate Symptom Score (DAN-PSS)
document_sections.content: DAN-PSS is used chiefly in Denmark and Finland. Its twelve questions, arranged in parts A and B, cover incontinence and the bother associated with individual LUTS.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.4 The Symptoms of Lower Urinary Tract Dysfunction Research Network (LURN-SI-10)
document_sections.content: LURN-SI-10 correlates strongly with IPSS while identifying additional symptoms, including incontinence and bladder pain.

document_sections.heading: 4.3 Frequency volume charts and/or bladder diaries
document_sections.content: An FVC records each void's time and volume; a bladder diary additionally captures information such as fluid consumption, pad use, activity, symptom severity or bladder sensation. They provide daytime and nocturnal frequency, total output, nocturnal urine-production fraction and individual void volumes. Measurements vary with circumstances and within individuals. Diaries are especially important for classifying nocturia mechanisms, although completing one may itself alter nocturnal frequency through a bladder-training effect. Duration should balance sampling error against adherence. A systematic review favoured at least three days; whether days must be consecutive or particular weekdays is unknown if they are representative. ICIQ-BD is the only fully validated diary. Evidence grades are LE 3 for contemporaneous recording and reduced recall bias, and LE 2b for comparable reliability and diagnostic accuracy of three-day versus seven-day FVCs. Use a bladder diary for storage-related male LUTS, particularly nocturia (Strong), and ask patients to complete it for at least three days (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 4.4 Physical examination and digital-rectal examination
document_sections.content: Examination should particularly assess the suprapubic region, external genitalia, perineum and lower limbs, and exclude urethral discharge, meatal stenosis, phimosis and penile cancer. Physical examination is part of medical evaluation (LE 4). Include physical examination and DRE when assessing male LUTS (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 4.4.1 Digital-rectal examination and prostate size evaluation
document_sections.content: DRE offers a simple assessment of prostatic size and texture but correlates poorly with actual volume (LE 3). Compared with TRUS, it underestimates volume increasingly as gland size rises, particularly above > 30 mL. One study found it sufficient to distinguish volumes > or < 50 mL. TRUS estimates volume more accurately.

document_sections.heading: 4.5 Urinalysis
document_sections.content: Initial evaluation must include dipstick testing or microscopy to identify possible UTI, microhaematuria or diabetes mellitus. Abnormal findings warrant further investigation according to relevant guidance. Evidence for its value is limited, and the diagnostic value for UTI without acute frequency and dysuria has been questioned. Urinalysis may reveal UTI, proteinuria, haematuria or glycosuria requiring assessment (LE 3); expert consensus judges benefits greater than costs (LE 4). Perform urinalysis when evaluating male LUTS (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 4.6.1 Prostate-specific antigen and the prediction of prostatic volume
document_sections.content: Pooled RCT data in men with LUTS and presumed BPO found PSA predictive of prostate volume, with AUC 0.76-0.78 across thresholds of 30 mL, 40 mL and 50 mL. For glands exceeding 40 mL, approximate PSA thresholds in men with BPH in their 50s, 60s and 70s are > 1.6 ng/mL, > 2.0 ng/mL and > 2.3 ng/mL, respectively, at 70% specificity and 65-70% sensitivity. A Netherlands community study found that PSA 1.5 ng/mL best predicted volume > 30 mL, with PPV 78%. Total and free PSA predicted TRUS volume within ± 20% in > 90% of cases. The evidence summary grades PSA prediction of prostate volume and growth LE 1b.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.2 Prostate-specific angtigen and the probability of PCa
document_sections.content: The potential advantages and harms of PSA testing to detect PCa in men with LUTS should be discussed with patients. Measure PSA if diagnosing PCa would change management (Strong), use it when it assists treatment decisions (Strong), and explain testing and the implications of an elevated result (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 4.6.3 Prostate-specific antigen and the prediction of BPO-related outcomes
document_sections.content: Serum PSA predicts prostate growth more strongly than prostate volume. Cited studies link PSA with changes in symptoms, QoL/bother and Qmax; baseline PSA predicted progression to retention, AUR and BPO-related surgery. In the Olmsted County Study, treatment risk was greater with baseline PSA > 1.4 ng/mL. Men with BPO appear to have higher PSA and larger glands; a study reported PSA PPV 68% for BPO. Elevated free PSA predicted clinical BPE independently of total PSA. Baseline prediction of AUR and BPO surgery is graded LE 1b.

document_sections.heading: 4.7 Renal function measurement
document_sections.content: Renal function can be assessed using serum creatinine or eGFR. Hydronephrosis, renal impairment and retention occur more often with signs or symptoms of BPO, although the mechanism is not conclusively established. One study found renal insufficiency in 11% of men with LUTS; symptom score and QoL did not correlate with creatinine, while diabetes mellitus or hypertension were the likeliest explanations for elevation. Another study concluded that kidney and bladder US was required only for elevated creatinine or reduced eGFR. The Olmsted County Study associated BPO signs and symptoms, but not prostate volume, with CKD. Among 2,741 consecutive patients, reduced Qmax and hypertension and/or diabetes history were associated with CKD (LE 3). Renal insufficiency increases postoperative complication risk (LE 3). Assess renal function if history or examination suggests impairment, hydronephrosis exists, or surgery for male LUTS is contemplated (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 4.8 Post-void residual urine
document_sections.content: PVR can be measured with transabdominal US, bladder scanning or catheterisation. Elevated PVR may reflect BOO, impaired detrusor function or both. At a 50 mL threshold, its BOO-prediction PPV is 63% and NPV 52% (LE 3). High PVR does not prohibit WW or drug treatment but may indicate poorer response, particularly to WW. MTOPS and ALTESS associated baseline PVR ≥ 350 mL with symptom progression. Serial PVR changes may help identify AUR risk (LE 3), particularly during antimuscarinic treatment; baseline PVR has little prognostic value for BPO-related invasive therapy during α1-blocker treatment or WW. Because results vary substantially and outcome studies are lacking, no treatment-decision threshold is established. BVE is calculated as [voided volume/total bladder capacity] × 100 and may be more reliable than PVR, especially with DU. PVR-R relates residual to BV and is defined as PVR/total BV) × 100; it may better represent emptying than PVR alone. Measure PVR in male LUTS assessment (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 4.9 Uroflowmetry
document_sections.content: Uroflowmetry is a non-invasive assessment of Qmax, voided volume, PVR and flow pattern. Prefer a voided volume > 150 mL; repeat testing is useful when volume is < 150 mL or Qmax or pattern is abnormal because Qmax varies within individuals. For BOO, Qmax 10 mL/s yielded specificity 70%, PPV 70% and sensitivity 47%; at 15 mL/s, corresponding results were 38%, 67% and 82%. BOO cannot be excluded when Qmax > 15 mL/s. Low Qmax can reflect BOO, DU or inadequate bladder filling, so flow alone cannot distinguish mechanisms. It can monitor treatment and relate symptoms to objective findings. Sound-based home prediction has shown acceptable correlation with conventional testing. Diagnostic accuracy varies with cut-offs; repetition can improve specificity (LE 2b). Perform uroflowmetry at initial assessment (Weak) and before drug or invasive treatment (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 4.10.1 Upper urinary tract
document_sections.content: Compared with the general population, men with LUTS have no increased upper-tract malignancy or abnormality risk (LE 3). Renal US avoids radiation, costs less and has fewer adverse effects than UROCT; it can characterise renal masses and assess the liver, retroperitoneum, bladder, PVR and prostate. US can evaluate large PVR, haematuria or previous urolithiasis (LE 4). Perform upper-tract US in men with LUTS (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 4.10.2 Prostate
document_sections.content: Prostate imaging can use transabdominal US, TRUS, CT or MRI; routine practice generally relies on transabdominal US or TRUS.

document_sections.heading: 4.10.2.1 Prostate size and shape
document_sections.content: Prostate size informs selection among OP, enucleation, transurethral resection, TUIP and minimally invasive interventions, and matters before 5-ARIs. Volume predicts symptom progression and complications. TRUS measures volume more accurately than transabdominal US. A median lobe can influence choice because some minimally invasive approaches may be contraindicated. Size assessment before intervention or 5-ARIs is graded LE 3. Image the prostate before drug treatment if imaging helps select the drug (Weak), and when surgery is being considered (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 4.10.3 Voiding cysto-urethrogram
document_sections.content: VCUG alone is not recommended for routine male LUTS evaluation. It may identify vesico-ureteral reflux, diverticula or urethral disease and may be combined with urodynamics. Retrograde urethrography may help investigate suspected stricture.

document_sections.heading: 4.11 Urethrocystoscopy
document_sections.content: Men with LUTS and a history of microscopic or gross haematuria, urethral stricture or bladder cancer should undergo urethrocystoscopy during diagnostic evaluation (LE 3). Assess a middle lobe endoscopically if it could affect an intervention such as Urolift. In a study of 122 patients, normal preoperative Qmax occurred in 25% of 60 without trabeculation, 21% of 73 with mild trabeculation and 12% of 40 with marked trabeculation; all 21 with diverticula had reduced Qmax. A separate study of 39 symptomatic men aged 53-83 years found no significant correlation between trabeculation grade I to IV and Qmax. Among 492 older men, cystoscopic appearance correlated with urodynamic indices, DO and low compliance, yet 15% with normal cystoscopy had BOO and 8% with severe trabeculation were unobstructed. No study established a strong endoscopy–urodynamics association (LE 3). Perform urethrocystoscopy before minimally invasive or surgical treatment when results could change treatment (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 4.12 Urodynamics
document_sections.content: Filling cystometry and PFS are commonly used invasive investigations. They help identify LUTS mechanisms and adverse-outcome risks and support shared decisions; DO, low compliance, BOO/BPO and DU are generally defined urodynamically. Because testing is invasive, it is usually considered after conservative and medical treatment fail. Prior neurological disease, including previous radical pelvic surgery, requires assessment under neuro-urology guidance.

document_sections.heading: 4.12.1 Diagnosing bladder outlet obstruction
document_sections.content: PFS identifies BOO through increased detrusor pressure and reduced flow, distinguishing it from DU, where both pressure and flow are reduced. The BOO calculation is pdetQmax - 2Qmax: BOO > 40 is obstructed, BOO 20-40 equivocal and BOO < 20 unobstructed. BCI is PdetQmax + 5Qmax: BCI > 150 indicates strong contractility, 100-150 normal and < 100 weak. DO was identified in 61% of men whose LUTS were attributed to BPO and independently related to BOO grade and age. Reported DU prevalence in men with LUTS is 11-40%. Contractility does not appear to decline during long-term BOO or improve after relief of obstruction. In the UPSTREAM non-inferiority RCT at 26 English hospitals, surgery occurred in 153/408 (38%) with UDS versus 138/384 (36%) with routine care; 428 adverse events and eleven unrelated deaths were recorded. UDS was non-inferior for IPSS but did not significantly reduce surgery; investigators considered routine UDS of uncomplicated LUTS of limited value. A prospective surgical cohort found significantly worse twelve-month postoperative Qmax in DU alone with BCI < 100 and BOOI < 40 than in DU with BOO or BOO alone. UPSTREAM exploratory analysis suggested greater surgical benefit with IPSS > 16, age < 74 yr, Qmax < 10 mL/s, BOO index > 47.6 and BCI > 123. The panel found limited evidence for age-specific indications and no consensus for surgery candidates with predominantly voiding LUTS and Qmax > 10 mL/s; when Qmax < 10 mL/s, BOO is likely and UDS may be unnecessary. UDS requires rigorous quality control. PFS should not routinely precede prostate surgery for everyone (LE 3). Use UDS selectively before invasive treatment or when further pathophysiological assessment is needed (Weak); perform it after unsuccessful invasive LUTS treatment before another invasive procedure (Weak), when candidates cannot void > 150 mL (Weak), when surgical candidates have bothersome predominantly voiding LUTS with Qmax > 10 mL/s (Weak), when invasive-treatment candidates with those symptoms have PVR > 300 mL (Weak), and in such candidates aged > 80 years (Weak) or < 50 years (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 4.12.2 Videourodynamics
document_sections.content: Videourodynamics adds anatomical and functional detail and may be recommended if needed to understand an individual's LUTS mechanism. Evidence supporting imaging added to UDS is low-level.

document_sections.heading: 4.13.1 Prostatic configuration/intravesical prostatic protrusion
document_sections.content: TRUS-derived PCAR describes how nearly circular the transverse prostate image is; values approach one with increasing circularity. PCAR > 0.8 diagnosed BPO with sensitivity 77% and specificity 75%. Suprapubic US measures IPP between the median-lobe tip and bladder neck with bladder volume 150-250 mL: grade I is 0-4.9 mm, grade II 5-10 mm and grade III > 10 mm. IPP correlated with BOO at PPV 94% and NPV 79%. A systematic review reported BOO-detection sensitivity 0.71 and specificity 0.77 at > 10mm. IPP may correlate with volume, DO, compliance, detrusor pressure, BOO index and PVR, and negatively with Qmax. For unsuccessful TWOC after AUR, sensitivity and specificity at > 10mm were 0.51 and 0.79. Observer variability and learning-curve data are unavailable; replacing PFS with IPP remains under evaluation.

document_sections.heading: 4.13.2 Bladder/detrusor wall thickness and ultrasound-estimated bladder weight
document_sections.content: BWT spans mucosa to adventitia; DWT measures the intervening detrusor. A study found anterior BWT 5 mm at bladder filling 150 mL best separated BOO from non-BOO. Anterior DWT > 2 mm at filling > 250 mL had PPV 94%, specificity 95% and 89% agreement with PFS. DWT thresholds 2.0, 2.5 and 2.9 mm identified 81%, 89% and 100% of BOO patients, respectively; meta-analytic sensitivity and specificity were 71% and 88%. Studies generally found BWT/DWT more accurate than free-flow Qmax or Qave, PVR, prostate volume or symptom severity, although one study without standardised bladder filling found no BWT difference across normal UDS, BOO and DO. Measurement lacks standardisation and evidence identifying the preferable measure; BWT/DWT is therefore not recommended in routine male LUTS diagnosis. UEBW identified BOO with accuracy 86% at 35 g; severe LUTS with UEBW > 35 g predicted prostate/BPO surgery during α-blocker therapy.

document_sections.heading: 4.13.3 Non-invasive pressure-flow testing
document_sections.content: PCT interrupts flow to estimate isovolumetric bladder pressure and has shown promising repeatability and interobserver agreement. A systematic review and meta-analysis reported BOO-detection sensitivity 0.85, specificity 0.78, PPV 0.74 and NPV 0.87, but obstruction definitions differed markedly. External-condom results correlated with invasive PFS in a high proportion. Resistive index and prostatic urethral angle remain experimental.

document_sections.heading: 4.13.4 The diagnostic performance of non-invasive tests in diagnosing bladder outlet obstruction in men with LUTS compared with pressure-flow studies
document_sections.content: A systematic review of 42 studies evaluated PCT, uroflowmetry, DWT/BWT, bladder weight, external-condom methods, IPP, Doppler US, prostate dimensions and near-infrared spectroscopy against invasive assessment. Most studies were prospective cohorts examining BOO rather than specifically BPO. Despite generally low risk of bias, varying BOO thresholds and definitions and few studies per test limited inference; sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV varied considerably (LE 1a). Invasive urodynamics remains preferred. Combining tests and clinical parameters might improve accuracy, but evidence is limited; a proposed BWT, prostate-volume and PVR-ratio model reported accuracy 0.82. Do not substitute non-invasive tests for urodynamics/PFS to diagnose male BOO (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 4.14.1 Visual prostate symptom score
document_sections.content: VPSS correlated positively with IPSS in prospective testing and may be an option for men with limited literacy.

document_sections.heading: 4.14.2 Micro-RNA
document_sections.content: Research suggests miR-221 may have potential as a biomarker and therapeutic target in early BPH diagnosis and treatment.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.1 Watchful waiting
document_sections.content: Assess men formally before choosing treatment to establish severity and distinguish uncomplicated from complicated LUTS. WW is viable when symptoms cause little bother: progression to AUR or complications is uncommon and symptoms may remain stable for years. One study found approximately 85% of men with mild LUTS stable after one year. In a comparison involving moderate LUTS, TURP improved flow and PVR particularly in those with marked bother; 36% of WW participants underwent surgery within five years, while 64% remained well with WW. Increasing bother and PVR predicted WW failure. An evidence summary reported five-year failure 21% and clinical stability 79% (LE 1b); another study found 81% stable after a mean seventeen months (LE 2). Offer WW for mild/moderate symptoms causing minimal bother (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.1.2 Behavioural and dietary modifications
document_sections.content: Conservative care commonly combines education, reassurance, monitoring and lifestyle measures: adjust fluid timing; limit caffeine or alcohol; use relaxed and double voiding; milk the urethra for post-micturition dribble; employ distraction for OAB; retrain bladder capacity and voiding intervals; review medicines, particularly diuretics; assist impaired mobility, dexterity or cognition; and treat constipation. Self-management within WW can reduce symptoms and progression. In a study, three additional self-care sessions improved symptoms and QoL over standard care for up to a year (LE 1b). A systematic review found significantly reduced IPSS at six months versus usual care, a reduction resembling that of drugs at six to twelve weeks, and a smaller additional benefit when combined with drugs at six weeks (LE 1b). Offer lifestyle and self-care advice before or alongside treatment (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.1.3 Practical considerations
document_sections.content: Individual self-management components have not been separately studied. Lifestyle suggestions arose from formal consensus; additional research is needed.

document_sections.heading: 5.2.1 α1-Adrenoceptor antagonists (α1-blockers)
document_sections.content: α1-blockers inhibit noradrenaline-mediated prostatic smooth-muscle activity to reduce tone and BOO, although their small effect on measured outlet resistance and poor correlation between symptom relief and obstruction suggest other mechanisms. Receptors elsewhere, receptor subtypes and vascular or central effects may contribute. Available drugs are alfuzosin hydrochloride (alfuzosin), doxazosin mesylate (doxazosin), silodosin, tamsulosin hydrochloride (tamsulosin), terazosin hydrochloride (terazosin) and naftopidil. Formulations differ in pharmacokinetics and tolerability but appear to have negligible efficacy differences; appropriately dosed agents have similar efficacy. Full effects take weeks, though placebo-adjusted benefit may begin within hours to days. Controlled studies generally report IPSS reduction approximately 30-40% and Qmax increase approximately 20-25%; open-label studies report improvement up to 50% and up to 40%, respectively. Storage and voiding symptoms improve. Prostate size has little effect over less than one year, although smaller glands (< 40 mL) may respond better longer term; efficacy is similar across ages. In pooled trials, silodosin 8 mg improved IPSS domains and QoL similarly across severity groups. These agents do not shrink the prostate or prevent long-term AUR, although alfuzosin, tamsulosin and silodosin may improve resolution of existing AUR; IPSS and Qmax benefits appear sustained at least four years. Common adverse effects are asthenia, dizziness and orthostatic hypotension. Vasodilation is more pronounced with doxazosin and terazosin, less common with alfuzosin and tamsulosin, and may particularly affect patients with cardiovascular co-morbidity or vasoactive drugs. Silodosin-associated hypotension resembles placebo. In men aged > 66 years, a retrospective cohort found falls OR 1.14 and fractures OR: 1.16; a population study linked long-term α-blockers to heart failure HR: 1.22, especially nonselective agents. A study of 24,602 dementia cases and 98,397 controls found no significant association with dementia. IFIS risk rises with exposure to alfuzosin, doxazosin, tamsulosin or terazosin (LE 1a), especially tamsulosin; avoid starting an α1-blocker before scheduled cataract surgery and inform the ophthalmologist. A systematic review found no adverse effect on libido or ED but abnormal ejaculation OR: 7.53. EjD was more frequent than placebo (OR: 5.88), particularly with tamsulosin (OR: 8.57) and silodosin (OR: 32.5); doxazosin and terazosin had lower reported risks (OR: 0.80 and 1.78). Younger age may increase susceptibility, and EjD reflects reduced or absent ejaculate rather than necessarily retrograde ejaculation. Greater urinary response correlated with EjD. Efficacy versus placebo and vascular-event and EjD findings are graded LE 1a. α1-blockers are usually first-line drugs because they act rapidly and are effective with generally limited adverse effects, but they do not avert retention or surgery. Counsel older recipients of nonselective agents about hypotension and sexually active recipients of selective agents about EjD. Offer α1-blockers for moderate-to-severe LUTS (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.2.2 5α-reductase inhibitors
document_sections.content: 5α-reductase converts testosterone to DHT; type 1 predominates in skin and liver, type 2 in prostate. Finasteride inhibits type 2, while dutasteride inhibits both. Epithelial apoptosis reduces prostate volume about 18-28% and circulating PSA about 50% after six to twelve months. Continuous finasteride and dutasteride reduce serum DHT approximately 70% and 95%, respectively, and both reduce prostatic DHT 85-90%. Relative clinical benefit emerges after at least six months. Over two to four years, 5-ARIs improve IPSS approximately 15-30%, reduce volume 18-28% and increase Qmax 1.5-2.0 mL/s in enlargement-associated LUTS (LE 1b); available comparisons suggest similar efficacy for dutasteride and finasteride. Benefit depends on baseline size: finasteride may not outperform placebo below < 40 mL, whereas dutasteride appears beneficial at 30 to 40 mL. Larger baseline volume or PSA predicts earlier, greater dutasteride benefit relative to tamsulosin. Unlike α1-blockers, 5-ARIs reduce long-term (> 1 year) AUR and surgery risk (LE 1a). Against placebo at four years, PLESS attributed to finasteride AUR relative-risk reduction 57% and surgery reduction 55%, with absolute reductions 4% and 7%; MTOPS reported 68% and 64%, with absolute reductions 2% and 3%. A pooled analysis at two years found reductions 57% for AUR and 34% for surgery, each with absolute reduction 2%. Dutasteride also reduces these outcomes. Finasteride might reduce operative bleeding, but clinically meaningful evidence is mixed. Adverse effects include reduced libido, ED, ejaculation changes and gynaecomastia with tenderness in 1-2% (sexual and breast effects: LE 1b). Studies suggested more high-grade cancers without proven causality. Population studies found no increased cardiovascular association; another found more type II diabetes with 5-ARIs versus tamsulosin, without a dutasteride–finasteride difference. A Swedish study reported depression HR 1.61 with finasteride and HR 1.68 with dutasteride, without a long-term dementia or suicide association. Consider 5-ARIs for moderate-to-severe LUTS with enlargement (> 40 mL) and/or PSA > 1.4-1.6 ng/mL; they are unsuitable for brief treatment, and PSA suppression matters for PCa screening. Use them when progression risk is increased, for example prostate volume > 40 mL (Strong), and explain the slow onset (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.2.3 Muscarinic receptor antagonists
document_sections.content: Acetylcholine stimulates detrusor muscarinic receptors; M2 and M3 predominate, with M3 more important functionally for contraction. Other tissues and central mechanisms may contribute to antimuscarinic effects. Licensed agents for OAB/storage symptoms are darifenacin hydrobromide (darifenacin), fesoterodine fumarate (fesoterodine), oxybutynin hydrochloride (oxybutynin), propiverine hydrochloride (propiverine), solifenacin succinate (solifenacin), tolterodine tartrate (tolterodine) and trospium chloride. Previous reliance on female studies does not establish that male LUTS require exclusively prostate-directed treatment. In pooled data, fesoterodine 8 mg surpassed tolterodine ER 4 mg for severe urgency episodes/24 hours and OAB-q bother at week twelve, with retention around 2%. Most male monotherapy studies lasted twelve weeks. Tolterodine improved selected urgency, frequency and UUI measures; solifenacin improved perceived bladder condition; fesoterodine improved frequency, urgency and UUI. In TIMES, tolterodine ER improved UUI episodes per 24 hours at week twelve versus placebo but not urgency, total IPSS or QoL significantly.
