Men with PSA < 1.3 ng/mL may respond more; studies also report benefit with concomitant BPO. Monotherapy improves urgency, UUI and daytime frequency (LE 2). Approximately 3-10% discontinue trials, similarly to placebo. Reported adverse events include dry mouth up to 16%, constipation up to 4%, voiding difficulty up to 2%, nasopharyngitis up to 3% and dizziness up to 5%. In men without BOO, fesoterodine 8 mg increased PVR +20.2 mL versus placebo -0.6 mL and fesoterodine 4 mg +9.6 mL. Retention with tolterodine was 0-1.3% versus placebo 0-1.4%; symptoms with fesoterodine 8 mg occurred in 5.3% versus 0.8% for both placebo and 4 mg, mainly within the first two weeks and at age 66 years or older. In mild-to-moderate BOO, a twelve-week tolterodine study found PVR 49 mL versus 16 mL but AUR 3% in both arms. Increased PVR can occur, while acute retention is rare with baseline PVR < 150 mL (LE 2). Long-term male studies and testing in all older groups are lacking; baseline PVR in trials was low. Prescribe cautiously, reassess symptoms and PVR, and advise stopping if voiding or stream worsens. Use muscarinic receptor antagonists for moderate-to-severe predominantly storage LUTS (Strong); do not use antimuscarinic OAB medication when PVR > 150 mL (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.2.4 Beta-3 agonist
document_sections.content: Beta-3 receptor stimulation is thought to relax detrusor muscle, but the full mechanism remains uncertain. Mirabegron 50 mg is approved for adult OAB. Trials, predominantly in women, found improvements in frequency, urgency, UUI and perceived benefit; a meta-analysis of eight RCTs including 10,248 patients (27% male) also found significantly improved nocturia versus placebo and tolterodine. In men, mirabegron 25 mg daily improved satisfaction and QoL, whereas validated symptom scores improved only without obstruction. Combination studies with solifenacin included mixed populations without separate male results. A small RCT reported significant IIEF-15 and IPSS improvement with Mirabegron + Doxazosin in concurrent BPO and ED, requiring larger confirmation. Common mirabegron adverse events include hypertension, UTI, headache and nasopharyngitis. It is contraindicated at uncontrolled systolic pressure ≥ 180 mmHg or diastolic pressure ≥ 110 mmHg; measure blood pressure before and regularly during treatment. Across thirteen studies with 13,396 patients (25% male), OAB drugs were not associated with greater hypertension or cardiovascular events versus placebo. Urodynamic assessment found no adverse effect on Qmax, detrusor pressure or BCI and only small overall PVR change. Studies suggest favourable tolerability in older adults, although male-specific long-term evidence is lacking. In an eighteenweek study of 3,527 patients (23% male), adverse events were 40% for solifenacin 5 mg plus mirabegron 25 mg and 32% for mirabegron 25 mg; retention was < 1% but somewhat more frequent with combination, which also slightly increased PVR. Among 21,996 patients (30% male), median discontinuation occurred at 169 days with mirabegron, 56 days with tolterodine and 30-78 days with other antimuscarinics, without a gender difference. EMPOWUR found once-daily vibegron 75 mg improved frequency, urgency and UUI versus placebo, but 85% of participants were women and vibegron was not licensed in Europe. Mirabegron improvement of storage symptoms is graded LE 2 and longer persistence LE 3. Use beta-3 agonists for moderate-to-severe predominantly storage LUTS (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.2.5 Phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors
document_sections.content: PDE5Is increase intracellular cyclic guanosine monophosphate and reduce detrusor, prostatic and urethral smooth-muscle tone; effects on neural pathways, perfusion and inflammation are possible, but the precise LUTS mechanism is uncertain. Only tadalafil 5 mg once daily is licensed for male LUTS. RCTs found reduced IPSS and storage and voiding symptoms and better QoL; Qmax generally did not significantly differ from placebo. A Cochrane analysis of sixteen RCTs reported a small placebo-relative IPSS change (MD 1.89 lower; 95% CI: 2.27 lower to 1.50 lower; n = 4,293), with no IPSS difference versus α1-blockers. Most evidence extends only to twelve weeks. Other meta-analyses found better IPSS and IIEF but inconsistent Qmax benefit; a meta-regression suggested greatest benefit in younger men with lower body mass index and more severe symptoms. Across four trials, ≥ 25% IPSS improvement occurred in 60% receiving tadalafil 5 mg and 44% receiving placebo; maximum trial duration was 52 weeks. Pooled analyses found benefit across baseline severity, age, prior treatments, testosterone and predicted volume; benefit in cardiovascular-risk patients did not extend to those taking more than one antihypertensive. In sexually active men > 45 years, tadalafil improved both LUTS/BPH and ED. One analysis attributed 92.5% of IPSS benefit directly and 7.5% indirectly through erectile improvement. Another found a small significant Qmax increase without PVR change. At twelve weeks, pooled tadalafil data did not show superiority over placebo for IPSS in men ≥ 75 years, unlike men < 75 years. In an open-label study of 71, BOO index changed from 61.3 to 47.1, DO resolved in fifteen (38%) of 38, flow rose from 7.1 to 9.1 mL/s and mean IPSS fell from 18.2 to 13.4. In a twelve-week RCT, tadalafil 20 mg did not significantly change measured urodynamics versus placebo. A study suggested solifenacin, tadalafil and dutasteride together could be effective and safe after previous treatment failure in OAB with LUT obstruction. Reported PDE5I adverse effects include flushing, reflux, headache, dyspepsia, back pain and nasal congestion. Tadalafil is contraindicated with nitrates or guanylate cyclase stimulators such as riociguat, when sexual activity is inadvisable because of cardiac disease, and with myocardial infarction within the last 90 days, unstable or intercourse-related angina, New York Heart Association Class 2 or greater heart failure in the last six months, uncontrolled arrhythmia, hypotension < 90/50 mm Hg, uncontrolled hypertension, stroke within the last six months or relevant anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy. Experience beyond one year is insufficient, evidence on gland shrinkage is limited and progression data are unavailable. Significant improvement of IPSS and IIEF but not Qmax is graded LE 1a. Use phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors for moderate-to-severe LUTS with or without ED (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.2.6 Plant extracts – phytotherapy
document_sections.content: Herbal preparations can contain one or multiple plant ingredients. Proposed compounds and in-vitro actions are varied; in-vivo effects and exact mechanisms remain uncertain. Products from the same plant may differ across manufacturers and batches, so results cannot be extrapolated between extracts without considering extraction methods and active content. Regulatory standards are heterogeneous. The HMPC distinguishes well-established from traditional use; Table 1 lists EU herbal monographs and their indications. Only hexane extracted Serenoa repens (HESr) received HMPC support for well-established use. A meta-analysis of 30 RCTs involving 5,222 men over four to 60 weeks found no benefit from pooled S. repens products versus placebo and no superiority over finasteride or tamsulosin for IPSS, Qmax or size, although similar active-treatment results might indicate equivalence; different extract types were pooled. A separate systematic review of twelve HESr RCTs found greater nocturia and Qmax improvement than placebo in enlarged prostates and LUTS improvements similar to tamsulosin or short-term finasteride. An updated review of fifteen RCTs and twelve observational studies reported versus placebo 0.64 (95% CI: 0.98 - 0.31) fewer voids/night and Qmax increase 2.75 mL/s (95% CI: 0.57 - 4.93); versus α-blockers, IPSS WMD 0.57; 95% CI: 0.27 - 1.42, and versus tamsulosin, Qmax WMD 0.02; 95% CI: 0.71 - 0.66. IPSS efficacy resembled 5-ARIs after six months; mean baseline-to-follow-up IPSS improvement was 5.73 points (95% CI: 6.91 - 4.54). A network meta-analysis incorporating only two HESr RCTs found no clinically meaningful short-term benefit for S. repens versus placebo or α1-blockers, but suggested benefit with prolonged use and greater IPSS improvement for HESr than other extracts. HESr gastrointestinal effects averaged 3.8%, with limited sexual impact (LE 2). In a cross-sectional comparison after at least twelve months (mean 13.5 months), clinically meaningful IPSS improvement occurred in 69.9% receiving HESr plus silodosin versus 30.1% with silodosin alone; improvement > 25% occurred in 68.8% versus 31.2%. This suggests, but does not establish, combination benefit. Trials use differing endpoints; combination studies and identification of likely responders are needed. HESr-associated Qmax and nocturia benefits versus placebo are graded LE 2. Offer HESr to men with LUTS seeking to avoid possible adverse effects, particularly sexual effects (Weak), and explain that efficacy may be modest (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.2.7.1 α1-blockers + 5α-reductase inhibitors
document_sections.content:
Combination treatment pairs the rapid symptom effect of an α1-blocker with the slower, months-long action of a 5-ARI. Trials have assessed finasteride with alfuzosin, terazosin or doxazosin, and dutasteride with tamsulosin. Early six- to twelve-month studies found α1-blockers more effective than finasteride for symptoms and no superiority of combination over α1-blocker alone. At four years, MTOPS and CombAT found combination superior to either monotherapy for symptoms and Qmax and to α1-blocker alone for prevention of AUR or surgery (LE 1b). CombAT found symptom and flow advantages from month nine and advantages for AUR and surgery after eight months. After tamsulosin was stopped following six months of treatment with dutasteride, almost three quarters reported no symptom worsening; baseline IPSS > 20 may justify longer combination treatment. After nine months of combination followed by finasteride alone, IPSS differences were 1.24 at three months and 0.4 at nine months; short study duration and post-discontinuation follow-up limit interpretation. Both MTOPS and CombAT favoured combination for clinical progression, defined to include IPSS increase of at least four points, AUR, UTI, incontinence or creatinine increase > 50%. MTOPS reported a 66% long-term progression-risk reduction with combination versus placebo, compared with 34% for finasteride and 39% for doxazosin alone (LE 1b); finasteride-containing treatment, but not doxazosin alone, significantly reduced AUR and BPO-related surgery over four years. At four years, CombAT found combination versus tamsulosin reduced relative risks of AUR 68%, BPO-related surgery 71% and symptom deterioration 41% (LE 1b). Treating thirteen patients for four years prevented one retention and/or surgery event versus tamsulosin, with absolute risk reduction 7.7%. In the two-year CONDUCT RCT involving 742 patients, fixed-dose dutasteride plus tamsulosin was compared with WW allowing later tamsulosin; both groups received lifestyle advice. At 24 months, IPSS differences were 5.4 in the active arm and 3.6 in the comparator arm. Combination reduced relative clinical-progression risk 43.1%, with absolute reduction 11.3% and NNT = 9. At 48 months, CombAT found consistent symptom advantages over tamsulosin across assessed baseline variables. A large RCT also evaluated finasteride plus tadalafil 5 mg against finasteride alone. Combined treatment produces adverse effects of both classes (LE 1b), more frequently than monotherapy; MTOPS found more treatment-related adverse events during the first year, and a meta-analysis found three-fold higher EjD risk than with either monotherapy. Reserve combination principally for moderate-to-severe LUTS with progression risk indicated by larger gland, higher PSA, older age, greater PVR or lower Qmax. It is intended for long-term treatment, more than twelve months; α1-blocker withdrawal after six months may be considered in moderate LUTS. Offer α1-blocker plus 5α-reductase inhibitor to men with moderate-to-severe LUTS and increased progression risk, for example prostate volume > 40 mL (Strong).

The CombAT study found that, after four years, combination therapy reduced relative risks versus tamsulosin by 68% for AUR, 71% for BPH-related surgery and 41% for symptom deterioration (LE 1b). Adverse effects characteristic of both α1-blockers and 5-ARIs occur with the combination (LE 1b). Offer this combination to men with moderate-to-severe LUTS and increased progression risk, such as prostate volume > 40 mL (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.2.7.2 α1-blockers + muscarinic receptor antagonists
document_sections.content: This combination targets α1-adrenoceptors and muscarinic receptors; not every possible pairing has been tested. Trials lasting four to twelve weeks assessed initial treatment for OAB with presumed BPO and add-on treatment for persistent storage symptoms. Compared with α1-blockers or placebo, benefits for urgency, UUI, frequency, nocturia and IPSS are marginal, although QoL improves. A review of six studies in treatment-naïve men and five in men with persistent symptoms found a small reduction in daily voids (standard mean difference - 0.19), no significant reduction in urgency episodes and more adverse effects. A Cochrane review found small improvements versus α-blocker alone in IPSS (mean difference 2.04) and QoL (mean difference 0.71), with moderate to very low certainty. Tolterodine alone mainly benefited men with PSA < 1.3 ng/mL, whereas combination-related symptom improvement was seen irrespective of PSA. A meta-analysis of sixteen studies involving 3,548 patients with BPH/OAB found no difference in total IPSS or Qmax with initial combination treatment. Benefit is chiefly apparent in moderate-to-severe storage LUTS; reported benefit persisted for up to one year. In men with storage and voiding symptoms and PVR < 150 mL, symptom reduction produced patient-relevant QoL improvement versus placebo or α1-blocker alone. A trial found combined behavioural and drug therapy better than drug therapy alone for OAB symptoms, but not better than behavioural therapy alone. Adverse effects of both classes occur; dry mouth is most common, and dry mouth or ejaculation failure may exceed what would be expected from the separate drugs. PVR may rise, generally without clinical importance, and AUR risk remained low through one year; Qmax did not clearly deteriorate. An RCT of solifenacin 6 mg or 9 mg with tamsulosin found non-inferior primary urodynamic results versus placebo and higher Qmax. Trials were generally brief, emphasised storage endpoints and enrolled men with low baseline PVR; monitor PVR during combination treatment. The evidence summaries grade QoL improvement and reductions in storage outcomes or IPSS as LE 2, combined adverse effects as LE 1, and low AUR risk when PVR < 150 mL as LE 2. Use the combination when moderate-to-severe LUTS have an inadequate storage-symptom response to either monotherapy (Weak); do not prescribe it when PVR > 150 mL (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.2.7.3 α1-blockers + Beta-3 agonist
document_sections.content: A beta-3 agonist may be added when OAB symptoms persist during α1-blocker treatment. In MATCH, 544 patients received tamsulosin 0.2 mg with mirabegron 50 mg or placebo: the mirabegron arm had 0.52 fewer voids per day, while the between-group improvement in total IPSS was not significant. Another trial in men with BPO receiving tamsulosin 0.2 mg daily found greater improvement with added mirabegron in OAB scores, urgency, daytime frequency, the IPSS storage subscore and QoL. In PLUS, after four weeks of tamsulosin 0.4 mg, 715 men received placebo or mirabegron 25 mg, increased to 50 mg after one month. The adjusted difference was 0.39 fewer voids per day; voided volume and urgency showed similar findings, but total IPSS, its subscores and OAB-q symptom scores did not differ significantly. In a comparison of add-on therapies to silodosin, fesoterodine 4 mg improved OAB, urgency and IPSS-QoL scores more than mirabegron 50 mg at three months and was also superior for DO. MATCH reported uncommon cardiovascular events. PLUS reported six retention episodes (1.7%), without a clinically significant specific change in Qmax or PVR; hypertension, headache and nasopharyngitis were frequent adverse events. A randomised open-label study found no clinically relevant cardiovascular or overall safety change when mirabegron or tamsulosin was added to the other drug. Another RCT found comparable efficacy but better safety with mirabegron than solifenacin. Available add-on studies are short-term; the small frequency benefit makes short-term value uncertain, and longer studies are needed. Evidence summaries describe slight reductions in daily voids and urgency episodes and adverse effects of both classes (LE 1b for each). Use an α1-blocker with mirabegron for storage LUTS persisting after α1-blocker monotherapy (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.2.7.4 α1-blockers + Phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors
document_sections.content: This pairing aims to improve LUTS beyond α1-blocker treatment alone. A meta-analysis of five RCTs—two using tadalafil 20 mg daily, two sildenafil 25 mg and one vardenafil 20 mg—found greater improvements with combination therapy in IPSS (-1.8), IIEF (+3.6) and Qmax (+1.5 mL/s). Reviews reported similar results; a network analysis of 55 RCTs excluding 5-ARIs ranked PDE5Is plus α-blockers above monotherapy and other combinations for IPSS improvement. Prospective studies also reported better IPSS QoL, IIEF-5 and Qmax. No serious AEs were reported for the association, and an RCT found similar AE incidence in combination and α-blocker-only arms. Compared with α-blockers alone, the combination improved LUTS, QoL, erectile function and Qmax without increased AEs, but the clinically significant effect on IPSS was small (LE 1a). Meta-analyses suggest that younger men with low body mass index and more severe LUTS might benefit most; larger, longer studies are needed. Use α1-blockers + Phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors for bothersome LUTS, particularly when improved erectile function is desired (Weak), and explain that the effect is modest (Weak). Counsel every patient about adverse effects of pharmacological options when choosing treatment.

document_sections.heading: 5.3 Surgical treatment of benign prostatic obstruction
document_sections.content: Surgery is central to LUTS/BPO care. M-TURP has served as the reference operation because of availability and efficacy, while alternatives seek comparable benefit and safety. The approaches are resection, enucleation, vaporisation, other ablative methods and non-ablative methods. Prostate size restricts many studies; only a small fraction of RCTs include glands > 80 mL, limiting high-level evidence for large prostates. Panel consensus defines short-, mid- and long-term follow-up as twelve, 36 and over 36 months. Durability includes re-operation, inability to stop medication and initiation of new LUTS medication, although most studies report only re-operation; long-term surgical RCTs are often absent. Some patients knowingly prioritise sexual function or perceived safety over maximal obstruction relief. For inclusion of a new device or intervention, the Panel requires adequate efficacy-and-safety RCTs and further studies establishing reproducibility and generalisability; an RCT alone does not ensure a recommendation. Promising approaches lacking this certainty remain under investigation, including some for which recommendations have been issued.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.1 Resection of the prostate
document_sections.content: The resection approaches discussed are monopolar and bipolar TURP, holmium laser resection, ThuVARP and TUIP.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.1.1 Monopolar and bipolar transurethral resection of the prostate
document_sections.content: TURP removes varying amounts of transition-zone tissue, reducing prostate volume and PSA by 25 -58%. Unlike M-TURP, B-TURP confines current locally and uses saline irrigation, eliminating TUR-syndrome. A meta-analysis of twenty RCTs found mean M-TURP changes of Qmax +162%, IPSS -70%, QoL -69% and PVR -77% through five years; studies extending eight to 22 years support durability. A study with mean thirteen-year follow-up associated failure with DUA rather than BPH regrowth. Repeat prostatic operations occur at approximately 1-2% annually; a review of 29 RCTs reported 2.6% retreatment after mean sixteen-month follow-up. In Austrian cohorts totalling 41,059 men, overall retreatment at three months, one year, five years and eight years was 0.9%, 3.7%, 9.5% and 12.7%, respectively; re-TURP at those times was 0.8%, 2.4%, 6.1% and 8.3%. Pooled evidence from 59 RCTs generally finds comparable B-TURP and M-TURP symptom, QoL and Qmax outcomes at twelve months and through 60 months, including 36-month IPSS and Qmax; trial quality was often poor. Ten TURis RCTs involving 1,870 patients found efficacy equivalent to M-TURP. Reported M-TURP peri-operative mortality and morbidity were 0.1% and 11.1%; Austrian data showed a 20% mortality reduction over time, to 0.1% at 30 days and 0.5% at 90 days. TUR-syndrome risk fell to < 1.1%; among 10,654 M-TURPs, transfusion-requiring bleeding occurred in 2.9%. Comparator RCTs reported transfusion-requiring bleeding 2% (0-9%), TUR-syndrome 0.8% (0-5%), AUR 4.5% (0-13.3%), clot retention 4.9% (0-39%) and UTI 4.1% (0-22%). Later problems include UI, retention, UTIs, BNC, urethral stricture, retrograde ejaculation and ED. B-TURP offers better peri-operative safety without a consistent efficacy difference; the largest meta-analysis estimated twenty fewer TUR-syndrome events and 28 fewer transfusions per 1,000 participants versus M-TURP, with potentially similar UI and short-term re-TURP rates (four fewer UI events and one more re-TURP per 1000 participants). TURis studies likewise reported improved bleeding and TUR-syndrome outcomes. Limited follow-up can miss late strictures or BNC. Most longer RCTs found similar stricture/BNC rates, but one reported more strictures with quasi-bipolar TURis for glands > 70 mL at 36-months and another more BNC with a true bipolar system among 137 patients at twelve months. Erectile and ejaculatory outcomes generally did not differ. In a comparative study continuing antithrombotic treatment during B-TURP, acetylsalicylic acid outcomes resembled untreated controls; oral anticoagulation increased median catheterisation (41-hours vs. 24-hours), median hospitalisation (four days vs. three days) and AUR (18% vs. 6%) without a transfusion difference; anti-platelet treatment increased transfusion (19% vs. 1%) and re-hospitalisation (19% vs. 3%). M-TURP is suitable for glands of 30-80 mL. The suggested 80 mL upper limit is Panel consensus, varies with surgical factors, and complication risk increases with size; surgery is safest under 90 minutes. Selection of B-TURP also depends on equipment, experience and patient preference. The evidence summary identifies either TURP as standard for bothersome moderate-to-severe LUTS/BPO with 30-80 mL glands and B-TURP as comparably effective with better peri-operative safety (both LE 1a). Offer bipolar- or monopolar-TURP for moderate-to-severe LUTS with prostate size 30-80 mL (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.3.1.2 Holmium laser resection of the prostate
document_sections.content: HoLRP is absent from contemporary treatment algorithms following the arrival of holmium laser enucleation and the absence of relevant new HoLRP publications since 2004.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.1.3 Thulium:yttrium-aluminium-garnet laser vaporesection of the prostate
document_sections.content: Tm:YAG emits continuously at 1,940 to 2,013 nm and can be used for ThuVARP. Meta-analyses, including a largest set of nine RCTs and seven non-RCTs, generally found no clinically important difference from M-TURP or B-TURP in IPSS, QoL or Qmax at twelve months. A multicentre RCT in 410 men found equivalent IPSS but superior Qmax with TURP at twelve months; the Qmax advantage was greater at age < 70 years and among men presenting with LUTS rather than retention. Patient-reported urinary outcomes were largely similar, with some evidence of less nocturia after TURP. A long-term RCT found similar efficacy and re-operation rates (ThuVARP 2.1% vs. M-TURP 4.1%). A prospective study of 2,216 patients reported sustained improvements throughout eight years. Some meta-analyses reported longer operations, shorter catheterisation and admission, and less blood loss with ThuVARP, without consistent transfusion or other short-term complication differences; two found significantly more transfusions after M-TURP. Trial quality and late-complication reporting were limited. The multicentre RCT found similar operative and recovery times, complication frequency and severity, transfusions and haemoglobin change; retention and LUTS presentations had similarly positive results. Three RCTs with 18 to 48 months of follow-up found no late-complication differences. A retrospective series of 103 patients found a greater haemoglobin fall with low molecular weight heparin bridging than with continued antiplatelet/anticoagulant therapy. Further study is needed. The evidence summary finds equivalent IPSS but superior TURP Qmax at twelve months, comparable short-term safety and limited longer-term comparison (LE 1b). Offer ThuVARP as a TURP alternative (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.3.1.4 Transurethral incision of the prostate
document_sections.content: TUIP opens the outlet by incision without substantial tissue removal, usually for prostates < 30 mL without a middle lobe. Conventional electrocautery and holmium laser TUIP were similarly effective for BOO in an RCT of glands ≤ 30 mL at twelve months, with similarly low re-operation rates. A meta-analysis of ten RCTs reported comparable symptom improvement but a smaller, significant Qmax improvement with TUIP. Among eight studies stating size limits, five used < 30 mL and three < 60 mL. A six-trial meta-analysis reported more re-operations with TUIP than M-TURP (18.4% vs. 7.2%). Conventional TUIP had shorter operating time and less retrograde ejaculation than holmium TUIP in an RCT; both had low complication rates. TUR-syndrome has not been reported and bleeding risk is small. Evidence summaries regard efficacy and safety for glands < 30 mL as comparable to M-TURP (LE 1a), with less retrograde ejaculation and transfusion risk but more repeat operations (LE 1a); size-based selection between TUIP < 30 mL and TURP 30-80 mL is LE 4. Offer TUIP for moderate-to-severe LUTS when prostate size is < 30 mL and no middle lobe is present (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.3.2 Enucleation of the prostate
document_sections.content: The approaches considered include open prostatectomy, bipolar, holmium, thulium and diode enucleation, alongside investigational techniques.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.2.1 Open prostatectomy
document_sections.content: Open prostatectomy (OP) removes an obstructing adenoma through a transvesical or transcapsular approach and is used for substantially enlarged glands (> 80-100 mL). Reported changes are LUTS -63-86% (12.5-23.3 IPSS points), QoL -60-87%, mean Qmax +375% (+16.5-20.2 mL/s) and PVR -86-98%, with efficacy lasting up to six years. In 2,452 Austrian patients, endourological re-intervention at three months, one year, five years and eight years occurred in 0.9%, 3.0%, 6.0% and 8.8%. Meta-analyses comparing OP with B-TUEP or HoLEP found no significant Qmax differences at three, six, twelve and 24 months, or PVR, PSA, IPSS and QoL differences through twelve months. One RCT found similar five-year Qmax, IPSS and repeat-operation outcomes with OP and HoLEP. Compared with B-TUEP, OP operating time did not differ significantly; it was shorter than HoLEP, but OP required longer catheterisation and admission and more transfusions. Other complications and IIEF-5 at three, six, twelve and 24 months did not significantly differ. Reported OP mortality fell to < 0.25%; a series of 1,286 men found mortality of 0.2% at 30 days and 0.4% at 90 days. Estimated transfusion frequency is about 7-14%; longer-term events include transient UI up to 10%, and BNC or urethral stricture about 6%. OP is effective and durable but the most invasive option. Without holmium or bipolar endoscopic equipment, OP is reasonable for glands > 80 mL with informed consent. Evidence summaries describe durability (LE 1b), comparable short- and mid-term efficacy to B-TUEP/HoLEP (LE 1a), worse peri-operative safety (LE 1a) and comparable long-term function to HoLEP (LE 1b). Offer OP for moderate-to-severe LUTS with prostate size > 80 mL when anatomical endoscopic enucleation is unavailable (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.3.2.2 Bipolar transurethral enucleation of the prostate
document_sections.content: B-TUEP endoscopically enucleates the adenoma using bipolar technology; PKEP and BPEP are described, followed by morcellation or resection. Meta-analyses found B-TUEP and B-TURP similar for IPSS, QoL and Qmax at twelve months and for IPSS and Qmax at 36 months. An RCT favoured PKEP over M-TURP for symptoms, flow and demonstrated de-obstruction at 36-months. RCTs in glands > 80 mL found no clinically important efficacy differences between PKEP or BPEP and B-TURP at six or 24 months, respectively. Other trials favoured PKEP in large glands at 36, 48 and 60 months. Reviews comparing B-TUEP with B-TURP found less AUR, haemoglobin decline and transfusion with B-TUEP, but generally similar recovery times, ED and other complications, including stricture/BNC through 24 months; another review found less bleeding than M-TURP with similar UI and post-catheter AUR. Individual RCTs reported shorter catheterisation/admission for PKEP than M-TURP in glands < 80 mL at 36 months, and shorter operation, catheterisation and admission than B-TURP for glands > 80 mL at six months, with some transfusion, BNC and retrograde ejaculation outcomes favouring PKEP. For glands > 80 mL, BPEP took longer than B-TURP but shortened catheterisation and admission without differences in transfusion, stricture or UI at 24 months. Stricture/BNC did not differ at 60 months. The evidence summary favours PKEP over TURP for mid- to long-term efficacy and peri-operative safety, with comparable mid- to long-term safety (LE 1b for each). Offer bipolar transurethral (plasmakinetic) enucleation instead of TURP for moderate-to-severe LUTS (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.3.2.3 Holmium laser enucleation of the prostate
document_sections.content: Ho:YAG emits at 2,140 nm; absorption by water-containing tissue limits coagulation and necrosis to 3-4 mm. An early review found similar short-term Qmax and re-intervention for HoLEP and M-TURP (4.3% vs. 8.8%); later reviews favoured HoLEP for short-term Qmax and IPSS, while a review found comparable IPSS and Qmax at 24-months. Reviews comparing HoLEP with B-TURP generally found similar short-term IPSS, QoL and Qmax. RCTs found comparable function to TURP at 24 months for glands < 80 mL and at seven years in a small M-TURP comparison. In glands > 80 mL, an RCT found similar function at 36 months but significantly less overall retreatment, resumed α-blocker use and re-operation after HoLEP. RCT comparisons with PKEP or B-TUEP generally found similar functional outcomes through twelve months or 3-year follow-up. A retrospective-series review found faster enucleation with en-bloc and two-lobe than three-lobe methods without superior function. Reviews generally found longer HoLEP operations but shorter catheterisation/admission, less blood loss and fewer transfusions than M-TURP, with similar stricture (2.6% vs. 4.4%) and SUI (1.5% vs. 1.5%) in one analysis. Findings against B-TURP varied by study; a national database of 2,869 laser enucleations and 37,577 TURPs reported longer operations, shorter admissions, similar overall complications and fewer infectious complications for laser enucleation. RCTs in glands < 80 mL favoured HoLEP for bleeding and recovery time; one in glands > 80 mL reported shorter operation, catheterisation and admission and fewer transfusions than B-TURP, without differences in UI or IIEF-5 at 36 months. Comparisons with PKEP found varying operating times and generally similar recovery or complications. A power comparison (2J, 50 Hz vs. 2J, 30 Hz) found similar peri-operative safety and durability. An RCT of Virtual basket found better haemostasis (18 vs. 29 min, p < 0.01) and shorter operation (101 vs. 126 min, p < 0.01) than conventional HoLEP; a review of seven studies supported shorter enucleation and surgery, while clinical and economic value remains undetermined. An RCT found no bleeding-safety difference with tranexamic acid. HoLEP has been performed safely during anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, but RCTs and separately interpretable drug-class and bridging data are lacking. Reviews found generally comparable sexual outcomes to TURP, although one seven-RCT review favoured long-term HoLEP IIEF-5; three quarters of sexually active men in one report had retrograde ejaculation, and ejaculatory/orgasm perception were particularly affected. Ejaculation-preservation attempts succeeded in up to 46.2%. Surgeon experience strongly influences complications; mentorship is advised. Evidence summaries report comparable mid- to long-term efficacy (LE 1b), comparable short-term safety (LE 1a) and longer operations but better peri-operative outcomes than TURP (LE 1a). Offer HoLEP instead of TURP or OP for moderate-to-severe LUTS (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.3.2.4 Thulium:yttrium-aluminium-garnet laser enucleation of the prostate
document_sections.content: Tm:YAG approaches include ThuVEP and blunt ThuLEP. Thulium:yttrium-aluminium garnet at 2,013 nm and thulium fibre lasers at 1,940 nm can enucleate water-containing tissue. Reviews found no clinically important short-term Qmax, IPSS or QoL difference between ThuLEP and M-TURP/B-TURP. An RCT found equivalent Qmax, IPSS, PVR and QoL against B-TURP at five years. A review and an RCT found similar results against HoLEP at twelve and eighteen months; an RCT found similar efficacy to PKEP at twelve months. Prospective ThuVEP series showed significant symptomatic and functional improvements; one retrospective comparison found similar clinical results for pulsed and continuous-wave ThuLEP. Reviews found longer ThuLEP operations and shorter catheterisation than M-TURP, shorter admission than B-TURP, fewer transfusions than M-TURP and less clot retention than B-TURP, with other complications similar. Against HoLEP, a review favoured ThuLEP enucleation time but found other operative and short-term safety outcomes similar; an RCT reported no urethral or bladder-neck stricture at eighteen months in either arm. Compared with PKEP, ThuLEP had less haemoglobin decrease and shorter catheterisation, with similar complications. One RCT favoured ThuLEP over B-TURP for IIEF-5 at twelve months. ThuVEP reports include patients with large glands or anticoagulation/bleeding disorders. One study reported adverse events in 31% and complications greater then Clavien grade 2 in 6.6%; another reported 2.4% re-operation at 48 month follow-up. ThuVEP lacks RCT support, and additional investigation is needed. Evidence summaries grade comparative efficacy and ThuLEP safety LE 1b and apparent ThuVEP safety in large glands or antithrombotic treatment LE 2b. Offer Tm:YAG enucleation (ThuLEP, ThuVEP) as an alternative to TURP, HoLEP or bipolar plasmakinetic enucleation for moderate-to-severe LUTS (Weak); offer Tm:YAG enucleation during anticoagulant or antiplatelet treatment (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.3.2.5 Diode laser enucleation of the prostate
document_sections.content: Diode lasers marketed for prostate procedures use 940, 980, 1,318 or 1,470 nm; few have clinical trial assessment. RCTs found no significant IPSS, QoL, Qmax or PVR difference between 1,318 nm or 1,470 nm DiLEP and B-TURP for mean gland size < 80 mL at six or twelve months. Three RCTs of 980 nm DiLEP versus PKEP in glands < 80 mL or > 80 mL found similar outcomes at twelve months; a 980 nm comparison with HoLEP was also similar through twelve months. One small 1,318 nm trial found longer operations but shorter catheterisation/admission and less blood loss than B-TURP, without different transfusion or complication rates. A 1,470 nm trial found shorter operation and recovery and less blood loss, likewise without transfusion or complication differences. Peri-operative findings across three 980 nm PKEP trials conflicted, but transfusion and complication rates did not differ; a HoLEP comparison found similar peri-operative outcomes. Limited, mostly low-quality RCTs and uncertain retreatment findings call for better trials. Evidence summaries assign LE 1b to comparable short-term efficacy and safety for 1,318 nm/1,470 nm versus B-TURP and 980 nm versus bipolar enucleation. Offer 120-W 980 nm, 1,318 nm or 1,470 nm diode enucleation as an alternative to bipolar plasmakinetic enucleation or B-TURP for moderate-to-severe LUTS (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.3.2.6 Enucleation techniques under investigation
document_sections.content: MISP and 532 nm (‘Greenlight’) laser enucleation are discussed as investigational enucleation approaches.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.2.6.1 Minimal invasive simple prostatectomy
document_sections.content: MISP comprises LSP and RASP, performed using personalised transcapsular or transvesical approaches. A review of 27 observational studies involving 764 patients found mean Qmax gain of 14.3 mL/s and mean IPSS improvement of 17.2; a comparison with OP found no significant functional or symptom difference. A multicentre RCT with median 26-month follow-up found no significant functional or peri-operative difference among LSP, RASP and HoLEP. A review of five non-randomised comparative trials found shorter admissions and higher postoperative Qmax with RASP than LSP. An RCT for glands ≥ 120 mL found longer catheterisation after LSP than RASP or HoLEP (p=0.002); MISP involved longer admission and fewer new storage symptoms. Compared with OP, meta-analyses favoured MISP for admission, blood loss and transfusion, but comparative studies found longer operations without different peri-operative complication rates. A robotic-versus-OP matched study found shorter admission and less blood loss but longer operation with robotics, with comparable Qmax, IPSS, QoL, PVR, PSA and complications. Much of the evidence is retrospective; adequately powered comparisons with OP and endoscopic options are needed, including costs and learning curve. MISP appears feasible for glands > 80 mL requiring surgery, but RCTs remain necessary (LE 2a).

document_sections.heading: 5.3.2.6.2 532 nm (‘Greenlight’) laser enucleation of the prostate
document_sections.content: KTP- and LBO-based enucleation can follow an anatomical blunt-dissection approach (GreenLEP), or use in-situ vaporisation after apical enucleation. Adequate, high-quality RCTs of KTP/LBO enucleation have not yet been conducted.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.3 Vaporisation of the prostate
document_sections.content: The document discusses bipolar transurethral and 532 nm (‘Greenlight’) laser vaporisation and investigational diode vaporisation.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.3.1 Bipolar transurethral vaporisation of the prostate
document_sections.content: B-TUVP forms a plasma field with a bipolar electrode to vaporise tissue. Its coagulation zone is < 2 mm, versus up to 10 mm with monopolar TUVP, potentially reducing irritation and SUI. Thirteen RCTs included 1,244 men with glands < 80 mL; most followed patients for twelve months, with maximum follow-up of 36 months in a small RCT (n = 40) and eighteen months in a later RCT (n = 340). Reviews generally found similar short-term IPSS, QoL, Qmax and PVR versus TURP. Possible inferior mid-term IPSS and Qmax with PK B-TUVP and methodological limitations prevent firm longer-term conclusions. Early pooled results found fewer peri-operative complications with B-TUVP, but did not directly report pooled comparisons for individual complications. A seven-RCT review reported shorter catheterisation (42.5 vs. 77.5 hours) and admission (3.1 vs. 4.4 days); another cautioned that heterogeneous, limited trials preclude firm conclusions. A meta-analysis found less clot retention and transfusion versus M-TURP but not B-TURP, with other complications generally similar. A six-RCT analysis of plasma B-TUVP found similar overall complications and transfusions versus TURP but fewer major Clavien 3, 4 complications and shorter catheterisation. Better standardised, multicentre and longer RCTs are needed. Evidence summaries describe similar short-term efficacy (LE 1a), favourable peri-operative but inferior mid-term efficacy of plasmakinetic B-TUVP (LE 1a), and lower short-term major morbidity with plasma B-TUVP (LE 1a). Offer B-TUVP as a TURP alternative for moderate-to-severe LUTS with prostate volume 30-80 mL (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.3.3.2 532 nm (‘Greenlight’) laser vaporisation of the prostate
document_sections.content: Reviews of 80-W and 120-W PVP generally found Qmax and IPSS comparable to TURP; a four-RCT analysis involving 559 patients found comparable outcomes for 120-W at 24-month follow-up, and two RCTs found similar efficacy at 36 months. An RCT found 180-W non-inferior to TURP for IPSS, Qmax, PVR, volume, PSA and QoL, with stable 24-month outcomes. In glands > 60 mL, one RCT found similar symptom change with PVP and HoLEP but better flow and PVR with HoLEP, and 22% conversion from PVP to TURP. An RCT found comparable 24-month IPSS and Qmax for B-TUVP and 180-W XPS. Reviews found shorter PVP catheterisation by mean difference 32 hours and admission by mean difference 1.85 days versus TURP, with fewer transfusions and clot retention, but generally similar urinary retention, infection and stricture outcomes. Operating time and repeat operations sometimes favoured TURP; one RCT found re-operation at 36-months in 11% after 120-W PVP versus 1.8% after TURP. For 180-W, peri-operative complications and 24-month re-operation-free survival were comparable to TURP. A retrospective outpatient series involved 537 patients, 517 treated as outpatients, with median 31-month follow-up and low readmission/complication rates. A Finnish retrospective study of 21,869 patients reported fewer bleeding re-operations after PVP but greater long-term cumulative re-operation (23.5% versus 17.8% after TURP). Evidence in anticoagulated patients comes mainly from case series; RCT representation is limited. One comparison reported more bladder irrigation with anticoagulation (17.2% versus 5.4%), while another found no significant difference. A mixed-laser series reported delayed gross haematuria in 33.8% at average 33 months; a series continuing anticoagulation during 180-W PVP reported peri-operative adverse events in 30.5%, including significant high-grade events. Short-term non-randomised studies addressed retention, poor contractility, older age and glands > 80 mL. Among 1,077 patients, older men had no greater complications (Clavien III 0.6%; overall 29.6%); at twelve months their peak flow improved 111.7% and IPSS decreased 69.5%, but gains were less durable than in younger men by median eighteen months. No RCT includes glands > 100 mL. Reviews found similar retrograde ejaculation to TURP, while IIEF-5 fell at six-, twelve- and 24- months in patients whose pre-operative score exceeded nineteen. In one B-TUVP comparison, redo TURP for recurrent adenoma occurred in 9.8% versus 1.7% after PVP by 24 months. The 180-W XPS is described as the current generator standard, but supporting studies, particularly for > 100 mL glands and long-term follow-up, are limited. Evidence summaries grade comparative 80-W/120-W safety and efficacy LE 1a, 180-W findings LE 1b, apparent antithrombotic-treatment safety for 80-W/120-W LE 2 and 180-W LE 3. Offer 80-W 532-nm KTP, 120-W 532-nm LBO or 180-W 532-nm LBO vaporisation instead of TURP for moderate-to-severe LUTS with glands 30-80 mL (Strong for each). Offer 80-W KTP or 120- or 180-W LBO vaporisation during anticoagulant or antiplatelet treatment when volume is < 80 mL (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.3.3.3 Vaporisation techniques under investigation
document_sections.content: The investigational approach discussed is diode laser vaporisation.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.3.3.1 Diode laser vaporisation of the prostate
document_sections.content: Few marketed 980 nm diode vaporisation systems have clinical trial assessment. In the first of two 120-W 980 nm RCTs versus M-TURP, IPSS, Qmax and PVR were similar at one and six months, but IPSS and Qmax favoured TURP at twelve and 24 months and repeat TURP was more common after diode treatment; the second RCT found equivalent outcomes at three months. A review found shorter catheterisation and fewer transfusions with diode vaporisation. One RCT found no significant difference in listed early and late complications, including retention, UUI, UTI, stricture and new sexual dysfunction. Studies indicate haemostatic potential during anticoagulant or platelet-inhibitor use, reported in 24% and 52% of patients, respectively. Several reported postoperative dysuria; early series reported repeat operations of 8-33% and persistent SUI of 9.1%. Limited, mostly low-quality RCTs and conflicting retreatment findings require better research. Evidence summaries describe favourable haemostasis and recovery but limited evidence (LE 1b), reports of severe storage symptoms and persistent incontinence (LE 3), and apparent haemostatic safety during anticoagulation (LE 3).

document_sections.heading: 5.3.4 Alternative ablative techniques
document_sections.content: The approaches discussed are Aquablation, PAE and investigational WAVE ablation.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.4.1 Aquablation – image guided robotic waterjet ablation: AquaBeam
document_sections.content: AquaBeam directs a high-velocity saline stream under real-time TRUS to remove prostatic tissue without heat; haemostasis may require catheter traction, diathermy or low-powered laser. A blinded multicentre RCT randomised 181 patients with glands 30-80mL to Aquablation or TURP. Mean total operation time was 33 vs. 36 minutes, and resection time 4 vs. 27 minutes. Six-month IPSS changes of -16.9 and -15.1 established non-inferiority. At one year mean IPSS reduction was 15.1 and 67% in both groups, without significant IPSS, QoL, Qmax or PVR differences. Five-year IPSS decreases were 16.9 versus 15.1 points, Qmax gains 125% versus 89% from baseline, and surgical retreatments 5.1% versus 1.5%. In WATER II, a cohort of 101 men with glands 80-150mL, twelve-month IPSS fell by mean 17 points, Qmax rose 12.5 cc/sec and PVR fell 171 cc among those starting with PVR > 100; 3% required surgical retreatment at 5-years. Urodynamic analysis of 66 WATER participants found six-month pdetQmax decreases of 35 and 34 cm H20 and substantial BOO-index improvement in both arms. WATER reported hospital stay and catheterisation durations of 1.4 and 1 day, respectively, and one transfusion after Aquablation versus none after TURP. A review of seven groups and 446 Aquablation patients found haemoglobin reduction of 2.06 g/dL without increased transfusion. At three months, persistent adverse events of Clavien-Dindo grade 1 or 2 or higher occurred in 26% versus 42%; anejaculation in sexually active men was 10% versus 36%. No procedure-related adverse events occurred after six months. In WATER II, bleeding events affected fourteen patients (13.9%): eight (7.9%) before discharge and six (5.9%) within one month afterward; eight needed transfusion, three theatre fulguration and two both. Antegrade ejaculation was retained in 81% versus 90% for smaller WATER I glands; new incontinence at twelve months was 2%. Analyses of WATER I and II found that two or more ablation passes versus one yielded IPSS lower by four points and IPSS QoL lower by 0.7 points at 24 and 36 months, and Qmax higher by 5 ml/ sec at 36 months. Functional non-inferiority versus TURP is supported for 30-80 mL glands, but better long-term evidence and assessment of bleeding are needed; bladder-neck cautery is often used. The efficacy evidence summary is LE 1b. Offer Aquablation for moderate-to-severe LUTS with glands 30-80 mL as a TURP alternative (Weak); explain bleeding risk and the lack of long-term follow-up data (Strong). Aquablation remains under investigation.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.4.2 Prostatic artery embolisation
document_sections.content: PAE selectively embolises prostatic arteries under angiographic guidance through femoral or radial access; it can be performed with local anaesthesia as a day procedure and requires specific training. In a six-month sham-controlled trial of 80 medically refractory patients, IPSS fell 5.03 +/- 8.13 with sham and 17.1 +/- 7.25 with PAE. A comparative review including 708 patients found TURP superior to PAE by mean postoperative differences of 3.80 IPSS points, 0.73 IPSS-QoL points, 3.62 mL/s Qmax, 11.51 mL prostate volume, 11.86 mL PVR and 1.02 ng/mL PSA. Other reviews found little or no short-term patient-reported symptom/QoL difference, including an eleven-RCT meta-analysis at twelve months, while functional measures generally favoured TURP. A non-inferiority trial found 21% of initial PAE recipients underwent TURP within two years. A retrospective series of 75 patients reported 87% catheter freedom among those with retention and haematuria resolution in 87.5% over three years. Comparative adverse-event findings conflict. One review found more overall events with PAE than TURP/OP (41.6% vs. 30.4%) and more AUR (9.4% vs. 2.0%); another found fewer overall events, comparable severe events, shorter admission (mean difference = -1.94 days) and longer procedures (mean difference = 51.43 min). A four-study analysis of 506 patients found no significant complication difference. Network evidence suggests possible reduction of major events but uncertainty spanning substantial benefit and harm; retreatment effects at 12 to 60 months are uncertain. Reviews variously found similar sexual outcomes, a PAE advantage in IIEF-5 change of 2.56 points, or less sexual dysfunction (OR 0.24); network evidence remains uncertain for erectile and ejaculatory effects. Non-target embolisation remains a concern, although recent studies report fewer events. A review of 22 studies estimated median radiation-related cancer-death risk of 0.117% for a 66-year-old and reduced life expectancy of 5.4 days; counsel about radiation, which may be reducible with appropriate protocols. Urologists and specifically trained interventional radiologists must jointly select patients; LUTS assessment for invasive treatment is the urologist's responsibility. Larger prostates might fare better in post hoc analyses, but larger trials are needed. Medium- and long-term evidence and comparisons with other minimally invasive approaches are needed; PAE remains under investigation. Evidence summaries rate inferior symptom and flow outcomes versus TURP LE 1a and longer procedure but favourable bleeding and recovery LE 1b. Offer PAE to men with moderate-to-severe LUTS seeking minimal invasiveness who accept less optimal results than TURP (Weak). Perform it only in collaborative units with urologist-led assessment and follow-up and trained interventional radiologists (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.3.4.3 Alternative ablative techniques under investigation
document_sections.content: The investigational method discussed is convective water vapour energy ablation.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.4.3.1 Convective water vapour energy (WAVE) ablation: The Rezum system
document_sections.content: The Rezum system transfers thermal energy from radiofrequency-generated water vapour into prostate tissue, causing necrosis; office-based treatment usually requires one to three injections per lateral lobe and, depending on gland size, one to two into the median lobe. An RCT randomised 197 men 2:1 against sham: IPSS and Qmax improved significantly at three months and benefit persisted in the active group to twelve months; PVR did not materially change. Clinically meaningful QoL response was 52% at twelve months, with improvement on other validated symptom measures. Follow-up of the active cohort supported durability at two and five years, with surgical retreatment of 4.4% over five year. A Cochrane review found no comparison with active treatment such as TURP. A network analysis at three to six months reported similar IPSS improvement with WAVE and TURP, but greater PVR and Qmax gains with TURP. Adverse events were generally mild-to-moderate and resolved promptly; validated measures found preserved erectile and ejaculatory function. One review judged symptom improvement clinically meaningful, sexual function preserved and four-year retreatment low. A Cochrane review rated certainty moderate to very low because of study limitations and imprecision; network evidence on retreatment versus sham at three months is very low certainty. RCTs against reference treatment remain necessary for longer-term efficacy and safety.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.5 Non-ablative techniques
document_sections.content: The approaches discussed are PUL and intraprostatic injections; iTIND remains under investigation.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.5.1 Prostatic urethral lift
document_sections.content: PUL uses permanent implants placed cystoscopically to compress lateral lobes and open the prostatic urethra. Reported improvements are IPSS -39% to -52%, Qmax +32% to +59% and QoL -48% to -53%. A Cochrane review found PUL less effective than TURP for IPSS and Qmax over short and long follow-up, while QoL might be similar. In a sham-controlled study, treated-cohort improvements at 60 months were 36% for IPSS, 50% for QoL and 44% for Qmax. A network analysis found similar IPSS improvement at three to six months but smaller objective PVR and Qmax improvements than TURP. In an observational cohort of 1,413 patients, 165 presented with retention; 69% of that group were catheter-free after five days, 83% after one month and 89% by study end. Reported postoperative adverse-event ranges include haematuria (1663%), dysuria (25-58%), pelvic pain (5-17.9%), urgency (7.1-10%), temporary incontinence (3.6-16%) and UTI (2.911%); most were mild-to-moderate and resolved within two to four weeks. An RCT found faster, more extensive recovery in the first three to six months than TURP and better ejaculatory preservation; reviews generally found stable or slightly improved sexual function at 24 months. A review of eleven studies involving 2,016 patients found annual surgical re-intervention of 6% per year (95% CI: 3.0-8.9), commonly TURP/laser (51%), repeat PUL (32.7%) or implant removal (19.6%). Five-year retreatment in a multicentre sham comparison was 13.6%. Evidence is limited for a protruding middle lobe, larger glands and comparative long-term durability. Evidence summaries grade functional benefit inferior to TURP at 24 months and low sexual-adverse-effect incidence LE 1b; the statement concerning unevaluated long-term effects is LE 4. Offer Prostatic urethral lift (Urolift®) to men wishing to preserve ejaculation who have LUTS, glands < 70 mL and no middle lobe (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.3.5.2 Intra-prostatic injections
document_sections.content: Intraprostatic agents studied include Botulinum toxin-A (BoNT-A), fexapotide triflutate (NX-1207) and PRX302. BoNT-A inhibits cholinergic neurotransmitter release; mechanisms for NX-1207 and PRX302 remain incompletely understood, although experimental work suggests apoptosis-related prostatic atrophy. A systematic review found no efficacy difference between BoNT-A and placebo and no evidence of clinical benefit in practice (LE 1a). Positive PRX302 Phase II findings have not been confirmed in Phase III. Two placebo-controlled NX-1207 trials enrolled 995 patients with mean 3.6-year follow-up and reported significantly better IPSS change and lower AUR in treated patients; trial authors concluded that intervention needs were reduced. A review found few procedure-related adverse events; NX-1207 trials found no significant long-term safety difference (clinical benefit LE 1b). One RCT found comparable IPSS changes with transperineal BoNT-A and TURP but better preservation of erectile function with BoNT-A at twelve months. More high-quality comparisons against reference treatments are needed. Do not offer intraprostatic Botulinum toxin-A for male LUTS (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.3.5.3 Non-ablative techniques under investigation
document_sections.content: The device discussed is (i)TIND.

document_sections.heading: 5.3.5.3.1 (i)TIND
document_sections.content: The nitinol iTIND has three struts and an anchoring leaflet. It is expanded within the prostate to compress obstructing tissue, producing ischaemic necrosis and an incision-like effect; it remains for five days before outpatient removal. A 32-patient prospective series reported significant IPSS, QoL and Qmax improvement at each visit through three years. In an RCT of 175 men randomised 2:1 against sham, 78.6% versus 60% achieved ≥ 3-point IPSS reduction at three months; at twelve months the active arm's mean changes from baseline were IPSS -9.25, QoL -1.9point and Qmax +3.52mL/s. In a separate 81-patient prospective study, mean IPSS changed from 22.5 to 8.8 at twelve months, and Qmax from 7.3 to 14.7 ml/s between one and twelve months. A network analysis found less improvement in IPSS, PVR and Qmax than TURP at three to six months. In the first series, four early complications (12.5%) comprised retention (3.1%), temporary incontinence after displacement (3.1%) and infection (6.2%); none occurred subsequently through 36 months. In the RCT, mostly transient Clavien-Dindo grade 1 or 2 events occurred in 38.1% versus 17.5% of sham recipients. No new ejaculatory or erectile dysfunction was reported. Over twelve months in the 81-patient study, two patients required medication, two TURP and ten were lost to follow-up. RCT comparisons with reference surgery are ongoing.

document_sections.heading: 5.4 Patient selection for LUTS/BPO treatment
document_sections.content: Treatment choice depends on assessment findings, achievable changes, personal preferences and expectations concerning onset, efficacy, adverse effects, QoL and progression. Behavioural measures, with or without medicines, are usually initial options. Surgery is usually required for recurrent or refractory retention, overflow incontinence, recurrent UTI, bladder stones or diverticula, treatment-resistant visible haematuria due to BPH/BPE, or upper-tract dilatation from BPO with or without renal insufficiency; these are absolute indications. Surgery is also usually needed if conservative or drug therapy does not adequately relieve LUTS or PVR, a relative indication. Choice of operation reflects gland size, comorbidity, anaesthetic fitness, patient preference and acceptance of adverse effects, equipment and surgeon experience. Figure 3 sets out conservative and medical choices by symptom bother, predominant nocturnal polyuria or storage symptoms, gland volume > 40 mL, persistent storage symptoms and whether long-term treatment is intended. Figure 4 organises surgical choices by operative indications or treatment preference, high-risk status, anaesthetic fitness, ability to interrupt anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy and gland sizes < 30 mL, 30 – 80 mL or > 80 mL; it identifies current standard/first-choice procedures and alternatives. Patient preferences may change the route selected.

document_sections.heading: 5.5 Management of Nocturia in men with lower urinary tract symptoms
document_sections.content: Nocturia is waking from sleep to void. Its occurrence reflects sleep-period urine production relative to bladder storage capacity. It may arise from LUTD, including OAB or chronic pelvic pain syndrome, but a causal connection with BOO is uncertain. Behaviour, sleep disturbances and systemic disease can also cause it, frequently in combination; nocturia is a LUTS only when LUTD contributes. Table 2 groups behavioural, systemic, sleep-related and LUTD causes according to excessive urine production or reduced void volume.

document_sections.heading: 5.5.1 Diagnostic assessment
document_sections.content:
Assess LUTD and the severity and bother of each LUTS using a symptom score and directed questions as needed; a validated bladder diary is mandatory. Review fluid- and sleep-related behaviours, medical history and medicines, including directed assessment for renal failure, diabetes mellitus, cardiac failure and obstructive sleep apnoea. Consider relevant medical expertise if a systemic condition or sleep disorder might contribute, is insufficiently managed or is newly suspected. Figure 5 follows assessment of bothersome nocturia with history, sexual function, symptom questionnaire, examination, urinalysis, conditional PSA and PVR, followed as indicated by prostate or kidney imaging, uroflowmetry, renal assessment and a bladder diary.

The nocturia assessment algorithm distinguishes polyuria or nocturnal polyuria, LUTS, sleep disorders, and mixed presentations. It directs evaluation of concerning findings according to relevant guidelines or clinical standards, assessment of significant PVR with kidney imaging and possibly renal function testing, and selection of treatment according to the identified cause. LUTS-related nocturia may lead to behavioural, drug, or interventional LUTS treatment; nocturnal polyuria may lead to behavioural or drug treatment; and medical or sleep-related causes call for treatment of the underlying disorder and shared care. Even nocturia that is not bothersome may justify a frequency volume chart when the history or examination raises concern about a serious underlying condition.

document_sections.heading: 5.5.2 Medical conditions and sleep disorders Shared Care Pathway
document_sections.content: The causative categories are bladder storage problems; 24-hour polyuria, defined as > 40 mL/kg urine output over a 24-hour period; nocturnal polyuria, defined by urine produced during the main sleep period exceeding 20% of 24-hour output in young people or 33% in people > 65; sleep disorders; and mixed aetiology. Systemic contributors can disturb water, salt or solute balance, plasma oncotic pressure, endocrine and cardiovascular regulation, renal function, or neurological control. Urologists should identify plausible mechanisms and seek relevant specialist input. A LUTD treatment pathway should not be pursued without a justified suspected causal contribution from LUTD and consideration of systemic and sleep abnormalities. History and examination should also consider early systemic disease in people whose nocturia is not bothersome. Potentially treatable non-urological contributors include obstructive sleep apnoea, congestive cardiac failure, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, and medications such as diuretics or lithium. Table 3 allocates diagnostic and treatment contributions between urological, shared, and medical care and lists potential nephrological, cardiovascular, endocrine, neurological, respiratory, and biochemical causes of polyuria.

document_sections.heading: 5.5.3.1 Antidiuretic therapy
document_sections.content: Arginine vasopressin (AVP) binds renal collecting-duct V2 receptors, increasing water reabsorption and urinary osmolality while reducing urine volume. Its V1-related vascular effects and short serum half-life make AVP unsuitable for treating nocturia or nocturnal polyuria. Desmopressin is a synthetic AVP analogue with strong V2 affinity and no relevant V1 affinity. Studies vary in dose, titration, formulation, and administration route; most have short follow-up, and study limitations, imprecision, heterogeneity, and inconsistency hinder an overall interpretation. A review of randomised or quasi-randomised trials in men found that desmopressin may change nocturnal voids by -0.46 versus placebo over up to three months and by -0.85 over three to twelve months, without an increase in major adverse events in the latter period. Another review found titrated antidiuretic treatment more effective than placebo for nocturnal voiding frequency and uninterrupted sleep. Reported adverse events include headache, hyponatremia, insomnia, dry mouth, hypertension, abdominal pain, peripheral edema, and nausea. Across three titrated-dose studies including men, seven of 530 patients (1.3%) had serious adverse events, including one death; seventeen (3.2%) had hyponatraemia, seven (1.3%) had hypertension, 53 (10%) had headache, and fifteen (2.8%) had nausea. Hyponatremia is the principal concern, particularly above 65 years of age, and may be life-threatening. Some protocols required baseline sodium over 130 mmol/L. Sodium must be assessed before treatment, following initiation or dose titration, and during treatment; desmopressin is not recommended in high-risk groups. In the sex-specific CS41 and CS40 trials of desmopressin oral disintegrating tablets (ODT), almost 87% had nocturnal polyuria and approximately 48% were > 65 years. Co-primary outcomes were the change in nightly nocturia episodes and achievement of at least a 33% reduction in mean nocturnal voids over three months. Compared with placebo, the difference in mean change was -0.3 [95% CI: -0.5 to -0.1] for women and -0.4 [95% CI: -0.6 to -0.2] for men; the respective 33% response rates were 78% vs. 62% and 67% vs. 50%. An analysis of three trials found more clinically significant hyponatraemia at ≥ 65 years than at < 65 years across dosage groups: among men given 50 mcg, 11% vs. 0%; among women given 25 mcg, 4% vs. 2%. Severe hyponatraemia, serum sodium ≤ 125 mmol/L, affected 22 of 1,431 (2%) overall. In a case series of men aged more than 60 given 50 mcg ODT, 12/80 developed non-severe hyponatremia after one week; it persisted in 4/12 after reduction to 25 mcg. Low-dose ODT is approved in Europe, Canada, and Australia for nocturia with ≥ 2 episodes, at 50 mcg for men and 25 mcg for women. The FDA initially declined approval because benefit relative to risk was uncertain; following resubmission in June 2018, it approved sublingual desmopressin acetate at those doses for adults waking at least two times nightly because of nocturnal polyuria, with a boxed hyponatremia warning. In two trials of nasal desmopressin acetate involving men and women with over two nocturia episodes and mean age 66 years, benefits versus placebo were statistically significant but small: -0.3 with 1.5 mcg and -0.2 with 0.75 mcg. Reductions exceeding 50% of nocturia episodes occurred in 48.5% and 37.9%, respectively, versus 30% with placebo; hyponatremia risks were 1.2% and 0.9%. The nasal product was FDA-approved in 2017 but is unavailable in Europe. Before prescribing desmopressin, assess non-urological causes such as sleep apnoea. For men < 65 years, start at 0.1 mg/day and, if needed, increase weekly to 0.4 mg/day; give once daily before sleep and avoid fluids for at least one hour beforehand and eight hours afterward. Low doses may be prescribed above 65 years, but must not be used in men ≥ 65 years whose sodium is below normal. Monitor all recipients for hyponatraemia, exercising particular caution in under-represented groups such as patients > 75 years.

document_sections.heading: 5.5.3.2 Medications to treat LUTD
document_sections.content: When LUTD is diagnosed and judged to cause nocturia, medications for storage or voiding LUTS may be considered, including selective α1-adrenergic antagonists, antimuscarinics, 5-ARIs, and PDE5Is. Their nocturia effects are generally small or not significantly different from placebo. OAB drug studies predominantly enrolled women; no studies specifically examining their effect on nocturia in men were identified. Combination-treatment benefits were inconsistent.

document_sections.heading: 5.5.3.3 Other medications
document_sections.content: Studies have associated sleep-promoting agents, diuretics, NSAIDs, and phytotherapy with a response or improved QoL, but their effects on nocturia are generally small or not significantly different from placebo. Larger reported effects lack confirmation in larger RCTs. One RCT found no difference in IPSS change between melatonin+tamsulosin and placebo+tamsulosin. Sleep-promoting drugs appear not to reduce nocturnal voiding frequency, although they may help people fall asleep again. Evidence statements assign LE 4 to the absence of trials of pathophysiology-directed primary treatment and robust behavioural-primary-treatment trials; LE 1b to reduced nocturnal voiding and longer uninterrupted sleep with antidiuretic treatment, increased hyponatremia risk at 65 years or older, and the possibility of timed diuretic treatment for nocturnal polyuria with sodium screening; and LE 2 to generally marginal α1-blocker benefits, small or non-significant nocturia reductions and more dry mouth with antimuscarinics, and reduced nocturia severity with 5α-reductase inhibitors in men initially voiding at least twice nightly. Recommendations are to address behavioural, systemic, sleep-related, and LUTD causes, including combinations (Weak), and discuss behavioural measures to reduce night-time urine production and nocturia and improve sleep (Weak). Offer desmopressin for nocturnal polyuria in men < 65 years (Weak), or low-dose desmopressin to men > 65 years with at least two nocturnal voids (Weak). Check for hyponatraemia at baseline, day three, day seven, one month, and periodically thereafter; check sodium more often above 65 years or with elevated risk (Strong). Discuss desmopressin benefits and risks, particularly above 65 years (Strong). For associated conditions, offer α1-adrenergic antagonists when nocturia accompanies LUTS (Weak), antimuscarinics when it accompanies overactive bladder (Weak), and 5α-reductase inhibitors when LUTS and prostate enlargement > 40 mL coexist (Weak). Do not offer phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors to treat nocturia (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.6.1 Epidemiology and Pathophysiology
document_sections.content: Urinary incontinence (UI) means involuntary urine loss. Its reported prevalence rises from 11% among men aged 60 to 64 years to 31% among men ≥ 85 years; it affects up to 32% of men with LUTS. The types addressed are stress urinary incontinence (SUI), urgency urinary incontinence (UUI), and mixed urinary incontinence (MUI). Overflow UI, post-micturition dribble, nocturnal enuresis, and total incontinence fall outside this section's scope. Table 4 describes prevalence, definitions, contributing factors, mechanisms, and presentations of these three types.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.2 Diagnostic Evaluation
document_sections.content: History and examination should distinguish SUI, UUI, and MUI, identify other UI types, and recognise presentations requiring prompt specialist referral. Validated instruments such as ICIQ-UI-SF can quantify severity. Voiding diaries document episode frequency and extent, voided volumes, and 24-hour or nocturnal urine output. Pad tests can measure severity and treatment response, but their ability to distinguish UI types or predict treatment outcome is uncertain; early post-operative pad testing may predict subsequent continence after radical prostatectomy. Urodynamics can characterise UI and accompanying storage or voiding dysfunction. In a retrospective series of 125 patients incontinent after BPO surgery, sphincter insufficiency predominated, but reduced compliance and DO were also implicated; impaired detrusor contraction or DO alone accounted for UI in 4 to 14%. A review after radical prostatectomy reported isolated intrinsic sphincter deficiency in 8-71%, associated detrusor dysfunction in 0–88%, DO alongside sphincter weakness in 0–100%, reduced compliance in 18-58%, and both DO and reduced compliance in 4-64%. Among incontinent patients without reported sphincter impairment, DO occurred in 0-4%, reduced compliance in 1-12%, and both in 1-7%. Of 668 urodynamic investigations in men with urgency with or without UUI, 258 (38.6%) showed DO and 293 (43.9%) showed BOO; reported UI correlated with DO. Evidence that UDS changes evaluation, management, or outcome prediction remains too weak to support a specific recommendation from those findings; consider it selectively, particularly before invasive treatment or after persistent or new post-surgical symptoms. PVR can help differentiate overflow UI, although its application in non-neurogenic male UI is uncertain. Selective urethrocystoscopy can exclude urethral or bladder-neck strictures, while bladder inspection can exclude tumours, stones, or diverticula that worsen UI; proposed sphincter repositioning tests have poor reliability. US, MRI, or CT may clarify relevant anatomy or function. Dipstick urinalysis can reveal infection, proteinuria, blood, or glycosuria requiring further investigation. Evidence statements give LE 3 to questionnaires and diaries for classification, pad tests for quantification and response, and the limited evidence that UDS or PVR changes treatment choice in uncomplicated UI. Take a full symptom, comorbidity, and medication history and perform a focused examination (Strong); use a validated symptom questionnaire, bladder diary, and pad test (Strong); measure PVR (Strong); and perform urodynamics when considering invasive UI treatment (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.6.3.1.1 Lifestyle interventions
document_sections.content: Obesity, smoking, activity, and diet may relate to UI, and changing them may help, but supporting studies predominantly involve women; evidence cannot adequately tailor advice to UI subtype. Base fluid advice on measured 24-hour intake and output. Intake should prevent thirst, and unusually low or high 24-hour urine production warrants investigation. A cross-sectional survey found no statistically significant caffeine–UI association. In an RCT, reducing caffeine alongside behavioural therapy reduced urgency, but not UI, compared with behavioural therapy alone.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.3.1.2 Treatment of co-morbidities
document_sections.content: Multiple comorbidities are associated with UI, particularly in older people. Treating an associated illness might lessen urinary symptoms, but concurrent diseases and individualised, combined interventions make attribution difficult. Medication effects can also be hard to separate from illness or ageing. Reviewing and possibly changing treatment of underlying diseases can be considered early, but evidence of UI benefit is limited and changes may cause more harm than benefit.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.3.1.3 Constipation
document_sections.content: An RCT enrolling mostly women found that a multimodal intervention for older patients reduced both UI and constipation and that behavioural therapy appeared to improve both. There is no evidence establishing that treating constipation itself improves UI.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.3.1.4 Containment
document_sections.content: Containment options include absorbent pads, catheters, external collection systems, and penile clamps. A review of six RCTs favoured superabsorbent over standard pads; a crossover trial in men with light UI found leaf-shaped pads preferable to rectangular ones. Reviews found no proven superiority among long-term indwelling catheter materials or types, or among intermittent catheter types or schedules. Non-randomised studies found similar UTI and upper-tract outcomes with suprapubic and urethral drainage but fewer urethral complications with suprapubic catheters. In an RCT of 56 men with post-prostatectomy incontinence (PPI), sheath systems, body-worn urinals, clamps, and pads had differing practical merits; most men preferred combining products. A hinge-type clamp was secure, discreet, and useful for brief vigorous activity, but almost all participants found it uncomfortable or painful. Evidence statements assign LE 3 to limited evidence for lifestyle or comorbidity and drug-regimen changes and LE 1b to the palliative role of pads or penile sheaths. Offer potentially helpful lifestyle advice while explaining the evidence gap (Weak); review drugs that might cause or worsen UI (Weak); and use pads or penile sheaths as palliative measures (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.6.3.2.1 Prompted or timed voiding
document_sections.content: Prompted voiding means a carer initiates toileting; two reviews found improved continence relative to standard care. Timed voiding uses predetermined intervals irrespective of cognitive impairment. A Cochrane review covering two RCTs found inconsistent continence improvement with timed voiding among cognitively impaired adults.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.3.2.2 Bladder training
document_sections.content: Bladder training seeks to modify frequent-voiding habits, increase control of urgency, intervals, and bladder capacity, reduce leakage, and restore confidence. Its ideal format, intensity, and preventive effect are uncertain. Adding it to anticholinergic treatment did not improve UI versus antimuscarinics alone, although frequency and nocturia improved. Across seven RCTs comparing training with drug treatment alone, only oxybutynin showed an advantage for UI cure or improvement.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.3.2.3 Pelvic floor muscle training
document_sections.content: A 2015 Cochrane review found no overall benefit at twelve months for post-operative pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) to treat PPI and considered conservative-treatment benefits uncertain. Later reviews found that PFMT, alone or with biofeedback or electrical stimulation, significantly shortened recovery time; guided biofeedback or pelvic floor muscle electric stimulation (PFES) added to PFMT significantly improved recovery at one and three months. Start PFMT as soon as possible after surgery, between seven and ten days after urethral catheter removal. One RCT found that a single pre-operative session with biofeedback benefited short-term post-prostatectomy UI and longer-term LUTS-related QoL. Two reviews following robotic-assisted radical prostatectomy found faster recovery with post-operative PFMT. Two RCTs found written instructions and supervised PFMT produced similar improvement. Other RCTs reported benefit for previously untreated men incontinent for at least one year after prostatectomy, no demonstrable effect through twelve months after TURP, and earlier recovery when training began before HoLEP. Studies also reported improved muscle strength or faster continence recovery with Pilates, an oscillating rod, biofeedback plus electrostimulation, whole-body vibration, or extended nursing care.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.3.2.4 Electrical stimulation
document_sections.content: Most stimulation evidence concerns women with SUI and is often low quality and heterogeneous. In an RCT of 70 men with PPI, surface and intra-anal stimulation each improved measured urine loss and QoL from baseline, without a significant difference between arms.
