A review of six RCTs found that stimulation may enhance PFMT in the short term but not after six months; it outperformed sham at six months but not twelve months, with more pain and discomfort. Reviews provide only weak evidence for electromagnetic stimulation, and a later review considered evidence insufficient to establish a benefit from electrical stimulation for male post-prostatectomy UI.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.3.2.5 Posterior tibial nerve stimulation
document_sections.content: Posterior tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS) conveys electrical input toward the S2-S4 sacral plexus. Percutaneous treatment uses a 34-G needle near the medial ankle and typically twelve weekly sessions of 30 minutes; transcutaneous treatment uses surface electrodes and typically self-administered twenty-minute daily sessions after instruction. In a predominantly female sham-controlled OAB trial, men represented 22.8% and 20% of the active and sham arms, and symptoms improved in 54.5% versus 20.9%. A non-inferiority RCT found improvement in frequency, urgency, and UUI after twelve weeks with either delivery method, without a significant between-arm difference. A review of predominantly female populations with males < 10% reported OAB improvement in 48-93% and UUI cure in 25-45%. Common adverse effects are mild puncture-site pain or discomfort; small haematomas, swelling, leg tingling, and vasovagal responses have occurred. Reported adherence was 89.7%. Contraindications include a cardiac pacemaker or skin disease at the stimulation site. Male-specific evidence is insufficient for a formal PTNS recommendation, although it can be offered as an alternative before more invasive treatment. Evidence statements rate improved continence with prompted voiding in care-dependent older people, lack of additional UI improvement from adding bladder training to antimuscarinics, conflicting evidence for PFMT adjuncts, and no additional benefit from pre-operative PFMT before radical prostatectomy as LE 1b. Potential stimulation benefit through six months, limited male PTNS effectiveness evidence, and absence of evidence that PTNS cures male UUI are LE 2. Implement prompted voiding when appropriate (Strong), offer bladder training as an adjunct (Weak), and offer PFMT alone or with biofeedback and/or electrostimulation to men undergoing radical prostatectomy to speed UI recovery (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.6.4.1 Drugs for urgency urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: Muscarinic receptor antagonists and beta-3 agonist are described as first-line drug treatments for UUI; their mechanisms, efficacy, and safety are addressed in the respective earlier pharmacological sections.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.4.2 Drugs for stress urinary incontinence
document_sections.content: A review of eight studies of duloxetine for post-prostatectomy SUI reported a mean dry rate of 58% (25–89%), mean pad-number improvement of 61% (12–100%), and mean one-hour pad-weight improvement of 68% (53–90%) over a mean one to nine months. Treatment was discontinued in 38%; fatigue, somnolence, and nausea were reported in 18%. Certainty was low because of heterogeneity and methodological limitations, and longer-term RCTs are needed. Duloxetine use for this indication is off label. Evidence statements rate antimuscarinic improvement in urgency, UUI, and daytime frequency; mirabegron superiority to placebo and comparable UUI efficacy to antimuscarinics; and short-term duloxetine benefit with substantial discontinuation as LE 1b. Offer antimuscarinics or mirabegron to adults whose UUI persists after conservative treatment (Strong). Offer duloxetine to men with SUI (Weak), and explain its possible adverse effects and off-label status in Europe (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.6.5.1 Bulking agents in men
document_sections.content: Urethral bulking adds volume to improve coaptation at a damaged sphincter and may be considered for small-volume leakage or when more invasive treatment is unsuitable. In the only qualifying RCT in a Cochrane review, 45 men received Macroplastique or an artificial urinary sphincter (AUS); both helped minimal incontinence, while AUS gave higher continence rates for total incontinence at 48 months (72% vs. 23%). A review of eight studies (n=142) of Macroplastique, Opsys, Durasphere, and Urolastic found short-term dry rates of 0-83%. In a matched analysis of 104 men with PPI, Macroplastique versus TiLOOP male produced twelve-month failure-free rates of 15.4% versus 76.9%, use of 0-1 pads daily in 21.2% versus 67.3%, and satisfaction of 3.8% versus 71.2%. Several small cohorts found no benefit. A review of 25 articles reported 54.3% success, 37.5% symptom improvement, and almost 30% dryness. Another review pooled two studies with 384 participants for a short-term cure rate of 26.1%; a study of 68 reported a 10.3% long-term cure rate, without describing reoperation rates. Dysuria and haematuria are usually transient; allergic reactions and migration to lymph nodes are possible. Reported retention ranges from 3-17%, generally with little need for catheterisation, and post-operative UTI from 6-7%. Cure rates are low, although use may remain an option when more invasive procedures are unsuitable. Very limited effectiveness evidence for PPI has LE 2. Do not offer bulking agents to men with post-prostatectomy incontinence (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.6.5.2 Male Slings
document_sections.content: Male slings target mild-to-moderate PPI, but those severity categories lack agreed definitions. Studies commonly define cure as no pad or one security pad per 24-hours; some require less than 2 g lost in a 24-hour pad test.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.5.2.1 Non-adjustable slings
document_sections.content: Fixed retropubic or transobturator slings are tensioned during implantation and cannot subsequently be adjusted. Synthetic devices act by compression or repositioning of the urethral bulb. A review of 33 prospective cohorts and one RCT reported overall cure rates of 60% (95% CI: 0.51-0.67) for slings and 56% (95% CI: 0.44-0.68) for AUS, with changes in 24-hour pad use of -3.33 (95% CI: -4.33 to -2.34) and -3.75 (95% CI: -4.56 to -2.93), respectively; a network analysis also found comparable efficacy. In the MASTER non-inferiority RCT, twelve-month continence was 87% with a sling and 84.2% with AUS (95% CI: -11.6-4.6, PNI=0.003]). A subgroup suggested poorer sling results above baseline pad weight > 250g, without statistical significance. For AdVance™ and AdVanceXP©, subjective cure averaged 49% (8.6 - 73.7%) after a mean three years among 136 patients. An AdVanceXP cohort reported, at 60 months, 57.6% cure, 25.4% improvement, and 16.9% failure. Another study reported cure of 66.7% and 71.7%, improvement of 26.5% and 24.4%, and failure of 6.9% and 13.3% at 24- and 48-months, respectively. With I-Stop TOMS, dryness declined from 38% at twelve months to 23% at four years and 15% at five years. A review of 1,170 men identified previous radiation, more severe UI, and previous surgery as failure predictors. After AdVanceXP, non-radiated versus radiated men had improvement of 49.6% versus 22.2% and satisfaction of 95% versus 64%. Pain and superficial infection are common; chronic pain was reported in 1.3%, transient voiding dysfunction in 4.3-10.3%, and erosions and chronic pain were uncommon at 0-0.4%. Fixed slings appear safe and improve continence, but may work less well with severe incontinence or previous radiotherapy.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.5.2.2 Adjustable slings in males
document_sections.content: Adjustable sling tension can be changed after surgery. The principal named systems are Remeex®, Argus®, and ATOMS®. Evidence includes one small RCT and mostly heterogeneous case series; a review found objective cure rates of 17-92%. For Remeex®, a nineteen-patient study reported 70% success over nearly seven years without explantation, infection, or erosion, whereas a fourteen-patient study found 36% satisfaction after 25 months, repeated adjustments, and 21% mechanical failure. Argus® reports include 404 men, few series above 40 participants, and follow-up up to 35-months; success ranged from 17-93%, with a mean 73.0% subjective cure. Argus T had similar efficacy to the other Argus approach at 44 months but more inguinal pain and explantation. In a 22-man randomised study, Argus T outperformed AdVance for eighteen-month 24-hour pad tests and satisfaction. An ATOMS review of 1,393 patients reported 67% dryness, 90% improvement after adjustment, 16.4% complications, and 5.75% expulsion. A review of 3,059 patients favoured ATOMS over ProACT for dryness (68% vs. 55%), improvement (91% vs. 80%), satisfaction (87% vs. 56%), adjustments (2.4 vs. 3.5), and daily pads (1.1 vs. 2.1). Pain, erosion, and infection are frequent concerns; chronic pain occurred in 1.5%, readjustment in 8-38.6%, explantation in 10-15.8%, and erosion around 10%. Reasons for explantation include infection (4.1-8%), erosion (4-12%), and perforation (2.7-16%). One review reported ATOMS versus ProACT explantation of 5% vs. 25% and major complications of 4.2% vs. 10.4%. Added benefit from adjustability remains unproven, so no recommendation is made; external comparisons suggest more explantation than with fixed slings.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.5.2.3 Autologous slings
document_sections.content: Autologous vas-deferens slings have been placed beneath the vesico-urethral anastomosis during RARP to encourage earlier continence. Two RCTs favoured a sling over none at one month, and another favoured a 6-branch over a 2-branch sling then. A larger RCT (n=195) found similar six-month continence (66% vs. 65%) and near-continence (86% vs. 88%). Evidence statements rate limited support for fixed transobturator slings in mild-to-moderate PPI and the absence of demonstrated six-month benefit from an intra-operative autologous sling during RARP as LE 1b; reduced fixed-sling benefit with severe UI, prior radiotherapy, or transurethral surgery as LE 2; limited evidence for adjustable slings and no demonstrated adjustability advantage as LE 3; and a possible higher adjustable-sling explantation rate in external comparisons as LE 4. Offer non-adjustable transobturator slings for mild-to-moderate postprostatectomy incontinence (Weak), explaining that these categories remain undefined. Warn that severe leakage, prior pelvic radiotherapy, or transurethral surgery may worsen results (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.6.5.3.1 Artificial urinary sphincter
document_sections.content: AUS is described as the standard treatment for moderate-to-severe male SUI. AMS 800 has an inflatable cuff, pump, and pressure-regulating balloon and the longest follow-up; ZSI 375 has two components. Robust evidence remains pending for Victo and Br-SL-AS 904. A review of 33 cohorts and one RCT found 56% overall cure and a -3.75 change in pads per 24-hours after AUS. AMS 800 observational studies reported 55-76.8% social continence; among 57 men followed for a median > fifteen years, continence was 77.2% and satisfaction 89.5%. In a 40-person cohort followed for a mean 53 months, low bladder compliance alone predicted worse outcome, whereas another study found no adverse urodynamic predictor. Greater surgeon experience and volume correlate with better outcomes and fewer revisions. Evidence for ZSI 375 is limited: one multicentre retrospective study found 84.4% success after 43 months, comprising 19.3% dryness and 65.1% improvement to 0-1 pads daily; another reported 72% success at seven years among 45 patients. In a single-surgeon series of 168 AMS 800 implants from 2008 to 2016, 63 patients (37.5%) required revision or explantation after median follow-up of 2.7 year. Among failures, balloon, cuff, and pump malfunction accounted for 36.5%, 7.9%, and 6.3%; urethral atrophy, erosion, and infection accounted for 22.2%, 19.0%, and 12.7%. Prior radiotherapy, urethral stricture, sling, and coronary artery disease independently predicted failure. A multicentre retrospective comparison of primary AUS after radical prostatectomy (n= 417) or BPO surgery (n=50) found three-month social continence of 79% vs. 72%. Reported AUS complications include infection or erosion (8.5%), mechanical failure (6.2%), and atrophy (7.9%). Radiation, greater age, and longer time since cancer treatment were associated with atrophy; previous irradiation and a penoscrotal approach were associated with erosion. Three-year revision rates ranged from 10-29.1%. ZSI 375 erosion and mechanical-failure risks were 8.2-13.3% and 2.2-2.5%. A retrospective comparison reported higher complications following BPO surgery than after prostatectomy, with figures stated as 8% vs. 18%, p=0.044; its ClavienDindo type 2 comparison was 20.6% vs. 44.4%, p=0.026. Specialised centres are advised. Patients must understand pump-operation requirements, possible future cognitive or dexterity limitations, device lifespan, and common long-term maintenance operations; maintenance should not itself be classified as a complication.

document_sections.heading: 5.6.5.3.2 Non-circumferential compression device (ProACT®)
document_sections.content: ProACT® comprises two periurethral balloons with tubing and scrotal adjustment ports, positioned near the bladder neck and adjusted after implantation. A review of nineteen studies involving 1,264 patients found 60.2% dryness, -3.1 pads daily, and improved QoL, with high heterogeneity. ATOMS comparisons favoured ATOMS for improvement, satisfaction, and complications. A quasi-randomised comparison with bone-anchored slings found similar SUI improvement (68% vs. 65%); another study found 50% remained substantially bothered. After radiotherapy, reported success was 46% versus 68% without radiotherapy, with more erosion. Bladder or urethral perforation is a principal implantation risk, estimated at 5.3%. Overall revision was estimated at 22.2%, including erosion (3.8%), leakage (4.1%), and migration (6.5%); prospective series reported explantation of 11-58%. Success is possible, but complications are frequent. Evidence statements assign LE 1b to primary AUS effectiveness; LE 3 to adverse effects of previous pelvic radiotherapy on AUS and explantation due to infection or erosion of up to 24% in some series; LE 2b to ProACT® efficacy accompanied by frequent failure and complications, especially after radiation; and LE 4 to the external-comparison suggestion of greater adjustable-sling explantation. Offer AUS for moderate-to-severe male SUI (Strong). Offer AUS or ProACT© implantation only at expert centres (Weak); explain the high risks of complications, malfunction, and explantation despite possible cure (Strong). Do not offer ProACT© after pelvic radiotherapy (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.6.6.1 Bladder wall injection of botulinum Toxin-A
document_sections.content: BoNT-A inhibits neurotransmitter release from cholinergic neurons. OnabotulinumtoxinA (onabotA; BOTOX®) 100 U is licensed in Europe for persistent or refractory non-neurogenic OAB with UUI in adults. In an RCT after inadequate anticholinergic treatment, onabotA 100 U reduced daily UUI episodes by 50% and micturitions by more than two; 22.9% became dry versus 6.5% with saline. A review comparing onabotA, mirabegron, and anticholinergics reported greater reductions and the highest odds of dryness or >50% UUI reduction with onabotA. A post-prostatectomy pilot trial found better QoL, ICIQ, and daily-frequency outcomes than placebo. Among 65 non-obstructed men, UDI-6 and IIQ-7 changed by -4.2 and -6.0 from baseline. In a 120-patient cohort, clean intermittent self-catheterisation (CISC) occurred in 28.6% without previous surgery, 7.5% after TURP, and 4.2% after radical prostatectomy. A phase IIIb trial with 10% men found UUI changes of -3.19 with onabotA, -2.6 with solifenacin, and -1.33 with placebo. A network analysis with male participation of 9.8-40.2% reported onabotA-versus-mirabegron differences of -0.43, [-1.22-0.37] for daily frequency and -0.46, [-1.46-0.53] for daily UUI. Retention and UTI are the most common adverse events; haematuria, dysuria, and pain also occur, and UTI and treatment-emergent adverse events were more frequent than with mirabegron. In men without prior prostate surgery, catheterisation occurred in 28.6%, versus 7.5% after TURP and 4.2% after radical prostatectomy. Evidence in men, particularly with BPO, and a standardised injection protocol are lacking; injections may need repeating, and a male series reported 68.8% discontinuation. Evidence rates single-session benefit over placebo at 100 U as LE 1b, absence of evidence for diminishing efficacy with repeat injections and high discontinuation as LE 3, and increased retention and UTI as LE 2. Offer bladder-wall onabotulinumtoxinA (100 U) for OAB/UUI refractory to drug treatment (Weak). Warn about limited response duration, UTI, and possibly prolonged CISC, confirming the patient's willingness and ability to catheterise (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.6.6.2 Sacral nerve stimulation (neuromodulation)
document_sections.content: Sacral neuromodulation (SNM) delivers low-amplitude impulses through an electrode near the third sacral root and a buttock generator; its precise mechanism is unknown. A test lead is placed near S3, or S4 if necessary, and permanent implantation follows when symptoms fall by more than 50%. RCTs cannot blind patients and assessors after response-based test selection; men account for around 10% of participants. A meta-analysis found no significant six-month difference in successful treatment versus onabotA (RR 0.93; 95% CI: 0.63-1.39). Reported adverse effects include implant-site pain (13-42%), lead migration (4.0-21%), leg or back pain (3.0-18%), and wound infection (5.7-6.7%); 29-33% require surgical revision. SNM is an alternative to onabotA for refractory OAB. Effectiveness after unsuccessful conservative treatment, without sham-controlled evidence, has LE 2a. Offer SNM to patients with UUI refractory to drugs who accept surgery (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.6.6.3 Cystoplasty/urinary diversion
document_sections.content: Augmentation cystoplasty adds a detubularised bowel segment to the bladder to increase capacity; diversion is an option for otherwise intractable UUI after pelvic procedures, radiotherapy, or pathology causing irreversible sphincter problems or fistula. No RCT compares augmentation with other refractory-OAB/UUI treatments. One large three-year study reported continence of 93% with idiopathic DO, 78% with neurogenic overactivity, and up to 90% when AUS was also implanted. The largest idiopathic augmentation series enrolled only women: after mean follow-up of 75.4 months, 53% were continent and satisfied, 25% had occasional leakage, and 18% had disabling UUI. A small mixed-gender prospective study found high satisfaction relative to onabotA. A small ileal-versus-colonic conduit study found no difference in upper-tract infection or uretero-intestinal stenosis, but did not specifically investigate intractable OAB/UUI. Pre-operative choices require detailed counselling, specialist nursing access, and attention to individual circumstances. Early risks include infection, bowel obstruction, bleeding, and cardiorespiratory complications. Long-term risks include metabolic disturbances, altered bowel habits, mucus, stones, perforation, and, rarely, cancer. Most patients require ongoing self-catheterisation after augmentation or diversion; conduit users require lifelong collection bags. Figure 6 outlines assessment, classification, specialist referral, and conservative, medical, and surgical options for male UI. Evidence statements assign LE 3 to limited evidence of efficacy for idiopathic OAB, frequent need for CISC after augmentation, high short- and long-term complication risks, and lack of comparative augmentation-versus-diversion evidence. Offer augmentation only after all other options fail and when the patient can and will self-catheterise (Weak); explain complication, CISC, and lifelong-surveillance risks (Strong). Offer diversion only after less invasive OAB/UUI treatments fail and if the patient accepts a stoma (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.7.1 Epidemiology and Pathophysiology
document_sections.content: Detrusor underactivity (DU) is a urodynamic concept involving insufficient contraction strength or duration and prolonged or incomplete emptying. Underactive bladder (UAB) denotes the associated clinical symptom complex, potentially including prolonged voiding, incomplete-emptying sensation, hesitancy, reduced filling sensation, and slow flow. General-population DU prevalence is unknown because cases may be asymptomatic or nonspecific. Video-urodynamic referral studies in men with non-neurogenic LUTS reported 10%, reaching 48% in people ≥ 70 years. Untreated DU may follow a chronic, relatively stable course. Normal voluntary contraction requires functional detrusor muscle, intact incoming and outgoing innervation, and integrated central control. Potential aetiologies are neurogenic, myogenic, iatrogenic, and idiopathic. BOO and diabetic cystopathy can contribute to myogenic dysfunction, but mechanisms remain poorly understood and clinical causes are probably multifactorial. Pelvic surgery, radiotherapy, anticholinergic drugs, and opioids may contribute. Although ageing has been proposed as a cause, evidence does not strongly establish that ordinary ageing reduces detrusor contractility.

document_sections.heading: 5.7.2.1 Medical history and physical examination
document_sections.content: Review comorbidities, medication, and storage, voiding, and post-micturition symptoms. No single symptom identifies UAB. Presentations extend from no symptoms to symptomatic chronic retention. Voiding symptoms generally predominate but may accompany storage symptoms, particularly with incomplete emptying or other bladder dysfunction. Concurrent suspected BOO/BPO complicates attribution, and no validated method distinguishes the respective contributions. Compared with men with normal pressure-flow results, one study found significantly more reduced or intermittent stream, hesitancy, incomplete bladder or bowel emptying sensations, palpable bladder, diminished or absent sensation, and consistent straining in UAB. Symptom-based predictive models have neither an established best-performing model nor published external validation.

document_sections.heading: 5.7.2.2 Questionnaires
document_sections.content: No validated questionnaire specifically diagnoses UAB. General male-LUTS instruments may be used, but their value for monitoring UAB symptoms or treatment is uncertain.

document_sections.heading: 5.7.2.3 Uroflowmetry
document_sections.content: Proposed methods use Qmax, flow patterns, or combined scores to distinguish UAB from BOO. Their accuracy is unestablished and they lack external validation.

document_sections.heading: 5.7.2.4 Ultrasound scan and post-void residual measurement
document_sections.content: In a single-centre prospective study of 143 men with LUTS, detrusor wall thickness ≤ 1.23 mm combined with bladder capacity > 445 mL predicted urodynamic DU with 42% sensitivity and 100% specificity. DU often accompanies slow emptying or residual urine, but no agreed diagnostic PVR threshold exists and one is unlikely.

document_sections.heading: 5.7.2.5 Urodynamics
document_sections.content: UAB is a clinical diagnosis; DU requires urodynamic diagnosis. Invasive urodynamics is the only broadly accepted diagnostic method, although diagnostic criteria lack consensus. Proposed measures include Griffiths’ Watt factor, combining voiding pressure, contraction speed, and bladder volume and expressed in W/m2; the appropriate measurement and threshold remain disputed, although expert opinion suggests Wmax 7.0 W/m2. Schafer’s detrusor-adjusted mean PURR factor (DAMPF) uses linPURR in the Schafer nomogram to classify contractility as very weak, weak, normal, or strong. Bladder contractility index (BCI), the most widely used in studies, is BCI=pdetQmax + 5Qmax: BCI>150 denotes strong, 100-150 normal, and <100 weak contractility. None of these models is validated, agreement between them is uncertain, and contraction strength alone does not describe all aspects of emptying.

document_sections.heading: 5.7.3.1 Behavioural interventions
document_sections.content: UAB management aims to relieve symptoms, prevent complications, and preserve or improve QoL through timely drainage, improved contraction, or reduced outlet resistance. High-quality male behavioural-treatment studies are lacking. Inform asymptomatic patients at risk, including those with diabetes or prior pelvic surgery or radiotherapy, because reduced sensation and increased capacity can delay recognition. Scheduled voiding can be recommended for sensory impairment. Double or triple voiding, Valsalva, or the Credé maneuver may reduce PVR in bothersome frequency, but trials have established neither benefit nor harm in non-neurogenic men. A descriptive cohort suggested that non-neurological DU can remain stable without CIC through five years and found no urodynamic predictor of subsequent CIC.

document_sections.heading: 5.7.3.2 Pelvic floor muscle relaxation training with biofeedback
document_sections.content: Relaxation of pelvic-floor muscles and sphincter initiates voiding; failure may impede flow and inhibit detrusor contraction. Relaxation physiotherapy is often used first for voiding dysfunction, but no adult male RCT tests it for UAB. In a paediatric DU RCT, standard urotherapy with or without animated biofeedback improved PVR, recurrent UTI, and urodynamic findings, with significantly greater improvement at every stage when biofeedback was added.

document_sections.heading: 5.7.3.3 Clean intermittent self-catheterisation (see section 5.6.3.1.4)
document_sections.content: For persistently raised PVR, clean intermittent catheterisation (CIC) is preferred for reliable emptying. No maximum acceptable PVR has been established, although UTI risk rises after 300mls. Compared with an indwelling catheter, CIC may reduce infection, colonisation, stones, and overflow UI. Independent use requires sufficient cognition and dexterity; another person may assist.

document_sections.heading: 5.7.3.4 Indwelling catheters
document_sections.content: Avoid long-term indwelling drainage unless other options are unsuitable and CIC cannot or will not be performed by the patient or a helper. When required, suprapubic drainage is preferred to urethral drainage because of traumatic hypospadias risk.

document_sections.heading: 5.7.3.5 Intravesical electrical stimulation
document_sections.content: Intravesical electrotherapy (IVES) stimulates A-delta afferents to reinforce bladder contraction and requires intact afferent pathways and detrusor muscle. Daily sessions are used, with ten to fifteen sessions considered a trial. In an RCT involving both sexes and predominantly neurogenic UAB, four-week IVES versus sham changes were PVR -97 mL vs. -10.5 mL, p < 0.01; bladder voiding efficiency +13.3 vs. 0.0, p < 0.01; and Qmax +1.3 vs. + 0.2, p < 0.04. A small retrospective study involving eleven women and five men found some voiding improvement in two-third; remaining evidence largely concerns children.

document_sections.heading: 5.7.3.6 Extracorporeal Shock Wave Therapy
document_sections.content: Extracorporeal Shock Wave therapy (ESWT) could theoretically aid contractility through neovascularisation and tissue regeneration. A small placebo-controlled RCT found improved PVR and UAB-Q at the 4th week but not the 12th week. Evidence statements assign LE 3 to attempting behavioural measures while avoiding Valsalva or Credé in poorly compliant bladders, using CIC first for high PVR over 300 mL, and indwelling-catheter complications and suprapubic preference; relaxation techniques have LE 4. Initiate clean intermittent self-catheterisation with upper-tract risk or PVR > 300mL (Weak). Offer transurethral indwelling catheterisation or suprapubic cystostomy only if other drainage methods fail or are unsuitable (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.7.4.1 Parasympathomimetics
document_sections.content: A review and meta-analysis of twelve RCTs involving men and women examined muscarinic agonists and acetylcholinesterase inhibitors. Some patients with post-procedure retention had a small benefit without increased adverse events, but PVR did not improve. Few small heterogeneous studies, weak data, and very short follow-up preclude firm conclusions about UAB treatment.

document_sections.heading: 5.7.4.2 Alpha-adrenergic blockers
document_sections.content: Reducing outlet resistance might help UAB emptying, although high-quality RCTs are lacking. A single-blind prospective RCT of 119 patients found greater symptom, PVR, and flow improvement with combined cholinergic and α-adrenergic treatment than either treatment alone. A propensity-matched study in non-neurogenic male DU reported improved QoL and voiding and urodynamic measures with tadalafil and silodosin. Evidence remains insufficiently rigorous to establish the drug class's efficacy for UAB.

document_sections.heading: 5.7.4.3 Prostaglandins
document_sections.content: Prostaglandins participate in bladder regulation; among five subtypes, E2 and F2a appear prominent in detrusor stimulation. A review of three RCTs suggested that intravesical PGE2 or PGF2a may reduce retention after catheter removal, but methodological shortcomings leave clinical use uncertain. In a nineteen-patient placebo-controlled trial, intravesical PGE2 plus bethanechol chloride reduced PVR, but its clinical importance was questioned. Efficacy for UAB is not established.

document_sections.heading: 5.7.4.4 Other drugs
document_sections.content: A study reported improved QoL, urodynamic measures, and voiding measures with PDE5Is such as tadalafil in men with UAB. Evidence statements assign LE 4 to insufficient evidence for parasympathomimetics, limited evidence for alpha-adrenergic blockers, and unestablished prostaglandin efficacy; potentially serious parasympathomimetic adverse effects warrant consideration. Do not routinely recommend parasympathomimetics for male UAB (Strong). Offer alpha-adrenergic blockers before more-invasive methods (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.7.5.1 Surgery for benign prostatic obstruction
document_sections.content: A review of surgery for BPO with pre-operative DU or acontractile detrusor reported mean IPSS changes from -3 to -19.5 points, IPSS QoL changes from -0.9 to -3 points, Qmax gains from +1.4 to +11.7 mL/s, and PVR changes from -16.5 to -736 mL; fourteen studies found >3 points IPSS improvement. Comparisons with patients without DU conflicted. One PVP study found worse one-month outcomes with DU and reported mean DU-group IPSS from 12.0 to 15.2, Qmax from 4.8 mL/sec to 8.2 mL/sec, and PVR from 918.3 mL to 325.9 mL; corresponding non-DU values were IPSS 17.5 to 9.7, Qmax 6.9 mL/sec to 17.6 mL/sec, and PVR 225.0 mL to 99.2 mL, with between-group p ≤ 0.05 for mean IPSS, Qmax, and PVR. Another PVP study reported smaller median IPSS change (-6.5 vs. -11) and Qmax increase (+3.5 mL/s vs. +8.2 mL/s) with DU. Its DU median IPSS changed from 17.5 to 9.5, Qmax from 9.7 ml/sec to 13.8 ml/sec, and PVR from 28 mL to 11.5 mL; non-DU values changed from 20.5 to 8, 10 ml/sec to 17.9 ml/sec, and 27.5 mL to 9 mL, respectively. Only follow-up Qmax differed significantly (p: 0.023). Other studies found no outcome difference. Reported mean BCI gains ranged from 4 to 44.6. After TURP or TUIP, a retrospective study found satisfactory QoL and voiding-efficiency improvement > 50% in 81.7% with DU or acontractility; among responders, mean BCI increased from 16.4 to 61.0 and 69.4% recovered detrusor function within 3 months. In a prospective series of HoLEP with DU or acontractility and BPO, 78% regained a sustained voluntary contraction at six months; 94.7% voided spontaneously with acceptable PVR and 5.3% needed post-operative CIC. Worse results have been associated with older age, absent obstruction, concurrent DO, weaker contractility, and TURP or photovaporisation rather than HoLEP. In a retrospective TURP study, severe DU meant BCI < 82, mild DU 82 ≤ BCI < 100, and no DU BCI ≥ 100, evaluated within obstruction categories 20 ≤ BOOI < 40 and BOOI ≥ 40. For BOOI ≥ 40, three-month success rates for IPSS, IPSS-Storage, IPSS-Voiding, QoL, and free Qmax were, respectively, 60.6%, 54.5%, 54.5%, 63.6%, and 66.6% with severe DU; 87.7%, 63.2%, 94.7%, 75.4%, and 75.4% with mild DU; and 94.1%, 82.8%, 95.6%, 90.6%, and 71.4% without DU. For 20 ≤ BOOI < 40, corresponding rates were 38.2%, 38.2%, 44.1%, 41.2%, and 38.2% with severe DU; 83.3%, 66.7%, 83.3%, 75.0%, and 41.7% with mild DU; and 90.9%, 90.9%, 90.9%, 90.9%, and 81.8% without DU. TURP in severe DU with 20 ≤ BOOI < 40 therefore warrants careful consideration after counselling. Limited long-term data suggest poor durability.

document_sections.heading: 5.7.5.2 Sacral neuromodulation
document_sections.content: Male evidence for SNM in DU or acontractility is scarce. A multicentre retrospective series excluded BOO, cognitive disability, and SNM contraindications and included 35 males with urodynamic DU lasting more than six months after unsuccessful earlier treatments. Of the males, 51.4% responded to testing and qualified for implantation; 72% of those implanted responded favourably. Among implanted men, voided volume changed from 75.0 mL to 300.0 mL, PVR from 350.0 mL to 90.0 mL, and mean Qmax from 7.0 to mL/sec to 16.0 mL/sec. Another retrospective study suggested better trial responses with residual contractility than acontractility. Evidence statements rate improved contractility, symptoms, flow, and PVR after de-obstruction in concomitant BPO/DU; predictors of poorer surgical outcomes; and statistically significant SNM improvements in refractory male DU without BPO as LE 3. Counsel people with DU or acontractility and concurrent benign prostatic enlargement about possible subjective and objective surgical benefits (Weak). Offer a test phase of sacral neuromodulation to men with DU but no BPO (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.7.6 Follow-up
document_sections.content: Long-term natural history of male UAB is inadequately documented. A small retrospective cohort found detrusor recovery in 43.9% at one year after medical or surgical treatment; bladder compliance < 80ml/cmH2O predicted better recovery. Follow-up intervals depend on patient characteristics, treatment, and urinary complications. Two retrospective studies suggested that contractility neither worsens with continuing BOO nor improves after TURP; the underactive detrusor appeared relatively stable.

document_sections.heading: 6.1 Watchful waiting (behavioural)
document_sections.content: Review patients choosing watchful waiting at six months and annually thereafter if symptoms do not worsen and no absolute surgical indication arises. Follow-up should include history, bladder diary, IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry, and PVR.

document_sections.heading: 6.2 Medical treatment
document_sections.content: After starting α1-blockers, muscarinic receptor antagonists, beta-3 agonists, PDE5Is, or specified combinations with α1-blockers, assess response after four to six weeks. Continue treatment if symptoms improve without troublesome adverse events; reassess at six months and annually if stable and without absolute surgical indications. Assess history, IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry, and PVR, adding a frequency volume chart or bladder diary for predominant storage symptoms or nocturnal polyuria. For 5-ARIs, review response and adverse effects at twelve weeks and six months using history, IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry, and PVR. Perform serial PSA testing when life expectancy exceeds ten years and PCa diagnosis would alter care; establish a new PSA baseline at six months and investigate a confirmed rise during treatment. With desmopressin, measure sodium on day three, day seven, at one month, and periodically, with frequency volume chart review. If sodium remains normal, later screening may occur every three months; monitor more frequently at ≥ 65 years or with hyponatraemia risk, and restart the monitoring sequence after dose escalation.

document_sections.heading: 6.3 Surgical treatment
document_sections.content: After prostate surgery, assess response and adverse effects four to six weeks after catheter removal. If symptoms are relieved and adverse events absent, further reassessment is unnecessary. The visit should evaluate IPSS/ICIQ-MLUTS, uroflowmetry, erectile and ejaculatory function, and PVR. Follow-up schedules for conservative, medical, and surgical care derive from empirical or theoretical considerations rather than evidence-based studies (LE 4). Follow all treated patients (Weak), tailoring intervals and assessments to the treatment received (Weak).

key_numeric_data.parameter: End of the reported follow-up range for symptom assessment
key_numeric_data.context: Open-label tolterodine trials reported significant reductions from baseline in daytime frequency, nocturia, UUI and IPSS.
A multicentre RCT comparing LSP, RASP and HoLEP found no significant differences in functional or peri-operative outcomes.
A retrospective feasibility study of outpatient PVP with the 180-W XPS laser reported low readmission and complication rates.
Two placebo-controlled trials of fexapotide triflutate (NX-1207) reported a significantly greater change in IPSS and a significantly lower AUR rate in the treatment arm.
Patients in the randomised iTIND-versus-sham study underwent follow-up assessment at this timepoint.
